PREFACE "The Old World" follows "Our Home | Europe must take a commanding place in any study of foreign nations and peoples. 

Asia, likewise, demands our careful attention. That we have serious and increasing political interest in the peoples of that continent cannot be ignored or denied. Our com- State and the New World," with which it is closely articulated. It covers the study of all the inhabited continents except North 

America and South America. It includes also, at the beginning, a brief study of the oceans and of the Polar Regions, and at the mercial transactions with China, Japan, and end a world-wide study of important prod- India give to parts of Asia an economic imucts, with an account of such mathematical | portance that even the breadth of the Pacific geography as all school students should have. 

The historical approach to the study of geography is given special emphasis in the case of Europe; for the story of the expansion of Europe includes most of the world, and is of great importance to the people of our own country.

The peoples of each continent are studied in their living environment. The treatment of the different regions and peoples has been expanded or restricted on the basis of their relative importance in our modern world. 

Europe is the continent that is, on the whole, closest to us physically, socially, commercially, and politically. News of importance from Europe figures prominently in our daily newspapers. Since the World War, Since the World War, the dependence of Europe upon our country, and the interest of our country in the countries of Europe, have become more and more evident. Europe is our original ancestral home. Its institutions, languages, laws, and customs have been transplanted across the Atlantic, where they are to be found today in more or less modified form. Our best foreign markets are in Europe, and from European countries we buy a large part of our imports. 

American tourists are to be found at all seasons of the year in every European country. 

For all of these reasons it is generally agreed that Europe and the leading countries of cannot minimize. Perhaps, too, no other continent affords the pupil such varied contrasts with his own, as does Asia. 

Africa and Australia, likewise, together with the important neighboring islands, are given accounts adequate to their importance. 

Thus all the lands of the Old World are covered. When a pupil has familiarized himself with the interesting materials of this volume, in addition to what he learned about the New World the year before, he has a world view and understanding into which he can fit his further study. He will know of the peoples of the world; of their geographical environments, their manner of living, their products, and the way in which the lives and work of distant peoples in all corners of the world affect his own. Moreover, he will know in what ways climate and physiography have helped to influence the lives of peoples in all parts of the world. 

Because of the decisive influence of relief and climate on the lives and fortunes of mankind, the text has been provided with a map equipment unequaled in any other textbook of its kind. That the pupils may always have before them the chief physical features of any region that is being studied, there is provided a physical map as well as a political map of each continent, and the colored maps of smaller regions are of the physical-political

vi 

PREFACE 

type. They are conveniently placed for reference throughout the text. In addition, an unusually large number of black and white maps have been included, each of which has been so made as to present clearly a chosen fact or group of facts. There are maps of each continent showing the various parts that have individual character, either physiographic or climatic. Besides an average annual rainfall map of the world, there are given two semiannual rainfall maps of each continent instead of the one annual rainfall map included in most textbooks. Among the other maps are those showing the distribution of population, important crops, mineral products, and other matters of importance in the several continents. All of these maps have been kept as simple as they must be to be used intelligently by young students. 

Great care has been taken in the choice of the illustrations, both as to size and as to placement, so that they can be easily studied. 

Each one was chosen because it helps to interpret the text not merely because it is a beautiful picture. However, taken as a whole, they constitute an unusually attractive as well as a valuable body of illustrative material. 

The teaching material is one of the special features of the book. This material is of far greater value than the formal map and review questions of an earlier day, and the lifeless summaries that frequently tempt children to take a short cut in their study. The interesting exercises here provided furnish abundant review material and emphasize the more important geographic relationships and principles. They have considerable variety in form, and thus avoid the monotony often found in checks and review exercises. Above all, they lead the learner to arrive at many conclusions for himself.

THE OLD WORLD 

In your study of the New World, you have learned much about the lands and the peoples of North America and South America.

Those two continents with their near-by islands include nearly all the land of the 

Western Hemisphere. 

In the Eastern Hemisphere you find the continents of Europe, Africa, and Australia, and almost all of Asia. Europe and Asia form a single large mass of land to which the name of Eurasia is frequently given. The continent of Africa is also joined to Asia by the Isthmus of Suez, across which a canal has been cut to connect the Mediterranean 

Sea with the Red Sea.

All three of these continents border on the 

Mediterranean Sea. Europe is on the north,

Africa on the south, and Asia touches it at its eastern end.

Long before the discovery of the New World, one great people after another arose in the lands that border the Mediterranean. 

In the valley of the Nile, in northeast Africa, the ancient Egyptians built large temples and palaces several thousand years ago. On the edge of the desert, too, they built huge pyramids, covering the burial 1 chambers of some of their kings. In southwestern Asia, about as long ago, some great cities were built by other nations. In southern Europe, a little later, the Greeks and the Romans erected temples of rare beauty.

Open-air theaters were built also, where plays were presented and orators spoke to the people, and where games and other exhibitions were held (A). Most of these buildings are today in ruins, yet people travel halfway around the earth to see and admire them. 

One by one these ancient peoples were conquered by less civilized invaders, who in turn built up new civilizations. The three continents of Europe, Asia, and Africa, of which this Mediterranean region forms a part, are truly the Old World. 

Most of your study in this book will be about the lands and the peoples of Europe, Africa, Asia, Australia, and the many islands near them. But before beginning that study it will be well to give some attention to the oceans that surround those continents, the world winds that blow across sea and land, and the interesting parts of the earth near the poles where no people live and which very few persons have ever seen.

A. - The Western Hemisphere and the Eastern Hemisphere. Which four oceans are partly in both hemispheres?

WESTERN HEMISPHERE SOUTH POLE OCEANS, WINDS, AND POLAR REGIONS THE OCEAN 

How large a part of the earth's surface is covered by water? Study a globe or the maps on this page and on page 84. You will see that the water surface looks about three times as extensive as the land surface. In fact the total area of the oceans of salt water is nearly three fourths of the total area of the earth.

The five great oceans, in order of size, are the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Arctic, and

Antarctic. The Pacific was so named by 

Magellan, the first explorer to sail into it from the east, because it was peaceful as compared with the stormy waters in the Strait of Magellan. The name Atlantic comes from the ancient Greek word Atlas, given to mountains in northwest Africa, and from

Atlantis, the name of a very large island which the Greeks thought once existed in the ocean to the west of Africa and Europe.

The Indian Ocean, of course, is the one near 

India and the Indies. The name Arctic 

comes from the Greek word for "bear" and for a group of stars called the Bear, seen always in the north. Thus the word came to mean "northern." The word Antarctic means opposite the Arctic"; that is, "southern." The Arctic Ocean is north of the Arctic Circle, and the Antarctic is south of the Antarctic Circle. 

the oceans together are sometimes called the sea, or the seas.

There are many bodies of salt water, large or small, called gulfs, bays, and seas, which are connected with the oceans but more or less landlocked. Some are almost surrounded by land on all sides, as, for example, the Gulf of Mexico, Hudson Bay, and the 

Mediterranean Sea. Others open very widely into the ocean, as the Arabian Sea, the Bay of Bengal, and the Gulf of Guinea (see map facing page 1).

Depth of the Oceans. For a long distance out from the shore of the continents, in most places, the sea water is less than 100 fathoms, or 600 feet, deep. Turn to the maps on pages 2

3 be. They find muds of different colors and various kinds of other deposits. The smallest particles of mud may be carried far out from the shore before they are deposited on the sea bottom. Stones and soil in icebergs may also be carried far out to sea before the ice melts and drops them. As millions of small-shelled animals, fish of all kinds, and larger sea animals die in the sea, their bodies break up and add to the ooze on the ocean floor. 

74, 244, 278, and 358, and notice the varying | bottom at the place where they happen to depths of the oceans. Areas where the depth is less than 100 fathoms are shown in the lightest blue tint, nearly white. The sea bottom of such areas near a continent is called a continental shelf. If some movement within the earth should raise the continent and shelf about 600 feet, the shelf would become a coastal plain. Beyond the outer edge of the continental shelf the sea bottom slopes down rather quickly to a depth of several thousand feet. The average depth of the Pacific Ocean is about 13,000 feet, and of the Atlantic about 11,000. The greatest known depth of the Atlantic Ocean is nearly 28,000 feet, or over five miles, not far north of Puerto Rico; while that of the 

Pacific is almost seven miles, near Mindanao Island, one of the Philippines. The greatest depth of the oceans is about one and a half times the altitude of the highest mountain. 

This makes a total difference in elevation of nearly fourteen miles between the lowest point on the sea bottom and the highest point on the land surface. 

Ocean Floors. Since each ocean is many hundreds of miles wide and the deepest waters are only a very few miles in depth, each of the ocean basins, taken as a whole, is very shallow. The sea bottom, too, is nearly flat in most parts. There are not so many irregular places as on land. The ocean floor is not being worn by the work of rivers and glaciers as is the land. It has, however, some steep slopes at the outer edge of the continental shelf, some deep canyons, many broad plateaus, and many volcanic cones. 

Some of the volcanic cones extend above the surface of the sea as islands.

The sea bottom, especially for a few miles off shore, receives deposits of sand, gravel, and mud from the streams which flow into the ocean. Seamen, knowing what muds have been found at various places on the ocean floor, sometimes try to find out their location by taking samples of the deposits of the sea 

Explorations. Much of our knowledge of the sea bottom has been gained in surveys for finding out about fisheries, for the laying of submarine cables, and for making maps used by seamen. The United States Coast and Geodetic Survey publishes hundreds of maps of our ocean shore lines and coastal waters for the benefit of navigators, the results of surveys continually being made along our shores. Beginning with the roundthe-world voyage of the "Challenger" in 1872-1876, many expeditions have been made also for the special study of the ocean. 

Ocean currents and temperature are studied because of their influence on climate and weather, and the plant and animal life of the deep seas has been carefully observed. 

Sea Water. The tropical seas are warm near the surface. At greater depths the water is cold, because cold water is heavier than warm water, and very cold waters from the polar regions flow along the sea bottom as they move toward the tropics. 

Thermometers lowered to great depths in the ocean show that the temperature near the bottom is only a few degrees above freezing. In general, as one goes toward either pole from the tropics the surface water of the oceans grows colder and colder. 

In the Arctic Ocean float vast fields of ice, from six to twenty feet thick. In warmer weather huge masses of this ice sometimes break off and float far southward in the 

Atlantic Ocean.

Similar great ice fields and icebergs are found in the Antarctic Ocean and the extreme southern parts of the other oceans. 

The ocean water contains much salt, and smaller quantities of other substances, in solution. Some salt is constantly being carried into the sea by streams. It comes from rocks slowly dissolved by rain water and by underground waters that afterward come to the surface in springs. In some parts of the world people secure salt by filling tanks or pools with sea water and letting it evaporate. Near the shores where streams 

Near the coasts of some of the West Indies, of Bermuda, and of the Santa Barbara 

Islands of southern California, glass-bottom boats are used for studying sea animals and plants. Marine plants grow best in shallow waters where they can have sunlight. Even in deeper waters where plants grow without touching the sea bottom they must have some sunlight. 

At great depths in the ocean there is no sunlight, and the pressure of the water is enormously great. Certain sea animals, however, are able to live there in spite of this

WAVES 

A. அங்குமா A bathysphere, a hollow metal ball in which a scientist can be safely lowered to great depths for the study of ocean life. tremendous pressure, and could not live anywhere else. When caught and brought up near the surface, they die. Some of the deep-sea animals are blind, but with highly developed organs of touch; others have eyes and furnish their own light somewhat as fireflies do on land. Because of the absence of sunlight, plant life is not possible at depths of more than 2000 feet. In the cold and still world below that level only some queer forms of animal life move about in silence and darkness. 

Waves. On the surface of the sea there is much wave motion. When you stand beside the ocean or a large lake on a windy day, you are interested to watch the waves that beat on the shore. You can see each wave coming in rapidly from a long distance out; but do you know that, away from the shore, each drop of water in the waves is moving, as a rule, only a short distance? 

It is moving only a little forward and up, and then back down, over and over again. 

Only the wave forms move steadily on and on in the same direction. Drop a small stick of heavy wood into a lake or pond when the surface is rippled by a strong breeze. The waves move along rapidly in the direction of the wind, but the stick teeters up and down and is blown along very slowly. Perhaps you have seen a field of full-grown grain across which a gusty wind was blowing. You remember how waves move across such a field, but you know that the individual stalks merely swing back and forth.

The top of a wave is the crest, and the depression between two waves is the trough. 

The height of a wave is measured by the vertical distance between the crest and the bottom of the trough; and its length is the distance between the two troughs separating it from other waves this distance being usually the same as that between two crests. 

On the ocean great waves are often twenty or thirty feet high, and sometimes in terrific storms they may be as high as fifty feet.

On the ocean, storms cause a ship to pitch as it rides across the waves, and to roll when sailing in a direction parallel with the waves. If it sails in a slanting direction, it will have both motions. Many passengers are made seasick by the pitch or roll of a ship, but the roll is more dangerous than the pitch. A ship may have to change its course during a bad storm so as to avoid rolling too much. Long waves, even if they are very high, are not so dangerous to ships as are short high waves, which sometimes pound a poorly built ship to pieces. People have been swept overboard from the decks of ships by the huge waves of a violent storm.

Some Things to Explain. -After reading pages 

1 to 5 of this book carefully, tell as clearly as you can: 

1. The meanings of the names given to each of the five oceans. 

2. What you understand a continental shelf to be. 

3. Which part of Europe (page 74) has the broadest continental shelf, and which part has a narrow shelf. 

4. What the floor of the oceans would look like if the waters that now fill the ocean basins could be drained away. 

5. Why we wish to know about the ocean floor and how we get this information. 

6. Why, in the different parts of the oceans, the water does not have the same temperature. 

7. Why some waters become brackish. 

8. In what ways drifting icebergs may be dangerous to ships. 

9. About at least three forms of marine life that are useful to man. 

10. How the blind fish living at great depths are able to move about without striking other things. 

11. How some fish with eyes are able to see in the darkness of the deepest ocean waters. 

12. Why no plant life is found at depths of more than 2000 feet.

Things to Do Outside of Class. 

life. 

Surf. When a large wave moves into shallow water, its length is lessened and its height is increased. As the wave drags on the bottom, it pitches forward and causes surf.

Such waves, which break at the crest and plunge forward, are also called breakers or rollers (A). Surf bathing is a popular amusement; and at some seaside resorts experienced bathers may stand on a plank to ride in toward the shore on great breakers. Surf bathing, however, may be very dangerous on a slanting beach where the water brought in by the waves moves back again down the slanting sea bed, underneath the incoming waves. The current formed by this water moving seaward along the ocean bed is called an undertow. Many a strong bather has been carried out to sea by the force of the undertow. 

Work of the Waves. The waves help to make smooth, sandy beaches. Stones and pebbles are ground into grains of sand by the long-continued action of the surf on the shore. 

During heavy storms the high waves may build up ridges on the land some distance inside the shore line. On coasts where violent storms and high waves may be ex- 1. Find pictures of different kinds of marine pected, it is dangerous to build summer

WAVES, CURRENTS, AND TIDES 

7 

Philip D. Gendreau 

A. High cliffs at Lands End, southwestern England. 

Where the sea is very shallow at some distance off shore, the waves may build up barrier beaches. Such beaches are formed of sand and pebbles heaped up by the waves.

The narrow band of open water left between a barrier beach and the actual shore is called a lagoon. Along the shores of North Carolina and Florida, for example, there are barrier beaches of sand and gravel extending for many miles.

Steep and rocky coasts also feel the pounding of great sea waves. As the rocks are worn away high cliffs may be formed (A).

Often, too, where softer layers of rock are worn away more rapidly than the harder layers, large caverns may be formed in the cliffs. There are such caverns or grottoes, for example, along the coast of California, in Norway, in Italy on the island of Capri, and in many other coastal lands. The sea is always at work changing shore lines. At 

Cape Cod Light, on Cape Cod, Massachusetts, the cliff is being worn back at the rate of about eighteen inches a year.

On the open sea where ships have plenty of room for navigation, the sailors on wellbuilt ships do not fear the large waves. The greatest danger comes when a ship is near shore and may be driven aground or dashed against the rocks by the violent waves. 

Ships grounded on a sand bar are sometimes pounded to pieces by the surf. 

Great storms may do much damage in cities on the seashore. Galveston, Texas, was partly destroyed in 1900 by storm waves which rushed in from the Gulf of Mexico.

In 1876 severe storm waves struck the coast of India, and at Calcutta 100,000 people were drowned.

Ocean Currents and Tides. - Besides the ordinary waves caused by winds, and the larger waves sometimes caused by earthquakes, there are two other kinds of movements in the surface of the sea. 

The prevailing world winds, which we shall soon study (page 11), cause ocean currents. These are slow, steady movements in large areas of the surface waters (78 A).

OCEANS 

The tides, or immense tidal waves which move over most of the sea surface at intervals of about 12 hours, are caused chiefly by the pull or attraction of the moon. When the sun is nearly in line with the earth and the moon, its attraction helps to cause higher tides than at other times. As the earth rotates on its axis, the tidal waves move across the great oceans, following, in a general way, the course of the moon. If the surface of the earth were all water, two immense waves on opposite sides of the earth, each only a few feet high but thousands of miles long, would go steadily around the earth from east to west. But where this movement is interrupted by lands, the tidal wave rises on the shores and is stopped. 

When, during each day, the tide rises to its greatest height at any place along the shore, we call it high tide for that place. When the water is moving out to sea again, we call this the ebbing of the tide, and when the water is at its lowest point at any place, we call it low tide (A). In some narrowing bays the tides rise and fall as much as fifty feet, but along most coasts the height is much less, usually not more than a few feet; at some seaports it is less than one foot. 

The tides both help and hinder navigation. 

Large ocean liners can sail from or enter some harbors only when it is high tide. For example, the very large steamers must wait in the Lower Bay at New York for high tide before they can safely follow the channel by which they reach their docks. Ships which run aground at low tide may have to wait until the incoming tide lifts them enough so they are afloat once more and can move forward again in safety. In 1688 when King 

James II of England deserted the throne and took flight, he was captured because his ship could not leave the lower Thames River during low tide. The Thames and many other rivers where great ports are located could not be used by the largest ships that now enter them if it were not for the tides.

Tidal movements also help to keep some harbors clean. They carry out to sea the sewage and other kinds of waste which would cause bad odors and might cause disease if they accumulated in the harbor. Stockholm in Sweden and Venice in Italy, with their many sea-level canals, are good examples of cities which are helped in this way by the ebbing of the tides. A.

Oceanic Islands. - There are countless | The dead corals made up the hard foundaislands in the ocean, some of which are large and many of which are small. New islands appear from time to time, and old ones sometimes sink into the sea. Some islands are much like the neighboring continents in their rocks and soil, and others, far out in the oceans, are made mostly of corals or of sand, or are built up by volcanic eruptions. 

The Hawaiian and Aleutian Islands in the north Pacific are examples of volcanic islands (A). Beginning at the ocean floor, volcanic eruptions, ages ago, piled lava and ash higher and higher until the material was pushed above sea level and became islands. 

Some islands, either near shore or out at sea, where the ocean waters were warm and shallow, have been built by sea animals called corals. Corals have hard skeletons and look like flowers. The islands they form are low and flat. At first they were coral reefs, below the surface of the water. 

Some of the oceanic islands are inhabited by strange and curious people. Their ancestors moved there from the neighboring continents or other large islands. Among the islanders of the Pacific are natives whose ancestors migrated from Asia and the East 

Indies in small boats, using the islands as stepping stones. They migrated farther and farther out into the Pacific in search of new and uninhabited islands, somewhat as the pioneers in our country moved in covered wagons from territory to territory in search of new lands which were less crowded. 

Some islands are especially important because they have good harbors (A) and can be used as fueling stations for ocean steamers, and as landing places for airplanes.

OCEANS 

A. The "Mayflower," which brought the earliest group of settlers to New England in 1620. 

Value of the Oceans. For thousands of years the oceans have furnished much food for man.

Most of the sea fisheries are in shallow waters, for it is there that the fish can find food.

The great oceans of the world are much used as highways for trade and travel. 

Most ships today follow well-known routes in the transportation of pas sengers and freight. The story of the growth of shipping, from the small vessels of early days, which were moved by oars or sails (A), to the immense ocean liners of today, is a very important part of the world's history.

Many sailing vessels are still in use on the ocean. Some of them are pleasure boats, and some carry cargo (B). Most of the ocean transportation of freight and passengers today, however, is in ships made of steel and driven by steam power. Coal and oil are the chief fuels used. Some of the great ocean liners are from 600 to over 900 feet in length, and can be driven through the water at a speed of twenty or thirty miles an hour. Most of the world's steamships, however, are much smaller and slower. Some ships are called "tramps" because they have no regular routes that they follow. They are sent to any port for which they can find a cargo, and from that port to any other where the next paying cargo can be found. 

The captains of all ships have instruments to help them find their position from time to time. By using these they are able to keep their ship on the course they wish to follow. 

In recent times the radio has been of very great value to ships at sea. It is used to send messages from ship to ship or to shore stations. Such wireless messages have been used many times in recent years to bring help to ships in distress. Many lighthouses and broadcasting stations on the coast are kept up by different countries to help make navigation safe. By listening to two or more stations, and noticing the direction of each, a ship can find its position at sea. 

Wide World 

B. A large modern sailing vessel. It is at least three times as long, and twenty times as large, as the "Mayflower."

WORLD WINDS 

11 The oceans are also of very great value to us because of their influence on climate. 

As you know, the waters of the oceans are usually warmer than the land in winter, and cooler than the land in summer. This difference causes a similar difference between the air over the land and that over the water. 

Winds from the ocean or from large lakes make the climate of regions near their shores more even than it would be without them. 

The oceans also furnish most of our water supply. Water from the surface of the ocean is taken up by evaporation into the air, is carried inland in the winds, and falls as rain. 

If there were no oceans on the earth, there would be very few living plants or animals such as we now have. Most of the earth would be without rain — a true desert land.

Some parts would be hot and some cold, but all parts would be too dry for living things. 

WORLD WINDS 

In many places on the earth, as you know, the winds blow sometimes from one direction and sometimes from another. In other from another. In other places, during some seasons of the year, they usually blow from about the same direction.

POLAR REGIONS 

Recent explorations of the polar regions are especially interesting, for several reasons.

They have been going on during our own lifetime. They are made largely by the use of airplanes, our newest means of transportation. Radio keeps us in touch with the expeditions and brings us day by day the news of thrilling adventures. When the explorers return home, we can see the moving pictures that they have taken and in this way share in their adventures. 

North and South Polar Regions. We are very apt to think of the Arctic and the Antarctic regions as intensely cold, with ice, snow, heavy clouds, and dense fogs. This is a true picture of the polar winters, but there are many hours of sunshine during the long summer days. At the poles themselves there is continuous day in a summer that is six months long; but in a winter of six months there is continuous night. In the summer time in the polar regions the sun's path in the sky is around and around almost parallel with the horizon, but climbing a very little higher each day until midsummer, after which it gradually drops lower and lower again until the summer season is over. The farther one goes away from the pole, in either of the Frigid Zones, the more difference there is between the height of the sun at noon and its height twelve hours later; and the shorter is the length of continuous day in summer and of continuous night in winter. 

The two polar regions are not entirely alike. Study pages 12 and 16 and make a list of some of the ways in which they differ. 

1. In the central part of the North Frigid 

Zone is the Arctic Ocean, mostly covered with ice fields and nearly surrounded by three continents. But the central part of the South Frigid Zone, covering the greater part of its area, is Antarctica, the vast 5. A. The airplane in which Byrd and Bennett flew over the North Pole in 1926. On their return they landed on the ice offshore. The picture shows the plane being hauled to port in Spitsbergen, shortly after that landing. 

2. The North Polar region can be reached rather easily by airplane from the surrounding continents. But the South Polar region is reached only by long sea voyages. An airplane trip to Antarctica from the nearest continent would be much longer and therefore more dangerous than one to the North 

Polar region. 

3. The region about the North Pole is a deep ocean. But the region about the South 

Pole is a plateau averaging 10,000 feet high, with mountain ranges reaching heights of from 5000 to 15,000 feet. 

4. Some people live in the North Frigid

Zone, and there, too, you will find the polar bear, fox, reindeer, musk ox, walrus (13 A), and some other animals; and, in the summer time, many plants. But in the South Frigid 

Zone there are no native peoples, and no native land animals or plants of importance. 

In both zones, however, there are fish and seals, and many birds in summer. In the South 

Frigid Zone there are millions of penguins, and there are many whales along the coast. 

North Polar Region. The Arctic Ocean, though nearly surrounded by Asia, Europe, 

and North America, may be reached by ocean voyages through several passageways: by Bering Strait between Alaska and Asia; by Davis Strait between Greenland and

Baffin Island; and by the much wider entrance between Greenland and Europe. 

Much of the Arctic Ocean freezes over in winter. Sometimes the thick ice which does not melt during the summer grows thicker in the winter. Ridges fifty or sixty feet in height are formed where the wind and waves push one ice sheet partly on top of another. It is very difficult to cross these ridges of ice with dog sledges; and in winter travel is especially dangerous because of the darkness. In summer, during the long days, travel is still dangerous as well as difficult because of cracks in the ice. 

Exploration by Sledge. For more than two hundred years after Columbus discovered America explorers tried to find a northwest passage from Europe to Asia. John

Davis in 1586 entered Davis Strait seeking such a route. Later, in 1610, Henry Hudson discovered Hudson Bay while seeking a water passage to the East. Fridtjof Nansen, a

A. The "Norge " in which the Amundsen-Ellsworth-Nobile expedition flew over the North Pole in 1926. 

Norwegian, was one of the earliest explorers to try to travel to the North Pole. From

From 1893 to 1895 he made a voyage in his ship, the "Fram," sailing it far into the ice pack north of Asia. Then with one companion he traveled by sledge as far as latitude 

86° 14′ in the region north of Franz Josef

Land- now called Fridtjof Nansen Land. 

An Italian explorer, Captain Cagni, in an expedition led by the Duke of Abruzzi, made a sledge trip a few miles farther north in 

1900. Robert E. Peary explored the Arctic regions north of our continent in 1892, in 

1902, and in 1906 in the attempt to reach the North Pole. It was not until his fourth expedition that he finally reached the pole, on April 6, 1909. Like the other explorers named above, he made the journey by dog sledges over snow fields and ice sheets, and sometimes had to cross, or travel around, lanes of open water between the sheets of ice. 

Nansen, the Duke of Abruzzi, Peary, and other explorers helped to increase our knowledge about the North Polar region. in 1930, their bodies and parts of their equipment were found on White Island near the 

Spitsbergen group.

The first flight actually made to the pole was by Richard E. Byrd and Floyd Bennett in an airplane, May 9, 1926. These two 

Americans flew from Spitsbergen over the pole and back again in less than sixteen hours (14 A). In 1909 it had taken many months before the world knew of the success of Peary's journey. The news of Byrd's success was received everywhere by wireless within a few hours. Aviation and the radio have almost conquered space and time. 

Exploration by Air. The first attempt to reach the North Pole by air was made by the Swedish explorer A. S. Andrée. He and his two companions left by balloon in 1897 from one of the Spitsbergen Islands in the 

Arctic Ocean. But nothing was heard from them until thirty-three years later. Then, Three days later the dirigible airship 

Norge " (A) flew over the North Pole from

Spitsbergen to Alaska. Roald Amundsen 

(a Norwegian), Ellsworth (an American), and

Nobile (an Italian) were the leaders in charge of that flight. The "Norge " flashed a wireless message of its success while flying over the pole. The world waited anxiously until word came two days later that it had landed safely in Alaska. In April, 1928, another explorer by air, George H. Wilkins, flew over the

Arctic Ocean from Alaska to Spitsbergen by way of Greenland, and in the following May, Nobile flew again over the North Pole in a larger airship, the " Italia." This airship was wrecked in some way on the return trip, and eight of its crew of fifteen men lost their lives.

South Polar Region. The Antarctic con- | 

tinent, often called Antarctica, has an area of about 5,000,000 square miles. Compare its size with that of the United States or of 

Europe (see Table 1 on page 392). Notice the location of the Antarctic Circle. How much ocean area does it surround?

The Antarctic continent itself is surrounded by a vast rim of ice, through which it is very difficult to find a channel. Explorers looking for a passageway have sailed many hundred miles along a wall of ice (A) over one hundred feet in height before finding one. The con- tinent of Antarctica is a high plateau, above which some mountains rise to greater heights. 

The ranges of South Victoria Land are the most important. Mount Erebus, an active volcano, is over 13,000 feet high. 

Study the map of the South Polar region on page 16. You will see that South America is the continent nearest to Antarctica. 

Africa and Australia are farther away. Notice also the location of New Zealand. The best way to reach the South Pole is from 

New Zealand, because the Ross Sea, on that side of Antarctica, reaches so far inland. 

Notice also the location of the Bay of Whales. 

Exploration by Sledge. - Charles Wilkes, of the American Navy, discovered and explored a part of the Antarctic continent, about 1840. In 1894 L. Christensen, captain of a Norwegian whaling ship, landed on the continent near Cape Adare. Ernest 

Shackleton, an Englishman, in 1909 led a party over ice and snow and reached a point only 97 miles from the South Pole. The honor of first reaching the pole was won by Roald Amundsen, who arrived there by a sledge trip on December 14, 1911. A little over a month later, on January 18, 1912, an 

Englishman, Captain Robert Scott, reached the South Pole after braving all the dangers of a sledge trip by a much more dangerous route. But a terrible Antarctic blizzard, which lasted nine days, took the lives of 

Scott and his three companions. They died on their way back, when only ten miles away from their advance camp.

A. A small part of Little America, beyond the combination mess hall and bunk house. The small tents were used to hold supplies, and some were used as sleeping quarters. expedition sailed for Dunedin, New Zealand, by way of the Panama Canal. In December the expedition was in the Ross Sea at the 

Bay of Whales. A base camp with houses and huts was made near the shore of the bay and was called Little America (A). A wireless station was set up that made it possible for the little colony to send messages to, and receive messages from, New York City, 11,000 miles away. Four airplanes were made ready for flights.

From Little America several explorations were made on sledges pulled by the Labrador dogs that had been taken along. These trips and short airplane trips added much to what was known about the geography of this region. During the flights many photographs were taken of the land below over a range of 1200 miles.

Byrd's greatest problem in trying to reach the South Pole by airplane was to carry enough fuel. Before he started his final flight he set up a fueling station about 400 miles south of Little America. 

Late on November 28, 1929, the weather was cloudy at Little America. News came, however, by radio from one of the sledge parties far to the south that the weather was clear. Four men left the base camp in the airplane named the "Floyd Bennett." Byrd was in command, Balchen was pilot, June was radio operator, and McKinley was the photographer. They made the journey of 

1600 miles from Little America to the South 

Pole and return in nineteen hours. They saw high, and until then unknown, mountain ranges, enormous glaciers, and flew over parts of the continental plateau never seen before. On their way toward the pole they flew into a strong head wind. The temperature was 10° below zero. There were clouds over the mountains. The airplane had to fly higher so as not to hit the mountain peaks. As greater and greater heights were reached, something had to be thrown overboard to lighten the load and, not wanting to lose anything else, the explorers threw over some of their bags of food. Second Byrd Expedition. -On October 

12, 1933, Byrd left New York on the " Jacob 

Ruppert" with seventy men and supplies for his second South Polar expedition. At the

From this camp explorations were made by dog sledges and airplanes. 

The Lincoln Ellsworth Expedition. Lin coln Ellsworth flew across the Antarctic Continent in 1935. He saw mountains having an elevation of about 12,000 feet, and high plateaus. He claimed for the United

View of the Bosporus, the much-traveled strait on which Istanbul is located. This city is still an important center of trade between Asia and Europe.

The map facing page 1, and the maps on pages 83, 137, and 178, show that several

European countries today control larger or smaller areas in other continents. This is particularly true of Great Britain, the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (Russia), and 

France. It is true, also, of Italy, Belgium, Portugal, and Spain, but for much smaller areas; while the Netherlands have the very important island possessions called the Dutch 

East Indies. 

This extension of European influence into other parts of the world is commonly called the "expansion of Europe." In connection with its study in this book, we may consider that this expansion began when Columbus discovered the New World.

To understand this spread of European influence over the world it will be necessary to study some of the causes that led up to it. 

One of these is to be found in the partial closing of trade routes between Asia and Europe which had been in use for many hundreds of years. Another, and a much more important, cause was the competition, among the nations of Western Europe, for the trade of the "East."

The Trade of Constantinople.- Much of the trade between Asia and Europe had centered for a long time at Constantinople the city now called Istanbul (A). At that city overland routes from the East met those from central Europe and also the water routes from southern Europe by way of the 

Mediterranean Sea. There, also, manufacturing developed, and from its workshops many articles were sent out to distant points in Europe. Among the most valuable of the manufactures were beautiful textiles, fine leather work, carved ivories, mosaics, engraved and enameled metal work, armor, and delicate pottery and porcelain. In exchange for these there came to Constantinople grain, furs, wax, amber, raw wool, unworked metals, and salt fish.

In Constantinople, also, the merchants of

Constantinople was long the capital of a great empire- the Eastern Roman Empire, or By zantine Empire - but it suffered from many wars, especially those with the Mohammedans or Saracens of southwestern Asia. The most powerful of the Mohammedan peoples, the Turks, at last conquered most of the others, and they took Constantinople in 1453.

Their presence in Southwestern Asia and in Constantinople cut down the trade on all the routes shown on the map (A). 

Even before Constantinople was captured by the Turks, its trade had began to decrease. 

Two Italian cities Venice and Genoa gradually took over much of the trade that formerly passed through Constantinople. 

Venice and Genoa. The city of Venice was built on a number of low-lying islands near the head of the Adriatic Sea. In the course of time it became a rich and beautiful city. Its war galleys brought the pirates of the Mediterranean under control, and in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries the ships of its merchant princes reached all the ports of the eastern Mediterranean. 

By way of the Brenner and the St. Gotthard passes, Venice sent forward goods from the East and from the workshops of Constantinople to the cities and towns of Germany and the Netherlands. But the merchants of Venice much preferred sea routes, and in the early part of the fourteenth century they were sending their ships to the western Mediterranean. Later their ships

By such sea routes northern and western 

Europe received pepper, cloves, ginger, indigo, and many other products at less cost than by the overland routes formerly used. 

On their return voyages the Venetian ships brought back wool, hides, and metals. 

Genoa and Pisa were rivals of Venice and were engaged in the same kinds of trade, and there were many wars between these cities. 

But each of them secured some part of the 

European trade with the East.

HOW THE PEOPLE OF EUROPE LEARNED ABOUT ASIA 

During the time when the control of European trade was in the hands of the Italian cities, much was learned about Asia that had not been known before. This was brought about in two ways. One of these was the knowledge brought back by the crusaders who had been to the Holy Land. The other was the knowledge of central and eastern Asia that came from travelers who had visited those distant lands. 

The Crusades. The purpose of the crusades of 1096 to 1270 was to take from Mohammedan conquerors the holy places of the Christian faith. Jerusalem had been captured by the Arabs in the year 637, and it remained in their hands until 1099, when it was taken by the European Christians in the first crusade. Later it was again captured by the Mohammedans (1187), and though the crusades lasted nearly a hundred years longer, the Holy Land did not again come under Christian control during that time, nor till hundreds of years later.

HOW EUROPEANS LEARNED ABOUT ASIA 

23 What were the results of the invasion of the 

Mohammedan East by the Christian West during nearly two hundred years? Here was an early expansion of Europe, because European colonies were established, for a time, east of the Mediterranean Sea. The crusaders found in the Eastern world a civilization that in some ways was more advanced than their own. They saw great wealth, magnificent buildings, fine clothes, new foods, and scientific skill. They brought back some new ideas about art, architecture, standards of living, and medicine. It was natural that routes were opened up by land and sea to reach the treasures of the East. Venice and Genoa became the leaders in this Eastern trade. 

Travelers to Central and Eastern Asia.

During the period of the crusades, certain of the European peoples greatly increased their knowledge of large parts of southwestern Asia. During that same period they learned, also, much about the geography of central and eastern Asia, and about the people who inhabited those lands and their ways of living. This knowledge came from the stories told and the written reports of travelers who passed through those lands. 

Some of the travelers made their way into China and returned by the same overland routes they had followed on their outward journeys. Others followed the sea routes that connect the Persian Gulf with the coast of the China Sea.

Among the most famous of these travelers were the Venetian trader Marco Polo, William of Rubruck, and the Venetian mis sionary Friar Odoric. 

Marco Polo. A family in Venice by the name of Polo was prominent in the commerce of that country during the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. About 1260, two brothers, Niccolò Polo and Maffeo Polo, were in the city of Bokhara in southwestern Asia on business. In that city, which is about 

300 miles east of the Caspian Sea, they met

A. 

Crusaders on the march. some men from the court of the great Mongol ruler Kublai Khan. These men were about to return to their own country and invited the Polo brothers to go with them. When the Polos reached the court of the great Khan they were pleasantly received, and while they were there they learned much about the riches of Cathay (China), over which he ruled.

When they were ready to return to their own country, the Khan asked them to arrange to have some Christian missionaries sent to his court. It was his hope that these missionaries would teach his people Christianity and the arts of the Western world. 

Unfortunately, the Polos were unable to have such missionaries sent. 

The two brothers reached home safely, and after two years they again started for the court of the Khan. On this trip, which began in 1271, they took with them Marco, the son of Niccolò. They went first to the mouth of the Persian Gulf, having it in mind to go on to China by sea. But they gave up this idea and went by land instead.

In the story that Marco later told of this trip, we get our first description of some lands that were not again visited and described by 

Europeans for hundreds of years.

The Polos reached the city of the great Khan in 1275. There young Marco became a great favorite. He was made an agent of 

He was made an agent of the imperial council and traveled through many parts of China, to the borders of Tibet, and into northern Burma. He took notes of what he saw on these trips, so that he was able to tell the Khan about each of the regions that he had seen.

With the passing of the years the Polos grew rich and began to plan to return to Venice. The Khan, wishing to keep them with him, especially the young Marco, would not for a long time give his permission. In 

1292 they were allowed to join an expedition that was to take a young Mongol princess to 

Persia. The trip was made by sea and the journey took over two years. This was because long stops were made at the island of Sumatra and in southern India. From 

Persia the Polos went overland to Constantinople, and from there to Venice, which they reached in 1295. 

How Marco's Story Was Written. We owe the story of Marco Polo's travels and the record of what he saw and learned to another, for Marco himself would not write it. It happened that a short time after the 

Polos returned to Venice the cities of Venice and Genoa were again at war. 

Marco was made a gentleman commander on one of the Venetian ships. In a battle in which the ships of Genoa were victorious, Marco was captured. He was put in prison in Genoa.

There he remained for almost a year, and during that time he told his story to a fellow prisoner from Pisa, who wrote it down (B). 

Unfortunately, at the time Marco lived there were many who thought that the stories he told were not true. The result was that the people of Europe learned less about Asia than they might have learned if they had not been such doubters.

Tartars by the people of Europe, had left their eastern homes and swept westward as far as central Europe. They hoped to add all Europe to the lands governed by their

EUROPE IN THE FIFTEENTH CENTURY 

By the time the fifteenth century opened there were many people in Europe who knew something about the resources and people of Asia. This knowledge had been gained through trade, through what had been learned by the crusaders, and from the reports of travelers who crossed that continent or sailed along its shores.

A. 

- An important German seaport, as shown in a picture made in the sixteenth century. 

The population and wealth of Europe were increasing and its people were beginning to enjoy greater freedom. The old system, by which the majority of the people lived almost as slaves under the rule of the few, was disappearing. More and more of the people were living in towns or villages, where skillful workmen were spending their time making things for sale to others. Because of their 

Because of their skill these workers became known as craftsmen, and the industries they followed were spoken of as crafts. In order to secure careful workmanship many of the crafts were under the control of groups of workmen who had united to form guilds. These guilds made rules about the materials to be used, about the way in which the work was to be done, and about the prices to be charged. 

The Growth of Towns and Industries. 

During the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, many towns grew up in England, France, Italy, and Germany (A). In the 

Netherlands, or "Low Countries," too, — the lands now called Belgium and the Netherlands (or Holland) there were many towns. 

Some settlements in each of these countries

EUROPE IN THE FIFTEENTH CENTURY 

27 A.

The chief seaport in the Madeira Islands. Notice the steamer and the small boats. were so favorably located that they grew large enough to be called cities. 

In most of these towns and cities there were workmen who specialized in particular crafts, and the products of their workshops became famous. Some of these products began to appear in the world trade of that time. Along with this increase in European manufactures and a steady growth in the purchasing power of a rapidly growing population, there was a greater demand for the products of the Eastern world. This was particularly true as to silks, spices, incense, precious metals, and the precious and semiprecious stones. 

New Routes to the East Needed. These products of the East had always been expensive because of the cost of overland transportation and the tax, or tribute, that traders had been forced to pay in countries through which they passed. It became clear to the countries in western Europe that the cost of these articles from the East would be much less if they could be brought all the way by sea. Venice had already shown that the cost of goods sent to England, the Netherlands, and Germany could be reduced if they went by sea instead of overland across the Alps.

It was in the fifteenth century, also, as you know, that the Turks conquered much of southwestern Asia and captured Constantinople. Their capture of the lands bordering the eastern Mediterranean greatly increased the difficulty of carrying on trade with the East. The result was that the countries of western Europe became even more active in their search for a sea route to the Indies and Cathay. Venice and Genoa did not, of course, lose all of their trade at once, but it was greatly decreased. The last of the great fleets to go from Venice to England and the Netherlands left Venice in 1532.

This was forty years after Columbus made his first great voyage to the New World and thirty-four years after Vasco da Gama had first reached India by sailing around Africa. 

The West Coast of Africa Explored. 

For a long time before the voyages of Columbus and da Gama, the exploration of the west coast of Africa had been going on. The man who had been directing these explorations for Portugal was Prince Henry the

Navigator. He sent expeditions to the 

Canary Islands, then and for a long time well known. well known. Other expeditions discovered the Madeira Islands (A) and rediscovered the

Azores, which had been almost forgotten.

One expedition after another followed more or less closely the west coast of Africa toward the south. One of these finally reached the coast of Guinea, and brought back slaves and gold dust. In the period 1444-1446, at least thirty ships were engaged in trade and exploration along the west African coast. 

In 1456 the Cape Verde Islands were discovered. Settlements were made in the 

Azores, in the Madeira Islands, and in the Cape Verde Islands. In these settlements we have some early beginnings of the expansion of Europe, which was in the course of time to make great changes in the lives and habits of the world's population. 

A Sea Route around Africa Is Found. 

Prince Henry died in 1460, but the ships of

Portugal still sailed south along the coast of 

Africa. In 1488 Bartholomeu Dias discovered the Cape of Good Hope (29 A) - first named the Cape of Tempests. At this time he sailed far enough east to note that the coast line extended toward the northeast. 

This fact made him believe that he had rounded the southern end of Africa, as he had, and that the way to India was open. 

On a later voyage, with Cabral, he touched the coast of Brazil, but he died on this voyage, off the cape we now call Good Hope.

It has been said of Dias that "he was allowed to see the Promised Land, but not to enter it."

Although the explorations of the Portuguese first led to the discovery of the sea route to the Indies, it was Christopher

Columbus who made the first voyage to the 

New World. However, it was only by the explorations and discoveries of those who followed Columbus that the people of Europe gained a true idea of the size and position of the new Western lands.

EXPANSION WEST AND EAST Columbus Crosses the Western Seas. 

You all know the story of the first voyage of 

Columbus to the New World. You will remember that the lands he found were some of the many islands that swing in a great curve from southern Florida to the northern coast of South America. You know, also, about the natives that Columbus found on these islands. He called those natives Indians because he believed that he had that he had reached the Indies, the southeastern part of Asia. 

You may, perhaps, know less about the discoveries that Columbus made on his third and fourth voyages across the Atlantic. 

Those voyages, like the first and second, were made for Spain. On his third voyage he touched the northern coast of the mainland which he called land of South America a New World, but in which he was not greatly interested. On his fourth voyage he explored the north coast of Panama, which he thought was part of the Indies. He was trying to find a passage through it, so that he might sail on to India, which he still believed was only a little farther west.

In letters written by himself and by his son Ferdinand the natives of Panama were described. They were found to be wearing large ornaments made of gold, and this fact was of great interest to the Spaniards at that time. From first to last, over the hundreds of years that Spaniards explored and made settlements in the New World, they had two things chiefly in mind. One of these was to find gold, silver, jewels, and spices. The other was to convert the natives to the 

Christian religion.

Strait of Magellan

A.- European possessions in the New World and in Africa in 1750. 

The Non-European World Divided be tween Spain and Portugal. .-In 1493, after the first discovery made by Columbus became known, Pope Alexander VI, who also knew of the explorations and discoveries being made by the Portuguese, tried to arrange matters so that Spain and Portugal would not get into trouble with each other. 

He divided the world outside of Europe between them. He gave to Portugal the lands east of a certain line drawn from north to south in a position that he fixed, and he gave to Spain the lands to the west of that line. He no doubt supposed that this line would run for its full length through the ocean, although, as the map on this page shows, it did not do so. What was to happen to lands that could be reached both by 

Portugal sailing toward the east and Spain sailing toward the west was not made clear.

In 1494, however, the position of the line as drawn by the Pope was changed by a treaty between Spain and Portugal. In this treaty the line agreed upon was to be drawn from the North Pole to the South Pole, through a point 370 leagues west of Cape

Verde, Africa. Notice the location of this line in the map (A) on this page.

A.-Balboa claiming the "Great South Sea" for Spain, as shown on a bronze tablet in the building of the Pan- 

American Union in Washington, D. C.

This division of all the non-European world between Spain and Portugal did not last for long. As we shall see, several other countries made successful explorations and settlements in the New World.

The map on page 30 shows the territories controlled by different European countries in North America and South America about 1750. The claims of each of these countries extended farther, so that large areas were claimed by two or three different nations. 

It was shortly after this (1754) that the conflicting claims to the Ohio Valley brought on war between English and French colonists in the New World - a war that led to great territorial changes of which we shall read more later.

Study the map carefully. Notice that the 

Spanish possessions included most of South America, but Brazil was claimed and settled by Portugal, because part of it was found to be east of the treaty line shown on this map. 

Spain claimed also all of North America, but made settlements only in Florida, Central America, and Mexico, and in parts of what is now southwestern United States.

Some of the Spanish Explorers. Spanish claims in these regions were made good by exploration and actual settlement. In the country that is now ours, Spanish explorations were led by Ponce de León, Hernando de 

Soto, Francisco Vásquez de Coronado, and others. It was Balboa, a Spaniard, who first crossed the Isthmus of Panama and discovered the Great South Sea, later called the 

Pacific Ocean (A). It was Magellan, a Portuguese who was sailing under the Spanish flag, who found a way from the Atlantic to the Pacific through the strait that bears his name. 

You will remember that one of

Magellan's ships, after crossing the Pacific, finally crossed also the Indian Ocean, rounded the southern end of Africa, and returned to 

Spain (2 A) (2A) -the first ship that ever sailed completely around the earth.

All of the explorers so far mentioned, and all who went with them, sought wealth for themselves and their king, but found little.

A few years later, however, Cortes seized. much gold and silver in Mexico, and Pizarro took much more in Peru. It was through them and many other leaders that Spain

A. - Fortifications at Gôa, which is still a Portuguese possession. made good her claim to lands shown as Spanish on the map (30 A). Many thousands of Spaniards settled in those lands, and in nearly all of them Spanish is the language most spoken today.

When Magellan's ships crossed the Pacific 

Ocean they stopped at the Philippine Islands, which Magellan claimed for Spain. Magellan was slain in a war with the natives of one of the islands, but later expeditions, crossing the Pacific, gained control of the Philippines and made them a Spanish possession.

Where Portugal Established Its Rule. - 

Portugal found Brazil, the part of South

America to which it laid claim, an almost empty land. But settlements were made and it became a real colony. In the East, however, in India and in the Spice Islands, Portugal never established itself as a conquering nation, as Spain did in Mexico and in Peru. Some commercial settlements were made, but in only one of them, Gôa (A), on the west coast of India, was there much intermarriage with the native population. 

Portugal did, however, try to gain complete control of the European trade with India and the Spice Islands. With this idea in mind the Portuguese seamen did their best to sweep the ships of the Arab traders from the 

Indian Ocean. They were so successful in doing this that the supplies of eastern goods that had formerly been reaching the Italian cities were at first greatly reduced and at last almost stopped. But the caravan traffic with the East was never completely destroyed. 

Portugal Loses Its Empire and Trade. 

The merchant traders of Portugal by their very cruelty raised up enemies against themselves. Also, as they grew rich, they became less eager and less careful in their business. 

Spain, having also grown rich and powerful, finally conquered Portugal and its empire in 1580, and it was not until the middle of the seventeenth century that Portugal once again gained its freedom. By that time the trade with the East had fallen into other hands, and today but little remains to Portugal of its one-time possessions. Brazil became independent in 1815.

The Spanish Empire Crumbles. The 

Spanish Empire, built up through the centuries by the swords of the conquerors and by the earnest efforts of its missionaries, also went to pieces. This was largely because the mother country allowed no liberty of thought or action to its people in the distant

Magellan's last battle. In the Philippine Islands Magellan made friends with the people of Cebu and helped them in a war with a neighboring island. In an attack there Magellan and his men were defeated, and Magellan was killed.

Neither was any encouragement given to industries that would lead to the development of the resources and the growth of the colonies. What Spain wanted from these New World lands was gold and silver and precious stones. Some of the native 

Indians put to work in the mines died off, and their places were taken by Negro slaves from Africa. But there are still many millions of Indians in the Spanish-American countries, besides millions of the Spanish race. 

There were many intermarriages also, and from them there resulted the people of mixed blood, called mestizos.

With the passing years the power of Spain decreased and that of other European nations began to rise. Most of the Spanish colonies in the New World declared themselves independent sometime between 1815 and 

1830. The last of the Spanish possessions in the New World and in the Pacific were lost in the Spanish-American War (1898).

Beginnings of Expansion by English, 

French, and Dutch. Even while Portugal and Spain controlled the sea routes of the 

South Atlantic, the Pacific, and the Indian oceans, other peoples had begun a search for routes to the East.

The three countries that were most active were England, France, and the Netherlands. 

Each of them sent out expeditions to search for either a northeast passage along the north coasts of Europe and Asia or a northwest passage through or to the north of North 

America. Although such passages were not found, important discoveries were made that were to have great consequences at a later time. Among these discoveries were the 

1. An English expedition found the White 

Sea and reached the port of Archangel.

This resulted in the opening of trade between the English and the Russians. 

2. Explorations along the eastern coasts of North America were made by the Cabots, for England. These were followed, later, by the establishment of successful English settlements along that coast. 

3. The Gulf of St. Lawrence and the great river of the same name were discovered by 

Cartier, a Frenchman. French settlements followed, and it was by this route into the interior of our continent that the French made their way to the Great Lakes and the Mississippi River territory. 

4. Important discoveries were made by an Englishman, Henry Hudson, while in command of an expedition sent out by the 

Dutch. He entered Delaware Bay and New 

York Bay, and explored the Hudson River as far as the place where Albany now stands. 

It was because of these discoveries that the Dutch claimed lands along the Delaware, the 

Hudson, and the Mohawk rivers.

England Wins the Freedom of the Seas. 

When Henry VIII was king of England, and later when Elizabeth was queen, much was done to build up a merchant fleet and to promote England's sea trade. In Queen 

Elizabeth's time, especially, English ships were to be seen in many ports seeking for cargoes. At the same time English privateers under the command of fearless captains were engaged in smuggling, in the slave trade, and in attacks on Spanish treasure ships. 

Francis Drake, the most daring and successful of all the English sea raiders, entered A. 

Drake accepting the surrender of a Spanish ship.

The Spanish Armada, attacked by English ships. the Pacific through the Strait of Magellan.

He followed the route of Magellan's expedition, and in doing so paid no attention to the fact that this route had been reserved to Spain. Along the western coast of South America he looted Spanish settlements, and he captured Spanish ships that were loaded with the treasures taken from the Indians.

Drake finally returned to England by crossing the Pacific and Indian oceans, rounding the Cape of Good Hope, and sailing northward through the Atlantic. Shortly after his return the queen made him a knight, and so he is known in history as Sir Francis Drake.

A few years after Drake's return from his voyage around the world, Spain attempted to destroy the growing sea power of England. 

In 1588 a Spanish fleet, so large that it has always been known as the Spanish Armada (A), was sent to the English Channel, where it was attacked by a much smaller English fleet that had gathered there. Drake was in command of one large squadron of this fleet, and after a seven-day battle the English ships destroyed part of the Armada and put the rest to flight. The Spanish ships, in escaping, had to sail northward and around the British Isles, and many were wrecked on the Irish coast on their way home. Spain's sea power was so badly broken that it was never fully rebuilt. From then on, the world's seas have generally been free to the ships of all nations except in times of war.

The French and the Dutch. - The English were not the only European people who were unwilling to allow Spain and Portugal to control trade routes and to keep for themselves the treasures of conquered peoples and the profits of the new world trade. The French and the Dutch made attacks upon Spanish treasure ships and each tried to gain the eastern trade that Portugal had controlled so long. 

All three nations looked both west and east from their home lands in Europe in their search for trade routes.

States purchased Alaska in 1867. 

The Growth of Dutch Power in the East. As you know, the English, French, and Dutch, in their expansion overseas, looked both to the West and to the East. In each of the three countries there were private companies formed to develop trade, and in some cases to encourage settlement also in the new lands of the West and in the old lands of the East.

Russia's Eastern Expansion. You will remember that at one time Mongolian hordes, under the command of their rulers, or Khans, invaded eastern Europe. When at last they withdrew into Asia again they left behind them, especially in Russia, many in whose veins there flowed a larger or a smaller proportion of Mongol blood.

During all the time that Spain and Portugal were creating their great empires overseas, the Russians were spreading eastward through Siberia. They moved so slowly and they were themselves so much like the natives of Siberia that their occupancy of the land was a matter of peaceful penetration, not of conquest by force of arms.

This eastward movement went on through the years until, at last, a very large part of 

New World, and you will read more about some of them a little later. You may not know so well what these three peoples did in the East.

The task that the Dutch set for themselves was to take away from the Portuguese the trade of the Spice Islands. This they were able to do with some help from the English. 

Much of the territory that they won at that time they still control today (A). In the Netherlands both the "Company of the 

West Indies" and the "Company of the 

East Indies" had help from the government. In England, however, the government was at that time less willing to take part in the affairs of the "East India Company" of that country. The result was that the English did not long try to compete with the Dutch in the East Indies. They turned their attention to India instead.

The English and French in India. - In In India the English had to compete with the French, but in this competition they were finally successful. During the struggle between the English and French in India the affairs of the English company were in the hands of a number of governors of great ability. Among these were Robert Clive, Warren Hastings, Lord Cornwallis, and Lord

Wellesley. In the period during which these men were in control in India, the Empire of the Great Mogul crumbled to pieces and the power of the native princes decreased. In later years it became necessary to bring more and more territory under British control. 

The mutiny of Indian soldiers (sepoys) serving in the British army, known in history as the the “ Indian Mutiny," finally led the British government to take over the control of all affairs in India. When this change was made the British East India Company came to an end. 

From the year 1743, when Robert Clive first entered the service of the East India 

Company as a boy of eighteen, to 1858, when Great Britain took full control of 

Indian affairs, was a period of only 115 years.

But during that time the British won a great empire in the East and the French lost one. 

Today the French possessions in India have an area of about 200 square miles, while the British possessions in that part of the world, India proper, total more than 1,800,000 square miles.

America in 1750. 

America in 1750. Let us turn again to 

North America. You have learned about the early settlements of the English, French, and Dutch in our continent. Turn to the map on page 30. It shows that the territory once claimed by the Dutch had passed under English control and that two nations held most of the continent from the Atlantic Ocean to beyond the Mississippi River. The early

English settlements, however, were for the most part east of the Appalachian Mountains.

West of the mountains the French claimed all the lands drained by the Mississippi, because they had explored tributaries of that river and had followed the main stream to the Gulf of Mexico.

The French claims in North America were made good by settlements along the St. 

Lawrence River and by the trading posts and mission stations that they had built in the interior. The French colony southwest of the Gulf of St. Lawrence was taken by the 

British in 1713. French trappers roamed through the lands around the Great Lakes, and in the Mississippi Valley.

France Loses Its American Possessions. 

In 1756 a war, known as the Seven Years'

War, broke out in Europe. Many European countries were engaged in it, but to us it was important chiefly because France and England were on opposite sides. The American part of that war was between the colonies of France and England, continuing a struggle that began in 1754; it was known as the 

French and Indian War because many Indians fought as allies of the French. 

In that war the French won some early successes, but later were badly defeated. The war ended with the Treaty of Paris in 1763. 

France turned over to Great Britain its territory north of the British colonies, and nearly all the land that it had claimed east of the Mississippi. New Orleans and the 

New Orleans and the

French were turned over to Spain. Later they were returned to France, but soon afterwards (1803) they were sold to the United

States. It was in this way that the hopes of 

France for expansion in the New World came to an end. 

Changes in Territory under British Con trol. One result of the French and Indian 

War was a great increase in the North 

American area under British control. It included most of the eastern half of the present United States and most of the present Canada. It must be remembered, however, that long before 1763 northern and much of western Canada had already been claimed by the Hudson's Bay Company. 

In 1776 the thirteen British colonies that stretched along the Atlantic coast declared themselves independent, fought for their freedom, and united to form one country. 

This was the beginning of the United States. 

By one treaty after another, between 1783 and 1846, the boundary between our country and 

Canada was agreed upon, from the Atlantic to the Pacific coast.

Present Possessions of European Nations. What is left to Spain, Portugal, France, Great Britain, the Netherlands, and Russia of the lands they once claimed in the New World? Three of these countries have nothing left. These are Spain, Portugal, and Russia. France has some small groups of islands and a small area in northeastern South America. The islands include St. Pierre and Miquelon, near the south coast of Newfoundland (page 42), and 

Guadeloupe and dependencies and Martinique in the Lesser Antilles (66 A). The combined area of all these islands is only 

1166 square miles. French Guiana in South 

America has an area of 34,700 square miles.

Within its borders is located a famous 

French convict settlement.

The New World possessions of the Nether lands include a small area in South America and two groups of islands. The South 

American area (54,300 square miles) is Surinam, or Dutch Guiana.

It was given to the Dutch in 1667, in exchange for the colony of New Netherland in North America, which the English had captured. The two island groups make up the Dutch colony known as Curaçao, named after the largest of the islands. The two groups are about 500 miles apart and their combined area is only 

403 square miles.

Out of all the European countries that explored and settled the New World, Great Britain alone has a land area of great size still loyal to the mother country. As you have already learned, however, France, the 

Netherlands, and Russia, as well as Great

Britain, expanded toward the east. There they still have possessions or territories, under their control, of great size and value. Great

Britain and France have each obtained large areas in Africa. In that same continent 

Belgium, Italy, Portugal, and Spain have each much smaller areas under their control. 

But none of these compare in size or importance with those of Great Britain and France. 

The continent of Australia and the neighboring islands of New Zealand are two of the 

British dominions. The scattered islands of the world's seas are either independent or are divided among many countries.

One European country that at one time had extensive colonies in Africa was organized as a nation too late to have any part in the exploration and settlement of the New 

World. This is Germany. Such colonies as it had in Africa, as well as its island possessions and its sphere of influence in China, were lost as a result of the World War. You will hear more about these one-time African possessions of Germany when you come to study the splitting up of Africa among world powers.
