THE BRITISH EMPIRE 

43 A. Parliament Building in London, the meeting place of the Parliament which governs Great Britain.

THE BRITISH EMPIRE 

Let us now turn our attention to the British Empire as it is today. It is the greatest empire of the modern world, and in many ways the greatest empire in the history of the world. Important parts of it, as you know, are in North America. In this study we shall need to think of the homeland of the British people and of all the areas where British rule, in any form, has been established. 

We shall want to know how and why many of the different parts of the empire were brought under British control or influence. 

First, however, we shall want to know something of the history of the homeland, Great 

Britain itself.

Great Britain. The central unit of the vast British Empire is the "Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland," usually called the United Kingdom, or simply Great

Britain. At the present time it is made up of England, Wales, Scotland, and Northern Ireland. Only a few years ago it included all of Ireland, but since that time the Irish Free 

State has been formed.

The parts of the British Isles that finally united to form the United Kingdom did not come together under a single government all at one time. It took a long, long time to bring the different parts of England alone under one ruler. It was many years after that before Wales, Scotland, and Ireland were added. 

England from Roman Times to William the Conqueror. You know that for many centuries the trade of Europe with Asia and 

Africa centered in the Mediterranean Sea.

As long as this was true the British Isles were on the fringe, or outer margin, of the world's trade. But in ancient times they were known and visited by the Phoenicians and later they were under the rule of Rome. Roman rule was established there in 43 A.D., and old

Roman roads and other remains show how far this rule extended. 

Even before the days of Roman rule in Britain there were groups in the British Isles that had crossed the that had crossed the "narrow seas" from the continent. After the Romans had left the British Isles, invasions of peoples from the continent still continued.

A. Conway Castle, one of the famous castles in Wales. 

The country that we know as England was conquered and settled largely by peoples called Saxons and Angles. Indeed, the name 

England is merely a shortened form of the name Angle-land. Anglo-Saxon England was at first divided among a number of rulers or kings. Each of these ruled over some part of the country and some of its people, and there was almost constant warfare among them. As early as the year 760 one of these kings had extended his rule over a large area and claimed to be "King of All England."

But the England over which he ruled was not the England of our present day. Shortly after he died his kingdom was again divided, and the king of another part of the country came to power.

While these wars were going on among the different rulers in England, invaders from the mainland of Europe continued to cross to Britain, where they made war upon its people. These invaders came from Denmark, from Norway, and at last a great army came from Normandy - now northwestern France. The leader of the Normans was William the Conqueror, and he succeeded in bringing all of England under his rule as William I. 

The so- 

Wales is Added to England. called English conquest of Wales was in 1283, when large parts of that land were brought under the control of the English. But there were still a number of small independent states in Wales. The "Act of Union" which finally brought England and all of Wales together under a single ruler was signed in 1536, when Henry VIII was King of England. 

Even before this act of union the title of Prince of Wales was given by several of the kings of England to their oldest sons. Nowadays "Prince of Wales" is a mere title, but at first that prince had some real part in the government of Wales.

Scotland Becomes a Part of the United Kingdom. - The Union of Scotland with 

England began when James VI, King of Scotland, became also King James I of England in 1603. Each country, however, kept its own separate parliament, or lawmaking body, until 1707. In that year, by an "Act of

GREAT BRITAIN 

45 

Edinburgh Castle.

Union," the two kingdoms were combined into one, the United Kingdom of Great 

Britain, with one British Parliament.

Ireland. Ireland became a part of the 

United Kingdom in 1801. But both before and after this date many of the Irish people were much opposed to the union. For a long time before the union was brought about, the English had been establishing their rule in that island. But they did not get on well with the Irish people. There was trouble over religious questions and over the fact that English landlords, who owned large parts of Ireland, charged high rents for their lands. 

Taxes and rents were so high that many people were forced to give up their homes and go to other countries to live.

In northern Ireland much of the land was taken from the owners because they had been at war with England. It was then given to new settlers who came chiefly from England and Scotland.

For a long time before Ireland was a part of the United Kingdom, many of the Irish people were not allowed to have any part in the trades, professions, or in education. 

They could not hold office, serve on juries, carry arms, or have a horse. After the union, laws were passed that gave the people the right to do many of these things, and conditions improved. More land was brought under cultivation and the manufacture of linen became an important industry. 

Unfortunately, during these years the population increased even more rapidly than the industries by which the people earned their living. Then came the great famine when for five years the potato crop, one of the chief food crops of the people, was almost a total failure. Food was sent from other parts of Great Britain, from the United States, and from other countries. But in spite of all that was done a large number of people starved to death. More than 1,000,000 died

Ireland to find homes somewhere elsemostly in America.

Many of the people of Ireland were never happy under the rule of the British government. They wanted to govern themselves. 

In 1922, after years of trouble, this "home rule," as the Irish called it, was arranged. 

In that year all of Ireland except its northern part was formed into the Irish Free State, a name that was changed to Ireland in 1937.

It, like Canada, is one of the self-governing 

Dominions of the British Empire. Northern 

Ireland is still a part of the United Kingdom. 

England under William I. - Early Eng 

Early Eng land was chiefly an agricultural country. 

In 1086, under William I of England, there was taken what we should now call a census. 

The king wanted to know many things about the land he had conquered. The facts learned as a result of the census were written down in a record known as the Domesday Book.

From the Domesday Book we are able to learn about England as it was at that time. were in England and how much land was cultivated. The names of the lords, or barons, who owned the great estates, or manors, are given.

The size of each manor also is given, and the way in which it was divided into cultivated fields, meadows, pastures, and forests. 

In some cases a baron owned a number of manors, each with some lord of the manor to look after it.

The home of the lord of the manor was the manor house. Most of the early manor houses were built at a time when the barons were often at war with one another. They were really great castles usually built of stone, and so they could be easily defended. 

The walls were thick, with only a few openings, and there were towers from which watchers could see any one who came near the castle during the day. It was usual to build these castles on high land. A wide ditch was dug around the castle, and when it was possible this was generally filled with water to form a moat.

A. Manor house.

To enter the castle one crossed the moat by means of a bridge which was raised at night or in times of danger, and lowered into place when needed. Later manor houses were more like the one shown here (A). - - Near 

The Village and the Villagers. 

each manor house there was a village, where most of the people belonging to the manor lived. A few of the villagers were free men who owned small farms. But most of them were not free. In a very real way they were the property of the lord of the manor, but he could not buy or sell them as slaves. If, however, the manor itself was sold these peasants, or serfs, went with the land. Most of the villagers were farmers called villeins, or laborers called cotters.

The manor land under cultivation was divided into great fields, of which there were usually three. Each of these fields was divided into many long, narrow strips. Some of these strips of land were for the lord of the manor, and the others were divided among the villeins (B). The strips that were given to each of the villeins were not all together in one small farm but were scattered over the three fields. To farm his land, therefore, the villein had to go from one part of the field to another, and from field to field.

Each year about one third of the cultivated land was allowed to lie idle or "fallow."

This was because growing plants are constantly taking their food from the soil. In fields that are allowed to lie idle one out of each three years, the food taken by the plants is not so quickly used up as in fields that are cultivated every year.

The villeins usually worked a part of each week on the lands of the lord of the manor, or in doing some other work for him. The rest of the time they could spend on their own work. They also gave to the lord of the manor, as rent for the lands that they cultivated for themselves, some part of the produce of their fields and some of the domestic animals that they raised. 

There was a common pasture in which the villeins were allowed to pasture their cattle, sheep, oxen, and horses with those belonging to their lord. They were allowed also to gather brushwood and peat with which to build fires to cure their bacon or to cook their food. But they were not allowed to hunt the wild game of the forest. That was kept for the lord of the manor and those whom he invited to hunt with him.

The homes of the villeins were small and poorly built and furnished. For people today such homes would lack all comforts. The only beds were piles of straw on the floor. 

There were no windows, no fireplaces, and no chimneys. Fires were built on a hard-packed dirt floor. The smoke escaped through a hole in the roof or through the doorway. 

The door was sometimes built in two parts. 

The upper half could be swung back to allow the smoke to get out, and the lower half was left shut to keep out any wandering animals.

In each village there were laborers who made tools; spun, wove, and made clothing from wool; tanned skins; and made articles out of leather. There was a miller who looked after the mill belonging to the lord, where all grain was ground. Each villein and cotter got along with such things as could be raised in the fields or made in the village. Little or nothing came to them from the outside world. The fields and pastures of the manor were surrounded by a forest, through which there were only narrow paths. 

There were then few roads and of course no railroads in England.

Fairs and Holidays. The serfs, both villeins and cotters, were generally allowed to visit any near-by village where a fair or celebration was being held. There they could enjoy the races or other sports, watch the clowns or jesters, and see the performances of trained animals. several weeks at a time. Merchants and traders came to them from all parts of Europe. Among the articles offered for sale there were rare and beautiful things from the 

East and from the workshops of distant cities.

Both at fairs and at church festivals or holidays there were traveling merchants with many things for sale. Some of the serfs were sure to take with them articles that they had made. These they would try to exchange with some of the merchants for articles that they wanted. As a usual thing the merchant would be willing to buy anything that was well made and that he thought he might sell in some other place at a profit.

In addition to small village fairs such as the serfs attended there were much larger fairs held from time to time in some of the chief towns or cities. These might last for

At fairs of this kind the lords of the manors and others could see miracle plays (A) and were able to buy many fine and beautiful things. There were silks from China, damasks from Damascus (in Syria), muslins from 

Mosul (in Mesopotamia, now Iraq), and spices, perfumes, and rare woods from the 

Spice Islands and other parts of the Indies. 

Here, also, would be found armor, fine swords, and many objects made of precious metals, as well as some glass ware, porcelain, and pottery. 

The Growth of Towns and Cities. Be sides the villages on the manor lands, there were in England some larger towns and a few cities, and these continued to increase in size ow-4

and number. In one way or another men of the villages who had become skillful in making things secured their liberty from the lords of the manors, and moved to larger places. There they became craftsmen and organized guilds (page 26). More and more these larger towns became centers of manufacture and trade. Merchandise from foreign lands was imported for sale, and English goods of different kinds were sent out of the country. Merchant guilds had charge of this foreign commerce. The roads over which these merchants transported their goods were very poor at first, being almost impassable in rainy seasons. But the roads were slowly improved.

The Black Death and the Labor Supply. 

In the fourteenth century an epidemic called the Black Death swept over much of Europe and finally reached England. Between one fourth and one half of the population in different parts of the country died from its effects. Vast areas that had been under cultivation could no longer be cared for. 

The lands that the dead villeins and cotters had held went back to the lords of the manors, but there were not enough laborers to keep it under cultivation. Much of the land that was once devoted to crops was turned into sheep pastures. 

Farms Are Rented. In earlier and more prosperous times many of the peasants had purchased their freedom from the lords of the manors. Now they asked for high wages and special privileges. Laws were passed by which it was hoped to make them serfs again, but the peasants rebelled and the new laws were only partly successful. Some of the lords of the manors met the problem in a much better and altogether kinder way. 

They stocked farms with domestic animals, furnished tools, and rented these to farmers who would pay rent. The old manor system was breaking up, manufacture and trade were increasing, and travel was growing easier and safer.

Pottery, Tiles, and Glass. - Not much is known about the early history of pottery in England. In the 

Domesday Book there is mention of several places in which this industry was carried on, showing that its manufacture was common in the eleventh century. There is also on record the fact that in 1260 an order was given for one thousand pitchers for use in the king's household. The potter's wheel was in common use; the art of glazing the pottery was well known, A. - Guild craftsmen: at the left, a goldsmith; at the right, a dyer. and much of the pottery was artisti- Some 

Early English Manufacturing. - You have learned how craftsmen began the manufacture of articles of various kinds (page 26). 

The work was usually done in their own homes by several members of the family. 

Sometimes other young people were taken into these family workshops as apprentices and taught the different processes. Sometimes, too, skilled workmen were employed and were paid a wage for the work they did. 

Each group of workers specialized in a particular industry. Metal working; the making of pottery, tiles, brick, and glass; the different processes in connection with the manufacture of cloth; tanning and the manufacture of leather goods; and brewing were among these industries.

Metal Workers. The name of "Otto the Goldsmith " is mentioned in the Domesday Book. He was the founder of the family of Fitz-Otho, who were workers in gold and the masters of the king's mint from 1100 to 1300. The goldsmiths (A) worked in gold and silver, and sometimes in other metals, such as bronze, which was a combination of copper and tin. Other metal workers were engaged in making pewter, a composition of tin and lead, to which, at times, small amounts of other metals were added. There were also founders, who cast guns (cannons), bells, images, and other things. cally and beautifully decorated.

Clay tiles of different sizes and patterns and for different uses were made in a number of places. We know that some tiles were made in England even before the Romans came to Britain. But the industry seems to have stopped during the Roman occupation. 

When it began again we do not know. Yet in 1212 builders in London were required to use tiles for roofs instead of thatch, because of the danger from fires. 

Bricks and floor tiles were in common use in building. Some of the floor tiles had patterns cut into the clay before they were hardened in the fire and glazed. Colors were also used in the decoration of the tiles, some of which were of great beauty. 

There are records to show that glass was made in large quantities in the early years of the thirteenth century, and the industry was probably much older. It is certain that glass was being made in some of the villages of southeastern England as early as 1225. No doubt it was made also in many other places where the necessary fuel and sand were found. 

Records show that " English glass was used in the windows of cathedrals built in England in the fourteenth century and later. 

The Making of Cloth. The making of cloth is an old, old industry. No one knows when or how man first learned to spin fibers of various kinds into thread or to weave

A. 

Part of a flock of sheep in Scotland. Many sheep have been raised in Scotland, partly because much of the country is hilly or mountainous. these threads into cloth. All of the early peoples knew how to do this work, and some of the methods they followed are still in use among primitive peoples.

It was always a household industry in the manor villages and it was one of the industries that was greatly improved by skilled craftsmen.

After the Black Death (page 50), so many fields were turned into sheep' pastures (A) that the production of wool was greatly increased. English weavers used much of the wool, but not all of it. A market for some of the surplus was found in the Netherlands. 

The weavers there had become famous for the fine woolen cloth that they were able to make. These weavers knew, of course, where the raw wool that they used came from. 

When troubles at home led some of them to move they were welcomed in England, and there they followed their trade.

The processes in the making of cloth included (1) sorting the wool to separate the fibers of different lengths and quality; (2) combing or carding it so that the fibers were made to lie parallel to one another; (3) spinning the carded wool into a thread; (4) weaving the threads into a cloth; and (5) dyeing and finishing the cloth.

The In the time about which you are studying, these were all home industries, and most of the spinning was done by women (53 A). most important of all cloth-making processes was weaving. The looms (53 B) were wooden frames with rollers at each end. On one of these rollers threads were fastened at a proper distance apart and then wound on the roller. 

The other ends of the threads were then fastened to the roller at the end of the frame where the weaver sat. These threads that ran from roller to roller were called the warp threads.

A. 

Spinning wheel.

B. A simple hand-worked loom. In a basket at the left are several shuttles. were made. In many places the right to use looms was taxed. That was to give the town or city an income from the work of the weavers.

In another city it was the rule that all looms should stand in the home or workshop where the weaving could be seen from the street or road. This was so that the weavers would not dare to use poor wool or do poor work. If the loom was placed where the work could not be seen, the owner of the loom was fined. It may have been for the same reason that in some places weavers were not allowed to work at night - a rule that was not insisted upon, however, just before Christmas.

Each of the warp threads passed through | But we can understand why most of them a loop of fine thread, or cord, which was fastened to the top and bottom of a vertical frame. There were usually two of these frames, but there might be several. It depended upon the pattern of the cloth to be woven. These vertical frames with the loops could be raised or lowered by the weaver. The frame that was raised would lift the warp threads that passed through its loops. When one frame was raised and the other lowered, thread wound on a long shuttle would be passed between the threads that were raised and those that were lowered. 

Then the frame that had been raised would be lowered and the one that had been lowered would be raised and another cross thread would be put in. These cross threads are the woof of the cloth. There was an arrangement by which each thread of the woof could be forced back tightly against the one that had been put in before it, and in this way a closely woven piece of cloth could be made. 

Rules and Laws Governing Weaving. 

The regulations and laws governing the use of looms varied in the different towns and cities, and in all places from time to time. 

Finishing Woolen Cloth. In finishing cloth the fullers scoured and beat it in water so as to clean and thicken it. The cloth then went to workmen who, by the use of the dried heads of certain thistles called the "teasel," drew up the loose threads from the body of the cloth. These loose threads were cut off by the cloth-shearers, or shear-men. 

The final appearance of the finished cloth depended upon the care with which the fullers and the shear-men did their work.

The Linen Industry. The making of linen was being carried on in England as early as the twelfth century. Records of purchases made for the king's household prove that the industry must have been a large one and that the quality of the product was high. common use.

In in 

Leather and the Leather Workers. preparing leather two processes were in

The hides of the ox, cow, and calf were tanned. The skins of deer, sheep, and horses were tawed. In tanning, an extract of oak bark was used, and the leathers made were rather stiff. In tawing, oil and alum were used, and the cured skins made a much softer and more flexible leather.

The trade in hides and skins and leather, both at home and with other countries, was almost as important as the trade in cloth.

There were several different grades of tanned leather. Those that were to be used as the soles of shoes or boots were always prepared by the best methods. The laws governing the leather industries were very strict. Poor workmanship in the preparation of the hides and skins, or the use of poor materials, was severely punished. 

The tawed or soft leathers were used in making gloves, saddles, purses, girdles, and for for many other purposes. Furs were finished by the tawers, also. At one time in London frauds were so common in their preparation that tawers were not allowed to cut off the heads of the furs on which they worked.

You know the importance of the sixteenth, seventeenth, and eighteenth centuries as the great age of discovery, exploration, and settlement in the New World. That was the time when

Spain, Portugal, France, England (later Great Britain), and the Netherlands built up overseas empires. It was also the period in which trade between Europe and the East developed. In the latter part of that period, and in the first half of the nineteenth century, these European countries, except Great Britain, lost nearly all of their possessions in the New World. Great Britain retained Canada, but the Canadian provinces were (in 1867) organized as a Dominion having a large measure of liberty in caring for its affairs.

Just what is meant by the industrial revolution? It means rapid and extensive changes in the way people did the work of manufacturing and in the way they lived. 

In all countries that have passed through the industrial revolution certain things happened. 

In those countries each different region no longer depended chiefly upon its own workmen to supply the needs of its people. They no longer did most of their work by hand with the help of a few simple tools. They no longer worked in their homes or in small workshops making a few articles, each of which had its own design and character. 

Instead they began working with great machines in mills or factories (A). They turned out a vast number of articles, each one exactly like others, produced in the same way. Manufacturers now think of large-scale" production of articles that are "standardized" in all ways. ers of machines. The food that they eat, the clothing they wear, the tools they use, the raw materials of their industries, and a vast number of other things are usually the products of other workers. Many of these things may have come from distant parts of the world. In order that this may be so, it has been necessary to build and to keep improving the means and the methods of transportation. "( The industrial revolution, as here described, came first in England. Other countries followed at later dates. In China and 

India it did not really begin until the opening years of the twentieth century. 

Coal and Iron. There were many reasons 

why the industrial revolution began so early in England, and why, after it began, it spread quickly to other lands. One of these reasons was that Great Britain had rich supplies of coal and iron, and an industrial Today most of the workers in mills and revolution requires the use of both these factories are not craftsmen - they are tend-minerals in large quantities. Another reason

DEVELOPMENT OF GREAT BRITAIN 

57 is that many of the machines whose use so greatly increased production were the inventions of Englishmen. The English also took advantage of the inventions of other peoples.

The fact that there were large deposits of coal and of iron ore in Great Britain was known for a long time before the industrial revolution began. Coal was burned as early as the twelfth century and iron was also made and used. 

But neither of these minerals had been mined in great quantities.

In the early days charcoal was used as a fuel in smelting the iron ore, and the production of iron was limited by actual needs. But there was constant destruction of the woodlands to furnish the necessary charcoal. By the beginning of the eighteenth century the iron manufacturers were worrying about a future fuel supply. Later inventions made it possible to use coal as a fuel in the smelting process. A. 

In some parts of the British Isles the coal and iron deposits were near each other and the supplies of both seemed enough to meet all needs. Iron furnaces were built near the coal fields. It was not long before the heaps of black coal piled on the surface, the coal dust that was everywhere, and the clouds of smoke that darkened the sky, gave the name "the black country " to the chief ironmaking region of England (A). 

Improvements in the Textile Industries. 

In the eighteenth century, also, a number of inventions were made that greatly improved the textile industries. You will remember that in early weaving, the shuttle, on which the thread that makes the woof of the cloth 

Ewing Galloway 

Pit head of a coal mine near Birmingham, England. is wound, was passed from one side of the loom to the other by hand. In 1733 John 

Kay invented a way by which this could be done by machinery. This "flying shuttle," as it was called, was one help in increasing the speed with which weaving could be done. 

A number of other inventions were made that increased the speed of spinning. In early days it had often been true that the spinners could not make enough thread to keep the weavers busy. A machine called a "spinning jenny was made by James

Hargreaves, about 1764, by which several spindles could be worked by a single wheel. 

Spinning methods were still further improved by Arkwright and Compton. The improved machines could be driven by water power, and before long the spinners were producing more thread than the weavers could use.

In 1786 Edmund Cartwright made a loom that could be driven by water power. It did not work well at first, but further improvements made it into a useful machine. The production of thread by the spinners and its use by the weavers could be kept in balance by controlling the number of machines.

The English spinners and weavers were working in cotton as well as in wool. At first the greater part of the raw cotton came from the West Indies. Cotton was also raised in southern United States, but it was difficult and expensive to separate the lint from the seeds. This work was done by hand and very little raw cotton was exported. 

In 1793 Eli Whitney invented a machine called the cotton gin. It separated the cotton fibers from their seeds so quickly and cheaply that cotton growing increased rapidly in the southern part of our country. The raising of cotton soon became a plantation industry there, and many slaves were brought over from Africa to do the work. The time finally came when the English cotton spinners and weavers had an almost unlimited supply of raw material. The result was that the industry rapidly increased.

Mills. One result of these changes in the textile industries in England was to cause men with money to build mills, put in machinery, and hire people, at a fixed wage, to work in the mills. At first these mills were built on the banks of streams, where there were waterfalls to drive the machinery. A Scotchman by the name of

James Watt worked for some time to build an engine that could be driven by steam. 

He was interested in the fact that underground water sometimes flooded the mines and made it necessary for the miners to stop work. He made a steam engine in which a piston was driven up and down in a cylinder, and he used the up-and-down motion to operate a pump for pumping the water from the mines. Later Watt built a steam engine in such a way that it produced a rotary mo- Wheel

Engines of this kind (A) were used to drive the machinery of the cotton mills and woolen mills. When that could be done, it was no longer necessary to depend upon water power for these or any other mills. Coal furnished an excellent fuel for these engines, and a large number of the more important mill centers changed their location from the waterfalls to the coal fields or other places.

The Mediterranean - Red Sea Route. - 

The trade route now most commonly used between Great Britain and India, Australia, and the East, passes through the Mediterranean Sea. Turn to the map of this sea on pages 162-163. Notice the narrow strait that connects the Mediterranean with the Atlantic Ocean. This is the Strait of Gibraltar. Notice also that near its eastern end the Mediterranean is connected with the 

Red Sea by the Suez Canal.

The Influence of Industry and Commerce | British Empire by right of discovery, by on the Growth of the Empire. What has the story of British industry and commerce to do with the growth of the British Empire? 

It was the development of British trade and the use of British shipping on all the world's seas that led to the building of a great British navy. When steamships began to take the place of sailing ships, it became necessary to have coaling stations at convenient points. Such stations were established on the coasts of some of the continents and on islands along ocean trade routes.

Coal for many of these stations was sent from British mines, to be sold to steamers following the routes on which they were located.

So far as it was possible, Great Britain, having more ocean commerce than other countries, wanted to control the coaling stations. In one way or another it gained possession of good harbors on continental coasts and annexed the areas in which these were located. This was easily done in lands that were unoccupied or occupied only by savage or semi-civilized peoples. But many other areas were taken by force of arms during the years that British commerce was expanding and the empire growing. In the oceans, the coaling stations were, of course, on islands, and these became a part of the

Gibraltar. The Rock of Gibraltar is an enormous mass of limestone about two and a half miles long and from one fourth to three fourths of a mile wide. On the north it rises in an almost perpendicular wall from the strip of sand by which it is connected with the mainland of Spain. It is nearly as steep on the east side, where the 

A. The Great Rock of Gibraltar as seen from a steamer in the Mediterranean Sea.

A. The chief seaport of Malta. Notice the old-style fortifications and the ships and boats of various kinds.

rocky wall rises from the sea. On the west side the Rock of Gibraltar has a somewhat more gentle slope and at its foot there is a narrow strip of land near sea level. Here are the harbor works, and here the town has been built.

At the point where Gibraltar looks out toward Africa the strait is not more than 10 miles wide. The Rock has been made into a vast fortress whose guns command the strait. 

Gibraltar was first fortified in 711. At that time the Moors from Africa were trying to conquer Spain, and they captured this point and worked from it as a military base. 

When, after several hundred years, the Moors were driven out of Spain, they held on to 

Gibraltar as their last stronghold.

Spain built a great fort in the rock in the sixteenth century. The work was done so well that for many years it was believed that this fort could not be taken. It was, however, captured by the Dutch and the British in 1704. Since that time Gibraltar has been in British hands, in spite of a seven-year attempt on the part of Spain, helped by 

France, to recapture it. 

In these days of oil-burning steamships, submarines, and airplanes from which bombs can be dropped, the control of the seas is less easy than it was once believed to be. 

Malta. The island of Malta has had a very important part to play in the history of commerce in the Mediterranean. This is not because of size, for the island is only seventeen miles long and eight miles wide.

It is chiefly because of Malta's position. It lies not far from the place where the island of Sicily, at the toe of the Italian boot, comes close to the northeast part of Tunisia in 

North Africa.

Mediterranean and on the North Atlantic.

Africa and southern Europe. Malta is important not only because of its position, but because it possesses a fine natural harbor (A).

Ιερου Ανεμόμυλους χρυσο φωνη 

A. 

Street scene in the chief city of Cyprus. The cart is loaded with jugs of water for sale. Many Asiatic cities lack modern systems of water supply. 

You will remember that at one time both the French and the English tried to control the trade of India (page 37). To help France in a later struggle Napoleon took Malta in 

1798, on his way to Egypt, which he hoped to capture as a stepping-stone to India. 

He was defeated in 1801 at the battle of the Nile, and because of this defeat he lost control of Malta to the British. They made it a coaling and naval station. For a long time they believed it necessary to control Malta in order to protect their trade route to the 

East by way of the Red Sea. In recent years its importance has become much less, as the British now feel that, in spite of its greater length, the open-sea route to Australia and the East is the safest one to use in time of war.

Cyprus. -Control of the island of Cyprus was turned over to the British government by the Sultan of Turkey in 1878, after Great 

Britain agreed to help in defending the Turkish lands in Asia against Russia. When 

| Turkey joined Germany in the World War, 

Great Britain at once made Cyprus a part of the British Empire. It became a crown colony in 1925.

The island might be used, under certain conditions, as a naval base for a fleet protecting the Suez Canal. But it has no modern fortifications, and the fact that Great Britain still has a great deal of influence in Egypt is of more importance, in the protection of the canal, than the possession of Cyprus. 

None of these Mediterranean possessions of the British Empire is large. None of them is important because of its wealth or its trade. But they are excellent examples of the way in which Great Britain has tried to establish control of the trade routes followed by its ships.

On to India, Australia, and the East. - 

From a point near the eastern end of the 

Mediterranean, the Suez Canal has been cut across the isthmus between the Mediterranean and Red seas. Since it was first

A. 

View of Jersey, the largest of the Channel Islands. It was on this island that the first Jersey cattle were raised. opened, it has been straightened and made wider and deeper. Other plans have been prepared, which, when carried out, will make the canal large enough to allow the biggest ships using it to pass each other without stopping. All the countries of the world that carry on trade with the East by way of the Mediterranean are interested in keeping the canal open. But the British government owns a very large part of the company that controls the canal, and more than half of the traffic of the canal is British. 

Turn to the map on page 276, and notice that at the southern end of the Red Sea the continents of Africa and Asia come close to each other. They are separated by the strait named Bab el Mandeb. South and east of this strait is the broad Gulf of Aden, which opens into the Indian Ocean. 

On the north shore of the gulf, at some distance east of the strait, is the port of Aden, which, with a large area in southern Arabia, is under British protection. The island of 

Socotra in the Indian Ocean, east of the Gulf of Aden, is also under British protection. 

Here again we see how Great Britain guards this sea route to India, Australia, and the East.

Some Subjects to Talk About. 

1. How modern roads are built. Be sure that you know (a) how the ground is prepared, (b) how the foundation is made and what materials are used, and (c) the different materials that are used for the surface of the road. 

2. The changes that are now being made in railroad passenger trains in our country. 

3. Why Great Britain became a center for the manufacture of iron and steel goods, and why that country has, in recent years, imported iron for manufacture into steel. 

4. Important foodstuffs imported by Great 

Britain and the countries from which they are obtained. 

5. Three important raw materials imported and the countries from which they come. 

6. Why the merchant marine and the navy of the British Empire have become the largest and most powerful in the world. 

7. Why Great Britain feels that the Mediterranean-Red Sea route is of so much importance to the empire, and what means have been taken to protect it. 

8. What is meant by saying that Malta is "important because of its position." 

9. The building of the Suez Canal and the improvements that have since been made. 

10. Why Great Britain is so interested in what takes place in any country at the eastern end of the Mediterranean Sea. 

11. Why the Suez Canal is of greater importance to Great Britain than it is to any of the other countries whose ships make use of it. 

12. How the Suez Canal differs from the

Panama Canal, why the Panama Canal cost more to build, and why it is more expensive to operate.

Other Islands in the British Empire. 

There are so many islands belonging to the British Empire that space cannot be taken in this book to give the names of all of them. 

Some of them are large, with rich and varied natural resources, a dense population, and important industries. Others are small and 

Others are small and barren, with few, if any, resources, and few, if any, inhabitants. Many islands, among them a considerable number of small ones, are refueling stations (both coal and oil), and there are cable and wireless stations. These islands and island groups came into the possession of England or Great Britain, or became a part of the British Empire, at different times, and for many different reasons. They are widely scattered over the earth, most of them being, of course, in the Atlantic, Pacific, and Indian oceans.

The Isle of Man and the Channel Islands. 

The Isle of Man is a possession of the English Crown. During the period of its known history, it has been ruled in various ways. At the present time it is governed under its own laws, and no act of the British Parliament is binding upon the Manx people unless that fact is stated in the law. 

The Channel Islands (64 A) are off the northwest coast of France. They are all that is left to England of the "Dukedom of Normandy" that was joined with England at the time William the Conqueror became king.

They are governed under their own laws. 

British Islands in the Atlantic. There are many British islands in the Atlantic that are not a part of Canada. Among the more important ones are Newfoundland, the 

British West Indies, and the Falkland Islands. 

Newfoundland. - Newfoundland is a selfgoverning dominion. You will remember that it was discovered by John Cabot in 

1497, only five years after Columbus had discovered the New World. But no successful English settlements were made there until the seventeenth century. Long before this, however, French, Spanish, and Portuguese fishing vessels were visiting the neighboring waters, and France had a fishing station on the island. The British came into possession of the whole island in 1713.

But the long use of these waters and the shores of the island by other nations led to many disputes that were not all settled until 1904. 

The chief industry of Newfoundland is fishing, its cod fisheries being the most famous in the world (A). Most of the fish are, of course, exported, and therefore, for the size of its population, it has a very great foreign Much of this trade is carried commerce. on in British-owned ships.

On a globe notice how close Newfoundland is to Ireland. This fact led, many years ago, to the laying of submarine transatlantic cables between these two parts of the British Empire. Many of the airplanes that have made or tried to make flights across the north 

Atlantic have made use of Newfoundland as one of the landing places on the way. 

Important wireless stations also have been built on the island. A.

were also famous for their production of sugar, during the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Cotton growing in the United 

States, Egypt, and India made the production of raw cotton in these islands of less importance. So, also, the manufacture of sugar from beets grown in Europe greatly decreased the demand for sugar from the 

West Indies.

West Indies are commonly divided into six groups of islands. These are (1) the Bahamas, (2) Jamaica with Turks Islands, (3) the 

Leeward Islands, (4) the Windward Islands, (5) Barbados, and (6) Trinidad and Tobago. 

Taken as a whole the British West Indies have always been of considerable importance to the empire. In connection with two continental possessions - British Honduras in 

British Honduras in

Central America and British Guiana in northern South America - they have furnished tropical products of great value. At about the time the British colonies along the Atlantic coast were fighting for their freedom, Great Britain felt that the West Indies were of greater value than the rebellious colonies.

It was from the West Indies that the British cotton spinners got an early supply of raw cotton. This was long before the United

Better agricultural methods have led in recent years to improvements in the growing of sugar cane, vegetables, and tropical fruits; and the island populations are becoming more prosperous again.

The Falkland Islands. - The Falkland 

Islands are in the south Atlantic Ocean, about 300 miles east of the Strait of Magellan. 

With their dependencies, South Georgia, the 

South Shetlands, the South Orkneys, and others (map, page 16), they are the most southerly colony of the British Empire.

Other British Islands in the South Atlantic. 

The other British islands in the south 

Atlantic include St. Helena, Ascension, and 

Tristan da Cunha. All of them have been built up from ocean depths by volcanic action. Only St. Helena is of real importance, because it lies on the route from Great 

Britain to South Africa. St. Helena is a naval fuel station and is connected by cable with Europe and Africa. It is famous as the place where Napoleon was held prisoner from 1815 until his death in 1821. 

British Islands in the Western Part of the 

Indian Ocean. The island and the island group of greatest importance to Great Britain in the western part of the Indian Ocean are 

Mauritius and the Seychelles (map, page 242). 

Mauritius must have been known to the

Arabs, although the credit for its discovery is given to the Portuguese. The Dutch were the first to establish settlements there. When these were given up the island was taken by the French, and during the troubles between the French and English in India it was used as a station by French privateers. It was taken by the British in 1810, and was made a British possession by treaty in 1814.

The early importance of Mauritius was due to its position on the trade route between India and South Africa. This early importance was largely lost when the Suez Canal was opened. However, if, because of war or for any other reason, the Suez route were given up for a time, Mauritius would again be a natural stopping point for British merchantmen trading in India and the East by way of South Africa. There are cables to Australia, Zanzibar, Madagascar, and

South Africa. A small body of British soldiers are stationed on the island.

The Seychelles group was discovered by the Portuguese, then fell for a time into the hands of France, from which they were captured by the British in 1794. They were at

There is only one good harbor. These islands are important to Great Britain because of their position on important trade routes between India and possessions in East Africa. 

British Islands in the Pacific. Great 

Britain is interested in many islands in the Pacific, only a few of which can be mentioned here. Among the island groups are the Fiji and Tonga groups, wholly controlled by Great Britain, and the New Hebrides, where they share control with France. From these islands Great Britain gets tropical products of great value, and on several of them there are wireless and cable stations.

There is more or less regular steamer service to most of them, but weeks may pass between voyages. Many of these islands lie on the extreme margin of the inhabited world. 

The Fiji group was discovered in 1643 and visited in 1769 by the famous English explorer Captain Cook. Great Britain took possession of them in 1874. They are connected by direct cables with Canada, Australia, and New Zealand, and there are several wireless stations in the group. There is also a wireless station in the Tonga Islands, or Friendly Islands, which are now a British protectorate.

The New Hebrides group is controlled by the British and the French jointly. This has never been a very satisfactory arrangement. Australia, because these islands are so near that continent, has strongly objected to certain agreements entered into between. 

Great Britain and France concerning the 

New Hebrides.

British interests in Ceylon, in the eastern half of New Guinea, and in North Borneo, are discussed in later pages of this book in the section on Asia. 

What the Island Possessions Have Added to the Empire. The actual amount of territory that has been added to the British Empire through the control of the many islands in the world's seas is, after all, very small. Their chief value is that they can be used in defending British possessions, as

Their trade with other parts of the empire in articles that these other regions need or can use is considerable. But in many cases Great Britain has found that the cost of carrying on their governments and keeping them in communication with other parts of the world is greater than any profit that can come from their trade. 

The Dominions. The really great units of the empire are the dominions. Three of these Canada, Newfoundland, and modern

Ireland you have already studied. You know when and how they became parts of the empire, and you have learned about them as they are today. The other dominions are the Union of South Africa, Australia, and New Zealand. These three dominions will be taken up for a full and careful study later in this book. 

At the close of the World War Australia and New Zealand were each made responsible islands. The directions to do this are called mandates. The areas to which mandates apply are called mandated territories. For a time, at least, the mandated territories controlled by Australia and New Zealand have become practically a part of the British Empire. So also have other areas for which mandates have been given to Great Britain. or any of its dominions or possessions. In our later study we shall give attention to some of them.

The Union of South Africa is part of a great continent, and will best be studied as a part of Africa. Its history is tied up with the history of that continent. That history includes the whole story of the partition, or the dividing, of Africa among the European powers. Some part of that story is told in connection with the study of Africa. 

Another part you are to study now, on the next two pages.

FINAL STAGES OF EUROPEAN EXPANSION 

Before turning to the study of the continents of Africa, Asia, and Australia, two important chapters in the history of European expansion should be known to you.

One of these is a part of the story of the dividing of Africa among the great powers of Europe. The other is the story of Russia's attempts to increase its territory, especially in southwestern Asia. 

Germany in Africa. - Northern and northeastern Africa were known to some of the peoples of the Mediterranean region early in history. The Arabs and others, whose ships sailed the Indian Ocean from earliest times, had traded with the natives of East Africa and the islands off the eastern shores of that continent. Under the direction of Prince 

Henry the Navigator, the western shores of the continent were explored by the Portuguese. It was Dias, a Portuguese, who first rounded the southern end of Africa, and a little later da Gama, another Portuguese, did the same thing and pushed on to the Indies. 

At different times the Portuguese, the Dutch, the English, and the French established small settlements along the coast. But it was a long, long time before the interior of the continent was explored. explored. It was not until the latter part of the nineteenth century that the division of the continent of Africa among the European nations was generally agreed upon.

In the meantime the British Empire had come into existence. It had enormously increased its area, it was governing hundreds of millions of native people in widely scattered parts of the earth. In the territories that had been brought under its control, there were natural resources of immense value. 

Then, in 1878, came the Congress of Berlin, and, as a result of this congress, some agreements that were to govern the taking of territories inhabited only by native peoples. 

Great Britain, France, Belgium, Russia, the 

Netherlands, Italy, and finally Germany annexed various territories lying outside the boundaries of Europe. Boundaries to separate the territories claimed were marked down on maps before the regions so claimed were explored. In this annexing of lands, unoccupied except by savage and semisavage peoples, Great Britain and France secured the lion's share. But in Africa, Germany, Belgium, and Italy each made claims. This marked the beginning of Germany's attempt to build up a colonial empire. 

It is this fact that you will find of interest.

British dominions. 

Russia's Further Expansion in Asia. - 

When the twentieth century opened, Russia already the second largest empire in the world tried to increase its territory at the expense of China. It especially wanted to secure control of the then Chinese province of Manchuria. Japan would not allow this to be done, and a war between Russia and Japan followed. In this war Russia was defeated, and since that time Japan has largely increased its influence in that part of the old 

Chinese Empire. 

For a considerable time, both before and since the World War, Russian influence in southwestern Asia has been increasing. been increasing.

Large areas have been added to Russia in that part of the world. Great Britain has found in this fact a threat against its control of India. Because of this, Great Britain has brought under the control of the Indian government more and more territory along its northwestern boundary. This has been done in part to stop the Russian advance and in part to secure control of the natives of that region.

You will learn more about this and about other parts of Asia under European control 

continent. Likewise, too, you will learn most about the European possessions in Africa and Australia in the parts of the book devoted to those continents.

The World Empires of Today. The three countries of the world that today have the most extensive territorial possessions are 

Great Britain, Russia, and France. When the Chinese republic was in actual control of all the territory supposed to belong to it, that country ranked fourth in size among the nations. At the present time fourth place must be given to our own country. 

Among other nations having foreign colonies or possessions are the Netherlands, Portugal, Belgium, and Italy.

POSITION AND SIZE OF EUROPE 

75 Just as we find the people and the cities of the Old World interesting to us, so do the people of many European countries find the New World interesting to them. Some of them have come to our country to make their homes here. Others have gone to some South American country. They believe that in these new and less crowded lieve that in these new and less crowded lands they can live better and be happier.

They have bought farms. They have found work in our mills and factories, and in our shops and offices, or they have started some business of their own. Others are students or travelers. They come to see our cities and their skyscrapers, to visit Niagara Falls, Yellowstone National Park, the Grand Can yon, or some other marvelous work of nature.

The ancestors of most of us came from Europe. In some European country many of you may still have relatives or friends. 

You could go back to the place from which your ancestors came and find the records of your family. For these reasons and many others you will enjoy studying the continent of Europe. 

The Position and Size of Europe. If you look at Europe on a globe, you will find it a very much cut-up peninsula extending west from the great land mass of Asia. But, although the large southern peninsulas of Asia almost reach the Equator, no part of Europe is as far south as the Tropic of Cancer. A small part of the continent extends northward beyond the Arctic Circle, but much less than in North America. Almost all of Europe, therefore, is in the North 

Temperate Zone. 

Europe is sixth in size among the continents only Australia is smaller. Asia is more than four and a half times as large, and North America is nearly two and a half times as large. How does Europe compare in size with the United States? How does it compare with Brazil? (See Table 1, page 

392, near the end of the book.)

Europe is less than half as large as North America and little more than half as large as South America, and yet it has a longer coast line than either.

A Mother Continent. 

Year after year | Sea to the Black Sea, then east of the Carpathians to the Baltic Sea. In following these routes is it necessary to cross any of the great mountain ranges? the population of many European countries has increased, except when disease or war has caused great loss of life. There are now more people in Europe, for each square mile of its surface, than in any other continent. 

Prove this by dividing the number of people in each continent by the number of square miles. This gives an average number for each square mile, or what is called the density" of population. The density of population for each country can be found in the same way. 

The increasing density of population in some of the European countries has had an effect upon the settlement and progress of many other countries. Through discovery and settlement, or through wars, some of the countries of Europe have spread their influence far beyond the boundaries of that continent. Some of them own or control large areas in other continents and many of the islands of the sea. Europe has been like a great mother. She has sent her children to fill empty lands and build new nations. 

The Highlands and Lowlands of Europe. 

Study the maps on page 74 and page 76. 

These maps show the larger natural regions of Europe and their relation to each other. 

You will remember that in both North 

America and South America the highlands and lowlands have a north-south direction. 

In Europe, their direction is east-west. 

The High Ranges of Southern Europe. 

Trace the mountains of southern Europe across the continent. Notice that they are made up of several mountain masses having different names. There are the Pyrenees, the Alps, and the Carpathians. Find each of these, and remember where they are. 

Notice also that there are mountains in 

Italy and in the Balkan Peninsula. What are the names of these ranges? Find a route past the western border of the Alps from the Mediterranean Sea to the North 

Sea. Find another from the Mediterranean

The Central Highlands. - North and northwest of the Alps and the Carpathians are the Central Highlands. They extend from south-central France across the continent to the great plains in its eastern part (map, page 76). There were once high mountains in this region; but long before any time of which we have a record, they were worn down to lowlands by the winds, and rains, and rivers, and ice. Later some parts were lifted again, and once more the forces that wear away the highlands of the earth began to work upon them. 

As a result, these lifted blocks of land have been carved into hills and valleys, with some lowland valleys where rivers flow out of them. 

The Spanish Plateau is another region in which almost the same changes have occurred. 

Northwest Highlands. The region known as the Northwest Highlands includes the mountains of the Scandinavian Peninsula, the highlands of the British Isles, and an area in northwest France. It is believed that these highlands are the remnant of a mountain range that at one time ran along the western coast of Europe from the Arctic Ocean to the Bay of Biscay. They are now much lower than they once were, and parts of the old highlands are covered by waters of the North Sea and the English Channel.

The present mountains of this region are broadest and highest in the Scandinavian

Peninsula. But they are much lower than the high mountains of southern Europe. 

It is fortunate for central and eastern Europe that there is now no great mountain wall like the Andes along the western coast. 

Such a body of mountains would almost entirely shut out the rain that reaches central Europe. The lowlands lying east of it would be largely desert instead of being fertile and densely populated as they now are.

Influence of the Ocean on the Climate of 

Europe. Have you ever stood on the banks of a river, or the shores of a lake or ocean, when the wind was blowing? Did you notice that the wind brushed the surface of the water and heaped it up in waves? 

If you did, you probably also noticed that when the wind was strong the waves were high, and that soon after the wind died down the waves did also.

Waves are not the only movement of ocean waters caused by the winds. Over some parts of the oceans the winds blow so steadily in one direction that the surface waters are driven along as a current or drift. 

On the map above, find the current off the eastern coast of North America called the 

Gulf Stream. One part of it comes out of the Gulf of Mexico through Florida Strait.

Its waters come from the equatorial regions and are warm. 

As the Gulf Stream moves northeast, it spreads out more, and is moved along in part

The Mediterranean Region. - 

The lands along the Mediterranean Sea are largely shut off from the cold winter winds of the interior of Europe by the east-west mountains. These southern peninsulas are themselves largely mountainous, and there are marked differences in the climate of the various parts. As a whole, however, the climate is more oceanic than continental. In addition to the southern lands of Europe, the

Mediterranean region is usually thought of as including parts of Asia and Africa.

Farming.-Farms average much smaller in size than they do in the United States, and as a rule the land is more carefully cultivated. 

Low lands along the North Sea have been protected, and some areas covered by shallow seas have been reclaimed, by building banks or dikes to shut out the ocean.

Hillsides and lower mountain slopes have been terraced. Some lands have been irrigated, and where possible more than one crop a year is raised. Fertilizers are used freely to increase the yield of the fields. A. 

Welsh shepherds are driving their sheep down from the mountains to the valley for their annual dipping," a precaution against disease. 

You can see the brands on some of the sheep. In the valley below you can see some fields.

Some of the food crops can be raised under a variety of conditions as to climate and soil. Such crops are widely scattered because each nation wishes, so far as it can. profitably do so, to raise food for its people. Other crops must have certain conditions of temperature and rainfall to do well. They will be grown in more limited areas. The distribution of the more important crops of both kinds will be shown on maps on later pages of this book. 

The Animal Industries. Grazing is car ried on where the land is too rough or too cold to be farmed; where the rainfall is too heavy or too light for cultivated crops; and in high mountain pastures. Most of the domestic animals, however, are raised on farms where mixed farming is carried on. 

Areas devoting special attention to sheep (A), goats, donkeys, horses, and hogs will be studied as they are found in learning more about the different countries. 

Unproductive Lands. Europe has only small areas that can properly be called unproductive. The high, rocky, snow- and ice-covered mountain areas are unproductive, but mountains that are covered with dra region bordering the Arctic Ocean furnishes pasture for herds of reindeer. 

Mineral Resources and Manufacturing. 

Minerals have been found in different parts of the continent but chiefly where old mountains have been worn down and where coal beds were formed. In these areas, metal and other manufacturing industries have been developed, and great modern industrial cities have grown up. The importation of raw materials not produced in Europe, or produced in only small amounts, has made possible the growth of other great manufacturing industries. 

Distribution of Population. You have already learned that Europe is the most densely populated continent. In what parts of the continent are most of the people to be found? Naturally there are more in the great manufacturing districts than in farming regions. The better agricultural regions and forest regions. THE BRITISH ISLES 

The British Isles include all of the islands shown on the map facing this page. They are separated from the mainland of Europe on the south by the narrow English Channel and on the east by the waters of the North Sea.

On the map of Europe (page 74) find the black line in the Bay of Biscay marked 100. 

It is the 100-fathom line and shows where the waters along the shore of the continent reach a depth of 100 fathoms, or 600 feet. 

Trace it around the west and the north of the British Isles, along the shore of the 

Scandinavian Peninsula, into the Arctic

Ocean. Within this line the edge of the continent extends out under the sea and is called the continental shelf There was a time in the history of our earth when no water covered the continental shelf and the British Isles were a part of the European mainland.

The largest island is Great Britain, and in it are England, Wales, and Scotland. 

The other large island is Ireland and in it The are Ireland, a country having the same name as the island, and Northern Ireland. Ireland (the country) has its own government. The three parts of Great Britain, together with 

Northern Ireland, make up the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, often called simply "United Kingdom," or "Great Britain." Learn the way in which each of these names should be used.

British Empire. The many parts of the earth over which the British government has more or less control are, taken all together, called the British Empire. This empire includes the United Kingdom itself, the country called Ireland, Canada and some smaller lands in America, Australia, large parts of Africa, India and some smaller lands in Asia, and several thousand islands. A few of the islands are large, but most of them are small.

Ireland (the country), Canada, Newfoundland, Australia, New Zealand, and South 

Africa are almost independent of British control, and together with the United Kingdom are called the British Commonwealth of Nations.

SOUTH AMERICA 

A. Nearly half of this hemisphere is land.

Great Britain and the Land Hemisphere. 

On this page there are outline maps of two hemispheres. One shows the half of our earth that has the greatest proportion of land. 

It is called the Land Hemisphere. The other shows the half of the earth with the greatest proportion of water surface. It is called the Water Hemisphere.

Notice that the British Isles are at the center of the Land Hemisphere. They are on the eastern edge of the north Atlantic Ocean the ocean over which most of the world's commerce moves. East of these islands is the mainland of Europe. West of 

West of them, across the Atlantic, is North America.

These two continents are the homes of the world's most progressive nations.

From the great ports of the British Isles and those of near-by lands more of the chief trading centers of the world can be reached in a shorter time than from any ports in any other continent. The central position of the British Isles in the Land Hemisphere has been of the greatest importance in aiding the growth of Great Britain and its expansion into the British Empire. B. 

Most of this hemisphere is water.

The British Empire and the Navy. - It has also been of great importance to the people of the British Isles that their homeland is separated from the mainland of the continent. All through the early history of 

Europe, different tribes and groups of people made war upon each other. Once in a while in those early days, armies and peoples from the mainland crossed the narrow seas and landed in the British Isles. 

Several of these invasions were successful, and for a time the countries from which these armies came controlled parts of the islands. islands. Always, however, the people of the islands succeeded in again setting up their own governments. The English people were the most numerous, and their kingdom the strongest, so that in time they gained control also over Wales and Ireland. Finally, in 1707, the kingdoms of England and Scotland were united in the one kingdom of 

Great Britain.

In early times the English built many boats for fishing, for they had discovered that fish in great numbers could be caught in the shallow waters of the North Sea

Courtesy Travel Association of Great Britain & Ireland, N. Y. Cuy

A. — Fishing vessels in port on the south coast of England. and other near-by waters. Gradually the fishing boats went farther and farther to sea, and the fishermen became brave and skillful sailors. The English built ships also to use in protecting their country from enemies, and manned them by sailors from the fishing fleet.

The English, later the British, navy has for many years been the largest and most powerful navy in the world. It has been nearly nine hundred years since an enemy army has been landed on the shores of 

Great Britain.

One great reason for the building of such a navy was the growth of the British Empire. 

When the age of exploration began, with the discovery of the New World by Columbus, England took part with other nations. 

During the course of many years, new lands were found, claimed for England or for Great Britain, and explored and settled by people from the British Isles. Many of these lands now form parts of the British Empire.

With this expansion of territory, the settlers in the new lands called more and more upon the mother country for manufactured goods, and offered raw materials in exchange. Trade increased, and ships to carry goods and passengers were built in constantly increasing numbers. More and more of the people in Great Britain gave their attention to mining, manufacturing, shipbuilding, and commerce instead of to agriculture.

Soon there was not enough food raised in the British Isles to feed the people. Much food had to be purchased in other lands, along with raw materials for mills and factories. These imports were paid for with manufactured goods and by carrying goods across the oceans for other people. 

To protect the distant lands of the British

Empire and the ships carrying on a worldwide trade, the government of Great Britain kept increasing its navy. But during the 

World War even this navy was not large enough to protect all food and supply ships, and many of them were sunk by enemy submarines. For a time there. was danger that the people of the British Isles would be short of food. But with the help of friendly nations and the building of many ships, actual hunger was prevented. The invention of the airplane has made possible a new method of attack upon these islands, and has made necessary also a new kind of defense. 

An Indented Coast Line and Good Har bors. At the time western Europe was high enough above sea level so that the continental shelf was dry land, rivers flowed across it. When, later, this west-coast region sank to its present position, some of the tributary streams of old river systems were left as independent rivers flowing into the surrounding seas. Their lower valleys were drowned, like the drowned valley of the Hudson River, about which you learned last year. This sinking of the land and the drowning of river valleys gave the British Isles their present irregular and deeply indented coast line.

The harbor of Southampton, on the southern coast of England, has up-to-date equipment and improvements. 

Point out Southampton on the map. In this picture you see a huge transatlantic liner lifted out of the water, in a floating drydock, for cleaning and repairs. At the right is a pier, with cranes for loading and unloading ships. 

The lower courses of some of the rivers became broad estuaries with channels deep enough for ships to sail a long distance inland. An ocean steamer going up the

Thames about 50 miles to London is almost in the center of southern England. Yet one that goes up the Hudson River 150 miles to the port of Albany has just entered the edge of our continent. Since much larger ocean liners have been built in recent years, it has been necessary to dredge the channels of some of the streams and to build docks and basins and other harbor works.

The outflowing tides in river estuaries have helped to keep them clear of sediment.

The larger ships also take advantage of the deeper water at high tide in getting in and out of the harbors. Ships moving with the tide are helped by its movement. Many excellent natural harbors along the western coasts of Scotland and Ireland have little value for commerce because the regions they might serve are small or unproductive. 

No part of the British Isles is more than seventy miles from a seaport, and this nearness to the sea has helped greatly in keeping down the cost of shipping goods to foreign markets. There are no long and expensive railroad journeys for either exports or imports between seaports and the places where goods are manufactured or used. In our own country, it is sometimes necessary to haul goods by rail from 500 to 2000 miles to get them to ports for shipment to other lands. This extra cost of transportation of course increases the price at which the goods must be sold. 

Surface. You have learned that there are no great mountains in the British Isles (page 77). The Highlands of Scotland are in the central and northern parts of that country and they are the highest and roughest part of the islands. This highland area is a region of valleys and ridges having a general northeast-southwest direction. It is cut into two sections by a trench-like valley.

A.- Valley and pass in the mountains of northern Wales. 

Some of the mountains in Wales are bare like these; others are covered with forests. 

Through this valley the Caledonian Canal was built to connect the Firth of Lorne and Moray Firth. In southern Scotland there is a hilly region known as the Southern Uplands, but it is not so high or rough as the highlands of the north. Between these highland areas is the Scottish lowland, deeply indented by the Firth of Forth on the east, and the Firth of Clyde on the west. There is also a coastal lowland along the North Sea.

The Pennine Chain is a range of low mountains running north and south through the middle of northern England. In northwest

England is a small highland area with a number of beautiful lakes - the English lake country famous in literature and art. Central and southeastern England is a lowland, flat in some parts and hilly in others. A part of the lowland between the Humber River and the Wash is so low that banks are built to keep out the sea, and the area is drained by pumping. Wales is a region of low mountains and many valleys (A). Ireland has a central plain surrounded by a rim of low mountains much broken in places so as to give easy communication with the sea. 

The great ice sheet that once covered so large a part of Europe (map, page 101) covered most of the British Isles. In parts of both the larger islands there are beautiful lakes formed by glacial action, as were many of the lakes in New York state and in New England.
