The cotton and woolen mills of northeast-northeastern France were in the hands of the ern France were much damaged during the World War. Since then the mills have been rebuilt and modern machinery put in, thus greatly increasing their output. A further increase resulted from the cession of Alsace and Lorraine to France from Germany, which added to the number of French-controlled mills.

Iron and Coal Regions. -France is im portant for its heavy metal manufactures as well as for the large amount and great value of its more artistic products. With the cession of Alsace-Lorraine to France, at the close of the World War, France obtained iron-ore reserves of enormous size and of great value. 

In addition there are iron ores in northwestern France, in the eastern Pyrenees, and in the region between St. Etienne and Le Creusot. 

France now has nearly half of the iron-ore reserves on the mainland of Europe (map, page 148). The coal resources of France are not so large as those of Great Britain and Germany, but some coal is imported and the mines damaged during the war are again in full operation.

With its increased supply of iron-ore France has greatly increased its manufacture of heavy iron and steel goods. The blast furnaces and iron and steel mills of Alsace- 

Lorraine are of the most modern type.

Here are made steel used in buildings and bridges; rails, locomotives, and cars; heavy machinery; and small metal articles.

At Le Creusot and St. Etienne there are other mills and furnaces, and many kinds of iron and steel goods are manufactured. 

Among them are armorplate, firearms of all kinds, structural steel, locomotives, electrical machinery, weaving machinery, and agricultural tools. France, however, is still far behind both the United States and Great 

Britain in these industries. At enemy. This led to a rapid building of hydroelectric plants in the French Alps, in the Pyrenees, and in parts of the Auvergne where there is much water power. Here, in valleys where for hundreds of years there had been only a few villages, a little land to cultivate, and some grass for pasture, there were many waterfalls and rapid streams. points where the best use can be made of the water power, the hydroelectric power plants were built. As the plants began to operate so that electricity could be furnished, the older industries of the neighborhood made use of the new power. Other industrial plants were built, and still others moved to points where the electricity could be brought to them by wires. So cheap and valuable is this kind of power that it is being still further developed. It should lead to a more active industrial life for southern France. 

Grenoble, the chief city in the French Alps, has grown in size and added new industries since electrical power became available. 

Transportation, Commerce, and Ports. 

France has many thousands of miles of broad, hard-surfaced highways. Some of them were seriously damaged during the war, and many others were neglected. Since that time, however, they have been repaired and are now in fine condition again. 

In describing the French railways it is fair to say that "all roads lead to Paris," as a study of the map on page 112 will show. 

The service on most of the railroads is excellent, although the cars and locomotives are much smaller and lighter than those used in the United States. The railroads extending to the north and east connect with those of Belgium and Germany. The line with the heaviest traffic follows the Saône-Rhone valley to Marseille, and two lines completed at great expense cross the Pyrenees into Spain.

Air transportation is developing rapidly in 

France, with Paris as the center. Regular air service is maintained to several French cities, to London, and to other large cities of the continent (map, page 133).

The most important of the French seaports have been mentioned on page 123. Ports on the English Channel, and Brest, are used chiefly in the trade with north European countries, the British Isles, and the United States. St. Nazaire is a naval station and has great shipyards. Place de l'Étoile, Paris. This open space was given its name because of the twelve radiating avenues. The tomb of the Unknown Soldier is beneath the Arc de Triomphe. An everlasting flame is kept burning there. 

Paris. Paris, the capital and largest city soldier, to honor all the soldiers of France of France, is also one of the world's largest who died during the World War. and most attractive cities. In parts of the city the buildings are old and the streets narrow, but much of the city has been rebuilt in modern times. When this was done, broad streets and wide avenues and boulevards were laid out. Most of these are shaded by fine trees. There are some large parks and many small ones with winding paths and pleasant places in which to rest. 

In the modern part of the city the buildings are all of nearly the same height and there are no such tall "skyscrapers " as are found in the larger cities of the United States. Indeed, there are laws to prevent the putting up of such high buildings.

The Seine River flows through the city.

A. The Louvre, once the residence of the rulers of France, now houses some of the world's most beautiful art work. 

Here is the "Mona Lisa," one of the matchless paintings of Leonardo da Vinci. Here also are such famous pieces of sculpture as the "Victory of Samothrace" and the "Venus de Milo."

Every day many students of art and hundreds of lovers of the beautiful visit this gallery to study or to see its many treasures.

Beyond the Louvre, toward the northwest, there are lovely gardens that reach as far as the open space called the Place de la Concorde (Harmony). Farther on in the same direction, other shaded walks and drives lead to the Arc de Triomphe. The shopping, busi ness, and banking center of the city, as well as the chief theaters, the beautiful Opera House, and many fine private residences, are also on the north side of the river. 

The part of the city known as the "Latin Quarter" is on the south side of the river. 

In this section there are government buildings and such schools and colleges as the School of 

Fine Arts, the College of France, and the 

University of Paris. Here live thousands of students. They come from all other parts of the world as well as from all parts of France. 

One of the many interesting sights is the line of bookstalls along the sidewalk on the south bank of the Seine. On top of the wall bor- dering the stream, hundreds of small square boxes have been fastened. Each of them is provided with a cover so that it can be closed and locked at night. In these little boxes the booksellers keep the books and prints that they offer for sale, and collectors of fine books have often found rare and beautiful volumes there. 

Many bridges cross the river. Over them trucks, busses, taxicabs, private cars, and foot passengers are constantly hurrying. If you pause for a moment, you will see swift river steamers carrying passengers upstream and downstream. They tie up for a moment at some landing place to land or receive passengers, and then dart off again. You will see also the slower-moving barges loaded with coal, building materials, or perhaps foodstuffs. You will remember that the Seine is connected by canals and other rivers with distant parts of France and with Belgium and 

Germany. Much of the heavy freight of

Paris-about half its total freight-is handled on barges.

Paris and surrounding towns have much manufacturing, and together make this the greatest manufacturing center of France.

Among the products of the shops and factories are fine automobiles, glassware and china, machinery and tools, leather and rubber goods, furniture, clothing, and jewelry. 

For many years Paris has been the style center of clothing for women, and Paris styles are copied all over the civilized world. This is because of the excellent taste shown by the French.

Population. The map on page 81 shows the distribution of the population of Europe. 

In France you will notice that there are three regions where the population is more dense than elsewhere: the manufacturing and mining region of the northeast, the area around Paris, and the part of the Rhone Valley region which is around St. Etienne and Lyon. Almost all of the coastal regions are also densely peopled. The highland areas, of course, have fewer people than the farming regions, but the fewest of all are found in the Alps, the Pyrenees, and in the newly forested areas of the Landes. - France and its outlying possessions. 

Foreign Possessions. - France, like Great 

Britain, looks to its colonies to furnish foods and the raw materials of industry for factories at home. So also, France seeks in these lands markets where its manufactures may be sold, and where some of its people may find new homes. Unfortunately, most of the foreign possessions of France are in hot countries where white people cannot live well. Even those who go out to develop or manage plantations must sometimes return to cooler lands for the sake of their health. To develop the resources of these distant lands means much hard work. More roads must be built, the jungles conquered, and native peoples must be taught what to raise and how to raise it. All of this calls for the spending of large sums over a long time, and the use of a great deal of patience with the natives. 

The map on this page shows the foreign possessions of France. Their total area is greater than that of all Europe, but much of it is in Africa and is largely desert. Algeria, Tunisia, and part of Morocco in North Africa are the most important. Algeria and Tunisia have been for a long time under French control, and as a result their industries and products have greatly improved and increased. On the lowlands along the coast, and in the fertile mountain valleys, the chief | industry of all three of these lands is agriculture (B). Wheat and barley are the leading cereals, and early vegetables are raised for French markets. Large areas are used for vineyards and for olive orchards. In other parts of these countries there are pine forests and many cork trees whose bark is used in making corks. There are many date palms and large areas of pasture land. B.

Potato field in Algeria. The potatoes have been dug by a machine, and are being picked up by native workers.

The island of Madagascar, off the east coast of Africa, is 980 miles long, and is nearly as large as the state of Texas. French Indo-China in southeastern Asia (map, page 137) exports much rice. The chief industry is agriculture, and there are many rubber plantations. There are rich deposits of hard coal, and there are valuable zinc and lead mines, and large teak forests.

GERMANY 

As a result of the World War the old German Empire ceased to exist. The treaty of peace signed at the close of the war gave parts of Germany to neighboring countries and turned over the German colonies to Great Britain, France, and other countries. Germany became a republic. At the present time Germany is not a true republic. 

It is controlled by a party having at its head a "Leader" (Führer) who is also the

Chancellor. Its official name is "The German Reich." Under the Leader and his cabinet the government is a dictatorship. 

They have assumed the control of the political, economic, industrial, commercial, and cultural life of the country. The present government has repudiated many of the provisions of the treaty that Germany signed at the close of the World War. It is also demanding the return of the lost colonies. They would furnish an outlet for a surplus population and a supply of needed raw materials.

Great Britain and France have vast foreign possessions (maps, pages 83 and 137) from which they get food supplies and raw materials for their industries. In them they have found markets for their manufactures, and many of their people have found new homes. 

Before the war Germany was larger than France. Today it is smaller than France, and about twice the size of Great Britain. 

But it has a larger population than either. 

With an area equal to three fifths that of 

Texas, Germany has half as many people as all of the United States.

The North German Lowland. The two natural regions of Europe that make up most of Germany are the Central Lowlands and the Central Highlands (map, page 76). In 

Germany these may be subdivided into: (1) the north German lowland, (2) a belt of low wooded mountains, (3) a high and rather level plateau, and (4) Alpine mountains.

EUROPE 

The lowland was covered by the ice sheet (map, page 101), and the soils left there by the melting ice were not very fertile. Large areas were covered by lakes and swamps. 

Some of the soils were stony, others sandy, and still others were stiff clays. To change these naturally poor soils into the fine farms and pastures of today has taken years of hard work by very industrious farmers. Many parts of the country have been drained, and much fertilizer has been used. 

Although this part of Germany is spoken of as a plain, the ice sheet left a number of ridges or moraines. They are roughly parallel to each other and to the Baltic coast. 

There are old glacial stream channels between them, and along some of those channels canals have been built to connect the northflowing rivers. Most of the rivers have been improved, and with the canals furnish a cheap method of transportation for heavy freight (map, page 146). 

The Climate of North Germany. In this part of Germany the summers are generally cool, although warmer in the eastern than in the western part. The winters are mild in the west, and cooler toward the east. 

In the winter, ice forms along the Baltic shore, especially toward the east, and ice breakers are used to keep the harbors open.

Rainfall is well distributed during the year (maps, page 79). Many days are cloudy, and there is much winter fog, especially in the northeast. The crops chosen for cultivation are naturally those that grow best under the climatic conditions found here. 

The Lowland Farmer and His Crops. - 

Although naturally poor, the soils of this region have been made productive. Year by year as the population of Germany has increased, so also has the demand for food. 

It has been the wish of the government that German farmers raise as much as possible of the food needed by the people. Fortunately for them, they can get chemical fertilizers at low cost. One reason for this is that A.

Potato-producing regions of Europe. 

Germany has the largest known deposits of potash, one of the materials used in making fertilizers. The deposits of Alsace now belong to France as that area became French at the close of the World War. The chief deposits, however, are in the region around 

Stassfurt, in central Germany. 

The German farmers have become students of agriculture, and many of the young people go to agricultural schools. There they learn of experiments made with seeds, soils, and fertilizers. Especially they learn about their own lands what crops to raise, what crop rotation to use, and how and what their farm animals should be fed. Even the hardworking French farmer does not now raise as much per acre on good soil as many of these German farmers raise on their one-time poor soils. Among the crops raised with very great success on German farms are potatoes, sugar beets, rye, oats, and wheat. 

Potatoes and Sugar Beets. Although potatoes are grown in many parts of Europe, the chief producing area is south of the Baltic and North seas (A). It stretches from the 

Netherlands across all of the German lowland into central Poland. The sandy soil and cool climate of much of this region are ideal for this crop. In proportion to their areas and in proportion to their populations 

Germany and Poland lead the world in the number of bushels of potatoes raised.

GERMANY 

141 Many of the potatoes are used for human food. Others are used in the manufacture of starch and alcohol. A large coarse-grained potato is raised as food for farm animals, partly taking the place of corn, which cannot be grown successfully in so cool a climate.

Map B on page 128 shows where sugar beets are grown in Europe. Experiments with seeds and with the raising of beets have greatly increased their size and the amount of sugar that can be obtained from the beet pulp. Germany has become the largest producer of beet sugar in the world.

East Prussia is chiefly an agricultural region. It has one large city, Königsberg, a seaport. There are linen mills in some of the larger towns. The chief crops are potatoes, rye, oats, and flax. Cattle, sheep, and horses are raised. Much of the land is in large farms owned by rich men who hire others to do the work.

Other Crops and the Animal 

Industries. Both rye and oats can be grown in the cool, damp region of north Germany, where the growing season is too short and the climate too cool for corn. The rye flour is used in making a "black bread" that is eaten by many of the German people. Hay, oats, nuts of forest trees, potatoes, root crops such as turnips and carrots, and the waste pulp of sugar beets are fed to domestic animals, and there are parts of the lowlands that are used for pastures.

Both dairy and beef cattle are raised, as are also some sheep. German farms furnish 

German farms furnish most of the meat, milk, butter, and cheese needed by the German people. The chief dairying region is in northwestern Germany, near the dairying regions of France, Belgium, the Netherlands, and Denmark.

EUROPE The Cities of Northern Germany. - There are many villages and a number of large cities in lowland Germany. The villages are chiefly trading centers for the farming regions around them, but in most of the cities there are manufacturing industries. These include sugar refineries, flour mills, starch factories, and plants where alcohol is made from potatoes. There are also linen mills and factories where farm tools and farm machinery are manufactured. Among the large cities of the lowland there are seven, each of which has a population of more than 250,000 people. 

These are Königsberg, Stettin, Hamburg, Bremen, Hannover, Magdeburg, and Berlin (Table 8, near end of the book). Farther south, where some large rivers of Germany flow out of the southern uplands into the northern plains, there are other important cities. 

Berlin. The largest city in Germany and one of the great cities of the world is Berlin, the capital. There has been a settlement at this point for more than seven hundred years, but it grew very slowly until it was made the capital of Germany in 1871. 

The broad avenues and shaded streets, the beautiful parks, and the handsome public and private buildings have all been built since that time. Berlin is therefore not like the older cities of Germany, whose interesting houses and narrow streets belong to an earlier day. In some ways it is like our capital city of Washington. Both have broad streets and fine modern public buildings.

One of the famous avenues of Berlin is "Unter den Linden" (139 A). In another way Berlin is not like Washington, for it has many mills and factories.

Berlin is like Paris and London in being both a capital city and a great manufacturing center. In its mills and factories many thousands of people find work. Textiles, clothing, machinery, shoes, paper, chemicals, and glassware are made. Raw materials are brought to the city and the manufactures are distributed by the railroads and waterways. The railroads are owned by the government, and the freight rates and passenger fares are low. Berlin is one of the great transportation centers of Europe, not only for railroads and waterways, but also for airplane routes (maps, pages 112-113, 146, and 133). 

Three German Ports. Three of the navigable rivers of northern Germany flow into broad estuaries. One of these estuaries opens into the Baltic Sea and two of them open into the North Sea. Near the end of each estuary is a river port that can be reached by ocean ships and may therefore properly be called a seaport. Stettin is on the Oder,

Hamburg is on the Elbe, and Bremen is on the Weser (map, pages 112-113).

Stettin is the smallest of the three ports. 

As it can be reached from the Atlantic and the North Sea only by way of the Skagerrak, Kattegat, and the Baltic Sea, or by the Kiel Canal and the Baltic, it is not so fortunately situated as are Hamburg and Bremen.

The Kiel Canal (see map) can be used by ocean steamers of large size and is open to ships of all countries. Stettin is chiefly important as a port because it is near Berlin, and because it furnishes an outlet for the industrial districts of eastern Germany and western Poland. The harbor is closed by ice for about two months in the winter. 

The port of Bremen (143 A) is larger than Stettin, with a harbor that can be kept free from ice at all times. It is not the natural outlet for any large industrial region. It is, however, connected by canal with the industrial district of the lower Rhine, and handles a part of its commerce.

Much more trade is carried on through Hamburg than through either Stettin or 

Bremen, and it ranks next to New York and

London among the world's great ports. Its position at the mouth of the navigable Elbe River makes it the natural port for central 

Europe, but its commerce, like that of Rotterdam and Bremen, is chiefly transit trade.

GERMANY 

143 A. 

Courtesy German Tourist Information Office, N. Y. City 

In the busy harbor of Bremen. Tugs are assisting one of the steamers to back into its proper dock. Bremen is the home port of some of the world's finest and fastest ships. 

Through these three German ports trade | extend southward to the Alps. In their is carried on with all the world. Each one has miles of docks and wharves, many storage warehouses, and the most modern machinery for handling all cargoes. In addition to ships from foreign lands, you will find in these ports hundreds of barges used on German rivers and canals. Hamburg and 

Bremen are the home ports of many great ocean steamships used in foreign trade. The largest and finest of the passenger liners are used in the New York service. 

All three of these seaports of Germany are manufacturing cities also. One group of industries has grown out of the shipping business and includes shipbuilding and the manufacture of machinery and marine engines. Another group is based on imported raw materials and includes the manufacture of cotton and woolen goods. 

The Highlands of Central and Southern 

Germany. Turn to the map on pages 112113. Notice that south of Hannover, Magdeburg, and Leipzig there are highlands that northern parts they are low mountains with heavily wooded slopes. Between these, fine fertile valleys reach back into the highlands.

The valleys and lower hill slopes are excellent farm lands. As a whole, this part of Germany is not much warmer than the lowlands of the north. It is, of course, nearer the 

Equator, and should therefore be warmer. 

At the same time, much of the region is higher above sea level, and should therefore be cooler. The one influence offsets the other here as it does in many other regions of high elevation-in the central part of Mexico, for example.

The average temperature of Germany from north to south is remarkably uniform.

South of the wooded hills and low mountains is a region that is high and flat, except where the rivers have cut their valleys across it. 

This is the Bavarian Plateau. Still farther south the surface of the plateau rises into the northern slopes, high valleys, and peaks of the Alps.

EUROPE 

Many parts of | Plateau or across it. On the southern edge of the plateau, where it joins the northern slopes of the Alps, dairying is an important industry.

Forests and Their Care. 

this highland area of southern Germany are covered with forests. Long years ago the 

German people began to look upon their forests as a crop to be tended and cared for as any other crop would be. About one fourth of Germany can be used for the growing of trees more profitably than it can for any other crop, and the forests are watched over by men trained for this work. When any part of a forest area is cleared, an equal area is at once planted to young trees. As these grow larger, some are cut to give those that are left more room to grow, and this is repeated as the trees grow larger and larger. 

Some profitable use is made of each tree that is cut down, whether it is large or small. 

The smaller ones may be used for fence posts or for poles in the vineyards or hop fields. 

The larger ones are used in the making of paper or for lumber. Even the twigs and small branches are collected and tied into bundles to be used as firewood.

Everything possible is done to prevent the starting of forest fires, and no country in the world has been more successful in preventing them. This interesting fact is all the more remarkable because under the law all forests may be visited by the people, and those belonging to the state or to cities are used as playgrounds. Because of the care given to its forests, Germany produces about two thirds of the forest products needed by its people, and needs to import only about one third. 

Agriculture and Manufacturing in the 

Bavarian Highlands. You have learned that there are fine farm lands in the valleys among the low mountains north of the 

Bavarian Plateau (page 143). That part of

Germany is its chief wheat-growing region; and rye, barley, hops, tobacco, and grapes also are raised there. The live stock includes fine horses, cattle, sheep, hogs, and poultry.

Other farming regions are found in the valleys of the streams flowing out of the Bavarian One of the large rivers of Europe is the

In the Bavarian Plateau, the valley of the Danube is a farming region in which fine cattle are raised. This part of the river is connected by a canal with the river Main, a tributary of the Rhine, and thus with all the improved waterways that are connected with the Rhine (maps, pages 112 and 146). Many locks are used in crossing the higher lands between the two rivers.

The Bavarian Highlands are not entirely lacking in manufactures, although there are no large deposits of coal or iron within the area. ECHOSLOVAKIA A. Chief waterways of Germany. 

From the Lake of Constance to Basel the 

Rhine forms the boundary between Germany and Switzerland, and from Basel north for about a hundred miles it is the boundary between Germany and France. The Rhine The Rhine has been "internationalized," which means that it is open to the commerce of all the world in times of peace. As you know, it is connected by a canal with the Rhone in 

France (page 132). This canal passes by

Belfort through a low pass between the 

Vosges and Jura mountains, called the "Burgundy Gate." By this route the Rhine is connected with the network of canals and navigable rivers of France. Farther north another canal, from Strasbourg (or Strassburg) by way of Nancy, joins the Rhine with the Marne River, and so with the Seine and Paris. Study the map on this page. 

In crossing the Netherlands, the Rhine becomes a part of the network of navigable waterways in that country, Belgium, and northeastern France. You have already learned that the Rhine and Danube are connected, and a water route thus provided to the Black Sea and to Istanbul. Another canal in northwestern Germany gives Rhine boats and barges a route to the estuary 50 100 130 of the Weser and the harbor of Bremen. Canals now being built will connect with other waterways, and greatly increase the area that can be reached from the Rhine. 

With all these connecting waterways, is it any wonder that the Rhine has become one of the most important rivers of Europe? It carries much more traffic, for example, than does the Mississippi River, which is much longer and serves a larger area.

The Middle Rhine. - The middle portion of the Rhine from Basel to Mainz flows through a level valley that varies in width from fifteen to twenty miles. This valley is spoken of as "The Garden of the Rhine," because it is so fertile and so productive. 

From Basel to Karlsruhe the western part of the valley is in France, but north of that city the Rhine Valley is wholly in Germany. 

On the west of the valley are the Vosges Mountains, and on the east is the highland region known as the Black Forest. The beds of ancient rocks underlying the valley floor were at one time much higher, and connected the highlands on the east with those on the west. west. Ages ago, during some disturbance of the earth's surface, breaks in the earth's crust allowed this block of the old mountain area to drop into its present position. A valley formed in this way is called a "rift valley." You have already studied a block of old land in southern France that was broken away from a larger area and tilted to form the Auvergne Mountains.

Among the crops grown in the valley of the Middle Rhine are grains, hops, tobacco, and some fruits. Along the hill slopes there are miles and miles of terraces, and on these sunny slopes there are great vineyards. Two important tributaries of the Rhine flow out

There are many towns and several cities in the middle Rhine Valley and on tributary streams. Frankfurt on the Main. It is usually given this name in full because there is another 

Frankfurt in Germany on the Oder River.

Frankfurt on the Main is not far from the place where the Main flows into the Rhine. 

It is a river port, and has breweries, chemical works, and machine shops.

Principal mineral products of Europe.

The Lower Rhine. The least picturesque part of the Rhine Valley is the part from 

Bonn to the North Sea. The land bordering the river is low and flat, and widens out rapidly to become a part of the Central Lowland of the continent. Industrially, however, this is a region of the greatest importance to Germany. Here are rich deposits of minerals; great furnaces, mills, and factories; a dense population; and many cities, so close together that each one seems to join the next. Germany is a great manufacturing nation, and mills and factories may be found in all parts of the country. More industries, however, are to be found in the basin of the Rhine north of Cologne than in any other part of Germany.

149 Mineral Resources of Germany. - The | is in the central part of the country. It mineral resources of Germany are large. Do you remember the potash deposits which are so necessary in the manufacture of chemical fertilizers? Read again, on page 140, about these deposits and their use. The copper deposits in the Harz Mountains are the largest in Europe. Before the World War,

Germany had made use of its enormous coal and iron resources to become one of the two great industrial nations of Europe. In 1914 it was already a serious rival of Great Britain as a manufacturing nation, and might soon have taken first place.

At that time, about one third of the iron ore and two thirds of the coal of the European mainland were in Germany. As a result of the war, Germany lost three fourths of its iron ore and one fourth of its coal; also nearly three fourths of its zinc. Most of the iron ore lost was in Lorraine, now a part of France; and France also was given control of the coal fields of the Saar Basin until early in 1935, when they were restored to 

Germany. Other iron and coal deposits went to Poland. With the smaller reserves of coal and iron, Germany has continued its iron and steel industries by importing iron ore from France, Sweden, Spain, and North 

Africa. Germany still has large coal fields left, and has found new ways to make use of low-grade bituminous coal and of lignite, which is a still poorer kind of coal, halfway between bituminous coal and peat. 

The chief coal regions of present-day Germany are: (1) in the Westphalian basin, east of the Netherlands and not far distant from the Lorraine iron fields, and (2) the

Silesian area, which extends into Poland and 

Czechoslovakia. Of the two, the Westpha- 

Of the two, the Westphalian basin is much larger, with an abundance of good coking coal, much more than will ever be needed to smelt all of the iron ore in Germany.

More than one third of the lignite deposits of Europe are in Germany; the largest area is easily mined by machinery and cheap labor, as the deposits lie on or near the surface. Coal and lignite are now much used as raw materials in the chemical industries, with such by-products as tar, gas, and oil. 

Much of the lignite is pressed into briquettes to be used as fuel in homes and factories. 

Because of boundary changes following the

World War, France came to have much iron ore but little coal. Germany was left with much coal but with little iron. These conditions have already led to some exchange of these products between the industrial regions of the two countries. Barge loads of ore move from France to Germany. The same barges carry coal back from Germany to

France. Much ore and coal are also carried by rail. It is probable that such exchanges will continue and increase. The industrial region of northeastern France, Belgium, and western Germany centers in the coal and iron mines. Here are important parts of three countries, with common needs and interests. 

Manufactures. The great industrial region of Germany centers in the Ruhr River Valley, and in districts near by. The whole region is crowded with blast furnaces and steel mills turning out iron and steel goods of all kinds. The center of the iron and steel industries is at Essen, where the great Krupp works are located. Duisburg-Hamborn and 

Düsseldorf are two ports on the Rhine that handle much traffic for the district. In this same region are the chief textile manufactures of Germany, using imported cotton, wool, flax, and silk. Much of this raw material, as well as the imported iron ores, comes through the port of Rotterdam. The various textile industries are scattered through many towns and cities, but Krefeld is the chief city manufacturing silk goods. 

No other country in the world has been so successful as Germany in the manufacture of dyes, drugs, and chemicals. These industries are found in the lower Rhine region.

EUROPE 

Outside of the lower Rhine district, Saxony has the most extensive manufactures, including large iron and textile industries. 

Leipzig and Munich have great publishing houses from which fine books, atlases, and color prints are issued. Cologne (German name, Köln) is famous for its perfumes, and more famous for its great cathedral. Dresden china, well known in the western world, is made not far from Dresden. Breslau is a textile-manufacturing center. 

Education. The German people as a whole are well educated, and have a great love of art and music. Their many schools have a high reputation. There are art schools, conservatories of music, technical schools of all kinds, and many agricultural schools. In Munich there is a great museum in which many machines connected with the world's industrial progress may be seen. 

In several cities, particularly in Munich,

Dresden, and Berlin, there are great art galleries. In these there have been gathered together fine paintings, much sculpture, and other objects of art. In Leipzig there is a famous school of music. Among the great universities of the world those of Germany take high rank, especially those in Berlin, Heidelberg, Leipzig, Munich, Bonn, and 

Jena. German men of science and German scientific institutions are among the best in the world.

Since the close of the World War, the German people have worked hard to make their country again one of the greatest of industrial nations.

You know that the chief mountain ranges of Europe, its Central Highlands, and its Central Lowlands have in general an east-Europe upon the climate of the continent, west direction (page 77). The main moun- read again what is said on this point on pages tain belt crosses the southern part of the 77-78. continent, and separates the Mediterranean lands from central and northern Europe. It does not form a continuous mountain barrier, however, but is broken into several mountain masses. Between these there are low places which have been used like gateways by traders and travelers for many centuries. 

It must be remembered that the mountains themselves can be crossed. During the thousands of years that men have known these highland areas all low passes have been found, and those most favorably located have been used. It is true that the passes of the Cantabrian Mountains, Pyrenees, Alps, and Caucasus Mountains are few in number and high above sea level. Such ranges are usually barriers between peoples. To cross them is difficult and at times dangerous. 

Trade and travel move around such barriers rather than across them, as do armies in times of war. Now, however, mountains are no longer the barriers that they once were. 

Highways and railroads furnish easy routes across most of those where there is much trade between opposite slopes.

In the early days of the settlement of our own country, our eastern highlands were very real barriers. They are now crossed by many highways and a number of railroads.

After gold was discovered in California (in 

1848), thousands tried the long and toilsome journey across our western highlands, and many died in the attempt. Today, there are highways for automobiles across these mountains; railroads that climb over tunnel through them; while airplanes roar their free way from one side to the other.

SWITZERLAND 

Switzerland is only about one third as large as the state of New York. Much of its surface is too high and rocky for farms and homes, yet it has an average population of over 250 people per square mile. How is it possible in such a land for so many people to find ways of earning a living?

The Land and Its Drainage. Switzer land includes the central parts of the Alps, with hundreds of mountain peaks. Among them are the Matterhorn (A) and the Jungfrau (map, page 112) in Switzerland; but the highest of the Alpine peaks is Mt. Blanc, 15,781 feet high, in France. 

Photo by Perren-Barberini, Zermatt

A. The Matterhorn. 

151

EUROPE 

Switzerland has much rain and snow. The rain falls in the lower and warmer parts, and snow in the colder and higher parts. 

Some areas are so high and cold that the moisture always comes in the form of snow. 

In other areas snow falls in the winter and rain in the summer, when much or all of the winter snow melts. The line along the mountains, above which moisture falls as snow, moves up and down the mountain slopes with the changing seasons. But the real snow line is the line above which the snow never entirely melts.

In the higher mountains there are places where the snow is blown into protected valleys and where it packs together and slowly changes to ice. From such snow fields, tongues of ice, called glaciers, move very slowly down the valleys. Each glacier begins to melt when it gets into the lower, warmer part of the valley. At some point it is all melted away and the water flows off as a mountain stream. 

On steep slopes the snow sometimes slides down in great masses, carrying along bowlders and stripping the soil from the underlying rock. These avalanches, as they are called, uproot trees, crush buildings, and sometimes, although rarely, destroy whole mountain villages.

The drainage of much of Switzerland is radial, like that in the Adirondack Mountains in New York state. This means that the rivers flow out in all directions from some high section of the mountains. In Switzerland the drainage is from the high region around Mt. St. Gotthard. The Rhone, the 

Rhine, and streams that flow into the Danube and the Po, are parts of this radial drainage. 

Trace these rivers on the map on page 112. 

Below the snow line are forests and pasture lands. The forests of the higher slopes are evergreens, and scattered among them and in warm, treeless spots among the snow fields there are summer pastures. On the lower slopes are such hardwoods as the beech and maple. Like the Germans (page 144), the

Swiss take great care of their forests. 

The northern part of Switzerland is a hilly plateau, 1000 to 2000 feet above sea level.

Here are most of the farms and all the cities and largest towns of the country. This region is sometimes called the Swiss lowland, because it is low as compared with the mountains. There are many lakes, of which the 

Lake of Lucerne, the Lake of Geneva, and the Lake of Constance are the largest. The 

Lake of Constance is on the boundary between Switzerland and Germany, and the 

Lake of Geneva is partly in France. 

Because Switzerland is an inland country it has a continental climate. The plateau and protected valleys are warm in the summer, and there is plenty of rain wherever crops can be grown. In winter the whole country is cold. 

The People. Life in the mountains tends to make people strong and brave. A mountainous country is easier to defend during war than one that is flat and open. Because of these facts and because surrounding nations find it convenient to have a small independent state between them, Switzerland has been free from foreign control for several hundred years.

The country is a republic, divided into a number of small states called cantons. Its government is somewhat like that of the 

United States. Three principal languages are spoken. In the east and north, most of the Swiss speak German. In the west, they speak French, and in the south, Italian. 

There are forests enough in Switzerland so that most of the farm buildings and village homes are built of wood. Some of the houses are large and are several stories in height. 

On many farms the houses and barns are under one roof, making it easier to care for the animals during cold and stormy weather. 

A Swiss chalet (153 A), with its carved woodwork, tiny windows, and overhanging roof, is a pleasant, attractive-looking house.

Farming and Dairying. 

Many of the Swiss farmers and their families spend the winter days and evenings, when there is no outdoor work to be done, in making articles for sale. Some of these farmers are expert wood carvers, and the women make beautiful embroidery, much of which is sold in our country.

Rütli house on the Lake of Lucerne. It is called the cradle of Swiss liberty, for here, in 1307, men met to plan the struggle for Swiss independence.

The farmers of the plateau and the lower valleys raise the common grains and vegetables. There you will find vineyards on sunny slopes, as you will also on the steeper slopes around Lake Geneva. In the higher mountain valleys the chief industry is grazing. During the summer months each family drives its cattle to the high mountain pastures, where men of the family or older boys take charge of them. 

All summer long the milk is made into butter or cheese, which is sent down the mountains to the towns to be sold. At the end of the summer, the cattle are driven down the mountains again to the home barns. The grass from fields that cannot be reached by grazing cattle, and from meadow lands, is cut and cured as hay. It is carried or dragged down the mountains to be stored with root crops grown on the farm. Both hay and roots are fed to the cattle in winter. Yet 

Switzerland as a Manufacturing Country. 

Switzerland has no good coal and no iron ore, and therefore has no large iron and steel industries such as are found in Great Britain, Germany, and the United States. 

Switzerland has important manufactures.

Some coal is imported for use in homes and shops and factories, but most of the power used for industry and to run the trains is electrical power. Swift streams and many waterfalls furnish a great deal of energy, and large hydroelectric power plants have been built. There is enough of this power for every use, and it is cheap.

HOCKEY CLUB DAVOS 

A. 

Photo by E. Meerkamper, Davos - An ice hockey contest in Switzerland. On the mountain side you can see some hotels; above them, a forest; and still farther up, a snow-covered slope. 

Most of the Swiss manufactures are small and use but little raw material. They are valuable chiefly because of the amount of expert labor necessary to make them fine or beautiful. They include jewelry, watches, clocks, laces, fine hand-made and machinemade embroideries, cotton and silk goods; delicate tools and instruments, and small machinery. 

Another Swiss Industry. One of the great industries of Switzerland is the taking care of summer and winter visitors. Because of these many visitors, Switzerland has long been called the "playground of Europe."

Summer visitors are attracted by the wonderful scenery, which combines beauty and grandeur, and by the clean, clear, crisp mountain air. With the aid of trained Swiss guides they climb the mountains and explore the ice fields and glaciers. They ride or walk along the roads through wonderful valleys, and enjoy the beauties of waterfall, lake, and river. There is much beauty, too, in the early spring flowers that cover the higher fields to the very edge of the snow.

Many winter visitors come chiefly to enjoy the winter sports. These include skating, ice hockey (A), skiing, bobsledding, sleigh riding, and toboganning. 

The running of hotels and boarding places, to take care of over half a million tourists a year, is a great business. It requires the work of many people, as does also the raising of the food for these tourists.

SWITZERLAND 

155 

Roads and Railroads. 

The summer and winter tourist trade is so valuable to Switzerland and its people, that fine highways and railroads have been built. The highways, of course, are used chiefly in the summer time. 

Some of them have been blasted out of rocky cliffs and along valley walls. Others wind back and forth along the slopes of hills and mountains. All of the main roads are broad, have a hard surface, and are well graded. 

The railroads connect with those of Italy, Austria, Germany, and France, and through these countries with the rest of Europe. 

Some long railroad tunnels have been dug through the higher Alps. The Simplon Tunnel, on one of the railroads into Italy, is about 12 miles long, and a train takes about twenty minutes to pass through. Unfortunately for Swiss trade, Switzerland has no seacoast, and therefore no seaport. Its trade with countries beyond those that border it must pass over the railroads and through the ports of its neighbors. This means that charges for such transportation must be paid to the people of other countries. It is one of the conditions that have forced Switzerland to develop the kind of manufactures that do not call for the moving of much heavy freight. 

Cities of Switzerland. You have learned that the greater part of the population, and most of the cities of Switzerland, are in the plateau regions in the north. Here you will find Zürich, Bern, Basel, Geneva (Genève), and a number of smaller cities. All of them have manufacturing industries of the kinds already described. Zürich is the largest city, and manufactures silks and cottons. Bern is the capital, and is visited by many tourists because of its beautiful location among the mountains. Basel is at the head of navigation on the internationalized Rhine River. 

By way of the Rhine, Basel can trade over the whole vast network of rivers and canals connected with that river (map, page 146). 

Geneva, on Lake Geneva, manufactures watches and fine instruments. 

Geneva is also the home of the League of Nations. This league was formed soon after the close of the World War, and includes in its membership most of the nations of the world. Its main purpose is to prevent wars by helping nations to settle their differences by peaceful means. Several times in the history of the world, some city in Switzerland has been selected as a place of meeting for the representatives of warring nations when peace was sought. Switzerland itself, partly because of its small size, and partly because of its position, is not likely to be involved in European or other wars. It is therefore an ideal place for meetings to talk over terms of peace.

EUROPE AUSTRIA 

Before the World War which began in 1914, the monarchy of Austria-Hungary was one of the large and powerful countries of Europe. It had rich coal and iron mines, oil wells, large forests, broad and fertile farming regions, and many busy factories. 

It had seaports on the Adriatic for easy trade with the rest of the world.

Some conditions were not favorable to the peace of the country. Although Austria and Hungary had the same ruler, in most matters of government the two parts of the monarchy were independent, and they did not get on well with each other. The Austrian Empire included several small countries that had once been independent. Some of these had come under Austrian rule willingly, others unwillingly. Their peoples spoke different languages, and many of them longed to be free from Austrian rule and to have their own governments again. 

Losses as a Result of the War. At the end of the World War, Austria and Hungary were separated, and each was much reduced in size. The shaded areas in the map (A) show the lands taken away from them.

Austria was left a small part of the fertile plains along the Danube; but the rest of the country is a part of the Alps. The greater part of the area left to Hungary is a region of plains on both sides of the Danube. 

On the south, some territory was given to Italy, including the Adriatic ports of 

Trieste and Fiume. The rest of the Adriatic coast in the old Austria-Hungary became a part of the new country of Yugoslavia. As a result of this loss of seacoast, both Austria and Hungary are now inland countries. 

They are able to trade with countries beyond the seas only across the land and through the ports of bordering countries. 

The northern slope of the Carpathians, including the Carpathian Plain, went to 

Poland. Other parts of the northern area, with rich iron and coal mines and large industrial regions, were made an independent country, named Czechoslovakia. Other territorial changes shown on the map (A) include the loss of a large area to Rumania, and transfers of territory between other countries, farther south. &Kiev Dniester R.

BES SARAB 

Pruth Austria Today. Nearly all of the present Austria is the home of a German-speaking people. It has an area less than two thirds that of New York state, and not quite as large as that of Maine. 

Much of it is mountainous, although the Alps of Austria are lower than those of Switzerland. The climate is continental, with great contrasts between the cold winters and warm summers. Farming can be carried on in the northeastern part of the country where there are fine fertile fields bordering the Danube.

Other small farms are found in the lower Alpine valleys. In the upper valleys, as in those of Switzerland, the chief industry is grazing. 

Butter and cheese are made, and dairying is increasing. Some hogs and sheep are raised.

-Parliament buildings and city hall on the Ring Strasse, which circles the heart of the city of Vienna. Other buildings on this street which date back to the city's days of greatness are the opera house, the former royal palace, the art gallery, museum, and university. 

Unfortunately, not enough food can be raised on the farms of Austria to feed the people, and so some must be imported. 

Other countries that import food, such as Great Britain, are industrial nations and have manufactured goods to sell. Most of the great industries of Austria built upon the raw materials of the country can no longer be carried on as they were before 1914. With the territory that has gone to other countries went much of Austria's iron ore, most of its coal, and many mills and factories. 

However, Austrian manufacturers are trying hard to build up their industries again. 

Manufacturing. - On the map, pages 112113, find a mountain mass named Eisenerz (iron ore). It is about a mile high and contains much iron ore. To smelt the ore, good coking coal must be imported. Most of this comes from mines once in the Austrian Empire but now in independent countries. Austria's own coal supply is small in quantity and of poor quality, much of it being brown coal or lignite. Machinery and automobiles are still made, and Austrian steel manufacturers have purchased a part ownership in some

Silesian coal mines so they can be sure of the coal they need.

The forests furnish material for the woodpulp and paper industries, but for the manufacture of textiles, fine leather goods, and shoes the raw materials are imported. Some cotton, woolen, and silk mills, and some shoe factories are operated, but not very profitably. Austrian manufactures may be made profitable again when the people of the newly independent countries made from the old Austria-Hungary lose their fears of each other. They will then be able to find some good way of exchanging raw materials and manufactured goods with each other.

Water Power and Hydroelectric Plants. — 

Austria has much water power in its swift mountain streams and waterfalls which can be used in developing electricity. Some hydroelectric plants were in operation before the war, but then Austria had large supplies of coal to furnish cheap power. Since the war and the loss of most of the coal areas, more hydroelectric plants have been built, and some of the railroads are now run by electricity. A market for some electric power has been found in parts of Czechoslovakia, to which it is sent over heavy wires. 

Cities of Austria. More than one fourth of the people of Austria live in the capital city of Vienna (in the German language, Wien). This city, the center of Austrian culture and fashion, was once one of the gayest cities of Europe. It is now less prosperous and less gay, but it is still one of the world's great musical and medical centers.

EUROPE 

Vienna is on the Danube River at a point where great trade routes center and cross each other. As you read about these routes of trade, trace them on the map, pages 112 and 113. Toward the west one route follows the Danube into southwestern Germany. There the Danube is connected by canal with a tributary of the Rhine. River trade from Vienna toward the west may therefore reach any place on the great network of inland waterways in Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium, and France, of which the Rhine is a part (page 146). Toward the east the river trade of Vienna may follow the Danube to the Black Sea, then by connecting waterways to the Aegean Sea and the Mediterranean.

Railroads take advantage of the Danube 

Valley westward, to reach the larger cities of central and western Europe. Eastward there are roads to the Black Sea. One route crosses Transylvania; another follows the

Danube where it breaks through the Transylvanian Alps at the Iron Gate. Other railroad lines bend southward along river valleys of the Balkan Peninsula to reach Istanbul in Turkey, and Salonika and Athens in Greece.

One route to the south leaves the Danube Valley to follow the Inn River to Innsbruck, where it turns south to cross the Brenner 

Pass to Italy. Another crosses the Semmering Pass to Trieste. Along the Oder River, north through the Moravian Gate, a railroad leads out on the German plains to the Baltic. 

Merely because of its position, Vienna still keeps, and will always keep, a large part of its old importance. It will probably be a long time, however, before it is as busy and important as it was when it was the chief city of a monarchy with 30,000,000 people.

At Salzburg, the Orient route through Germany unites with the Orient route from France that enters Austria from Switzerland. 

Graz is on the railroad from Vienna across northern Yugoslavia to Trieste.

CZECHOSLOVAKIA 

Czechoslovakia is one of the new countries formed from lands that were taken from Austria-Hungary after the World War. It is a long, narrow country made up of the old 

Austrian provinces of Bohemia, Moravia, and

Silesia, and the northern part of Hungary. 

Its name was chosen because most of the people are Czechs in the old Austrian provinces, and Slovaks in the eastern part of the country, in what was northern Hungary.

Both the Czechs and the Slovaks are Slavic peoples, and though they were long under foreign rule, they have kept their Slavic languages. What are the resources and possible future of this country?

Bohemia. The western part of Czecho slovakia has long been known as Bohemia, and before it came under Austrian rule it had been an independent country. It is a plateau region bordered by mountainous and hilly uplands. On the northwest are the 

Erzgebirge (Ore Mountains), rich in minerals.

On the southwest is the Böhmerwald (Bohemian Woods), largely covered with fine forests. On the southeast a hilly region, the 

Moravian Heights, leads into Moravia; and on the northeast, the bordering highlands are known as the Sudetes. 

Most of the plateau is drained by the Elbe and its tributaries. This river cuts across the Erzgebirge northwest of Prague, and forms a navigable water route to the port of 

Hamburg. Through this same mountain gateway there is a railroad to Berlin. From

Berlin as a center, travelers and goods can reach all important points in northern Germany and the other countries bordering the 

North and Baltic seas.

The southeastern part of the plateau is drained across the Moravian Heights by tributaries of the Morava River. The valley of one of these tributaries is the route of a railroad from Prague to Vienna. Another railroad line connecting these two cities crosses the highlands a little farther west.

Agriculture in the Plateau. - A large part of Bohemia has good soils. This is especially true of the river valleys. Wheat, rye, barley (A), and oats are raised. Potatoes and sugar beets are very important crops, and Czechoslovakia, like Germany, manufactures and exports much beet sugar.

Cattle and hogs are raised, but most of the milk and meat are used in the country itself. 

As a whole the climate of the country is continental. For the rainfall, study the maps on page 79. 

Manufactures of Bohemia. There is coal and iron ore in various parts of the plateau. 

Some of the better coal is exported, but much of it is the brown coal known as lignite.

The forests furnish the raw material for large wood-pulp and paper industries, and for the manufacture of furniture and toys.

Cereals, potatoes, sugar beets, and other crops are raised on the fertile plains along the

Slovakia. - East of Moravia is the part of Czechoslovakia known as Slovakia. Most of it is a region of mountains the southern slopes of the Carpathians. Small parts in the south are plains like those of Hungary. 

These plains and the mountain valleys are the chief farm lands of the country. 

Prague is one of the old cities of Europe, and it has had a long and interesting history. 

Travelers enjoy its quaint and crooked streets, the fine and noble old buildings, its monuments and other memorials of its past. 

Under Austrian rule it lost much of its importance and influence, but is now regaining them, since it has become the capital of an independent country.

Transportation and Trade. - Czechoslo vakia is an inland country with no seaport of its own. Yet it is able to reach the sea over three internationalized rivers - the Elbe, the Oder, and the Danube — and it is fairly well equipped with railroads (pages 112-113). Its trade is largely with European countries, but some of its manufactures are shipped to our country, and it gets raw materials for its industries both from our country and from other distant lands.

Pronunciations. 

Most of the people of Slovakia are peasants who plant and harvest their crops in the same way as their ancestors did before them. 

They have never had much education, and they know little or nothing about scientific farming. Their farms therefore produce less than the better-farmed lands of France and Germany, and less than the farms of Bohemia and Moravia. The Slovaks are just as willing to work hard as the Czechs are, but the Czechs are better educated and have become skillful workers in mills and factories, and so work more intelligently. 

There are many forested mountain slopes, these three terms to indicate the main sources of and some lumbering is carried on, but the Slovaks have made much less use of their Then place the name of each product of the counforest resources than the Czechs have. 

There are mineral deposits in various parts of Slovakia. A small but increasing amount of iron ore is mined.

An Old City. - Prague (Praha), the cap ital and the largest city of Czechoslovakia, is on the Moldau River, a tributary of the Elbe. It is in the center of the busy industrial regions of Bohemia, and is the chief railroad center of the country. It manufactures machinery, textiles, and chemicals. A water route by way of the Elbe connects it with Hamburg, through which it imports raw materials for Czechoslovak factories and ships their products. Prague has become a great trade center, although it is not easily reached from all parts of the country.

THE MEDITERRANEAN SEA AND SURROUNDING LANDS 

The map on pages 162-163 shows the 

Mediterranean Sea and parts of southern 

Europe, western Asia, and northern Africa.

This great sea is about 2300 miles long. 

It varies greatly in width; from Marseille in southern France to the coast of Africa the distance is about 450 miles.

The Inclosing Highlands. In southern 

Europe, western Asia, and northwestern

Africa there are narrow lowlands along much of the coast. Back of most of these there are highlands, some of which also extend to the sea. The Iberian Peninsula (map, page 

74) is a plateau bordered and crossed by mountain ranges. It is cut off from France by the Pyrenees (A).

East of the Pyrenees, beyond the Rhone Valley, are the Alps. From them a range of mountains, the Apennines, runs southeast through the length of the Italian Peninsula. Measure that length on the map. 

You should find it to be about 600 miles. 

You will have a better idea of these distances if you will measure them on some part of the map of our own country. For example, the length of the Mediterranean measured from New York City across the United States toward the Pacific Ocean will reach almost to the western boundary of 

Nevada. The width from Marseille to

Africa is about equal to the distance between In the toe of this boot-shaped peninsula, the the northern boundary of New York state and the southern boundary of Delaware. range turns toward the west. It appears in the island of Sicily and in northwest Africa. 1 164

MEDITERRANEAN LANDS 

165 In Africa it is called the Atlas Mountains, and continues to the Atlantic Ocean. A northern part of the Atlas Mountains bends toward the Strait of Gibraltar. The range turns eastward again in southern Spain, where it has been given the name of the Sierra Nevada.

Trace these mountains on the map as they have been described. You will notice that they nearly surround the western part of the Mediterranean basin. 

East of Italy is the Balkan Peninsula.

It is separated from Italy by the waters of the Adriatic and Ionian seas. Its mountains are a part of the Alps that have turned southward. In the west they are called the 

Dinaric Alps. In the east they are the southward continuation of the Carpathian Mountains and the Transylvanian Alps. 

The several parts of these mountains have been given separate names. 

Find the Aegean Sea and the Black Sea.

Notice that these two bodies of water are connected by a long strait of varying width. 

Its several parts have been given the names of the Dardanelles, the Sea of Marmara, and the Bosporus. The boundary between 

Asia and Europe follows these waters. 

South of the Black Sea, and north of the eastern end of the Mediterranean, is the peninsula of Asia Minor, also called Anatolia.

It is a highland that is partly plateau, and partly rugged mountains. At the eastern end 

At the eastern end of the Mediterranean find Syria and Palestine.

Notice that here also the highlands are close to the shore. It is only in southern Palestine, northern Egypt, and westward along the coast as far as Tunisia that there are no mountains near the coast. 

Look again at the map, pages 162-163, and notice the many peninsulas and islands of the Mediterranean. Remember that the 

Remember that the only ships of ancient and early modern times were small vessels, propelled by oarsmen or by sails, and suitable only for short voyages, such as can be made easily from one Mediterranean port to another. Sicily, near the 

Sicily, near the center of the Mediterranean, was more important in the commerce of early days than in that of today, largely because its harbors were convenient places for breaking long voyages into short ones. 

Mediterranean Rivers. So much of the

Mediterranean region is bordered by mountains that most of the rivers that flow into it are short. They offer no good navigable waterways into the interior of the continents. 

The Rhone in France and the Nile in Egypt are much longer than the other rivers, but their delta mouths are blocked by silt brought down by the rivers to the sea. In England, as you have learned, the rise and fall of the tides acts to scour out the river mouths, but the tides of the Mediterranean are not high enough to do this. Even the Po River in northern Italy has a delta at its mouth.

Inland from their deltas the Rhone and the Nile are navigable for parts of their lengths, and the river valleys furnish natural routes of travel that have been used for centuries. 

The Rhone route leads across France into northern Europe and to the British Isles.

The Nile Valley forms a part of a great route from Cairo to Cape Town at the southern end of Africa. areas. 

Mediterranean Climate. You know that the mountain wall of southern Europe cuts the continent into two unequal parts. 

The northern and larger part is a region of plains, with some plateau and mountain On the west the plains are open to the winds from the Atlantic. Near the ocean the climate is oceanic. Toward the east it grows gradually more and more continental. 

The climate of the Mediterranean lands is neither oceanic nor continental. They have hot, dry summers and mild, rainy winters. 

Regions that have such a climate are said to have a "Mediterranean climate."

You will remember that the areas of calms and winds on the earth's surface move north and south with the changing seasons. In the Northern Hemisphere the calms of the

EUROPE 

horse latitudes are farthest north in the summer. At that time the prevailing westerlies in Europe are north of the east-and-west mountains. The trade winds are blowing southward toward the equatorial calms, and rain falls only on higher and cooler lands. 

In the winter the horse latitudes are farthest south. The westerlies blow over the Mediterranean, and there is rain over the lands that they cross.

Climate of Corresponding Latitudes in North America. - The shape of the Mediter ranean Sea is irregular. The northernmost point, about 46° north latitude, is at the head of the Adriatic Sea. Its southernmost point, about 31° north latitude, is on the Gulf of Sidra, where it most deeply indents the North 

African coast.

The latitude of two of the Mediterranean cities will also help you to fix its boundaries in mind. Marseille, in France, is about 43° north latitude, and Cairo, in Egypt, a short distance up the Nile from the sea, is about 

30° north latitude. Corresponding latitudes on the west coast of North America include all of the coast of California and part of lower California, and on the east coast they extend from Boston to St. Augustine. In North

America the only region that has a Mediterranean climate is southern California. On the east coast the climate shows a greater range of temperature and a different seasonal distribution of rainfall. 

Influence of Climate on Agriculture and 

Grazing. In those parts of the Mediterranean border lands that have the true Mediterranean climate, the cereals, vegetables, and fruits raised are those that can best be grown under such conditions. The chief cereals raised are wheat and barley. They are planted in the fall, get their growth during the period of winter rains, and are harvested during the sunny days of late spring. 

Quick-growing vegetables are planted while the ground is wet with winter rains, and can be gathered before midsummer.

It is fortunate for the people of this region that at all times during the year it is warm enough so that subtropical fruits can be grown. These include olives, figs, grapes, oranges, and lemons. Olive, date, and fig trees, and grapevines can thrive and mature their crops with the moisture that soaks deep in the ground during the winter rains. 

The orange and lemon groves, however, must be irrigated.

The olives are used largely in the manufacture of olive oil. Much of the oil is used by the people of this region in place of butter. 

The grapes are used in making wine, which the Mediterranean people drink with their meals. Enough olive oil and enough wine are made so that there is a surplus for export. 

Dried grapes are exported also, as raisins and as currants. Other exports are dried figs, and such nuts as almonds and chestnuts. 

Farms are small and much of the work is done by hand. Only the simplest of tools are used. The spade, the hoe, and small plows are used here instead of the powerdriven machinery that is so common in the farming regions of our own country. 

On some of the broader plains in the Mediterranean region there is considerable rain in the summer half of the year as well as in the winter half. Such plains are found in the southern part of the Rhone Valley, along the Po River in northern Italy, in Yugoslavia, and in Rumania. These are better farm lands and the crops are larger than in most of the region of the true Mediterranean 

Most

On the hillsides and lower mountain slopes, terraces have been built where crops can be grown, but the rougher and steeper lands of the mountains are used as pastures. of these pasture lands are too rough and steep for crops, and have only a scanty growth of poor grass. Cattle and horses usually cannot find food enough, and sheep, goats, and donkeys are raised instead. On some farms oxen take the place of horses,

167 and camels from the desert are used in North Africa. It must not be supposed, however, that there are no cattle in these lands. In the Po 

Valley there are many cattle, but their number cannot compare with those raised in the countries of northern Europe. In most Mediterranean countries where they are found, they are used chiefly as draft animals. In the drier parts of 

Spain and Asia Minor, the chief business of the people is the raising of sheep and goats.

Forests and the Lumber and

Fuel Supply. In regions of scanty rainfall with long dry spells, trees grow slowly, even when the temperature is favorable. Many, many years ago the forests of most A. of the Mediterranean region were cut down to be used as fuel, in shipbuilding, and for other purposes. They have never grown up again. This is largely due to three reasons: (1) the surface soil was washed away; (2) no young trees were planted to take the place of the trees cut down, as is done in Germany (page 144) and in other lands where forests are carefully cared for; and (3) grazing sheep and goats eat any tender young shrubs and trees before they get a chance to grow. In much of this region, lumber must be imported, so most of the houses are built of stone. There is so little fuel that most of the poorer people get along with only enough to cook their food. The cork trees and olive trees (A), both of which can thrive in regions of scanty rainfall, have been carefully kept and cared for, because of the valuable products that they yield. 

Minerals and Native Manufactures. - 

In Spain, Algeria, and Tunisia there are valuable deposits of iron ore, but as there is little good coal for smelting, most of the iron ore is exported. Sulphur, phosphate rock, and fine marble are found, and some of all these are exported. You will learn more about the mineral resources of this region as you study the different countries. 

Some manufacturing is carried on in mills and factories in a few of the larger cities. 

These are the products of modern industrial methods. Among the native manufactures, however, are leather goods, and the weaving of tapestries and rugs. For some of these, different parts of the region have become famous. 

Fisheries of the Mediterranean. Fish caught in Mediterranean waters furnish an important part of the food supply of some of the people of this region. Large quantities of tunnies and sardines are taken, and some of them are canned and exported. To replace the high-priced fish that are exported, cheaper dried and salted codfish are imported from Newfoundland and Norway. There are sponge fisheries along the shores of Greece and Libya. There are many little villages along the shores of the Mediterranean from which small fishing fleets go out almost daily, to fish in neighboring waters.
