Mediterranean People of Long Ago. 

For many centuries the Mediterranean Sea was the center of the civilized world. The people along its borders were more or less separated from each other so that each group was able to do what it wished. The mountains that rose behind them shut out, for a time at least, the uncultured and unfriendly races from the interior of the continents. 

One group after another rose to power. 

The earliest of these were at the eastern end of the sea. Each group in its turn built great cities and temples, developed their arts, cultivated their fields, tended their flocks, and carried on wars. Each in turn was conquered and passed away. From among those who lived at the eastern end of the Mediterranean there was one group, of which history tells us, that we know as the Phoenicians. They lived on the coast of 

Syria and became the great traders of their time.

In the early development of their trade the Phoenicians at first followed the Mediterranean coast. Growing bolder, they sailed from headland to headland, and from island to island. In the course of time they learned to know about the peoples and resources of the islands and all the coast lands of the Mediterranean. 

The Phoenicians founded many settlements, including a number along the north coast of Africa. One of these was Carthage, which grew to be a large city and became Ruins of this city may be seen today (169 A), powerful when Phoenicia began to decline. not far from the modern city of Tunis.

It is known that Phoenician traders passed through the Strait of Gibraltar into the Atlantic Ocean. They founded the city of 

Gades (now Cádiz) in southwestern Spain.. and grew rich from their trade with that part of the Iberian Peninsula. They also obtained tin from the mines in northwest Spain and from the Scilly Islands off the southwest coast of England.

Some of the goods that Phoenician merchants collected and redistributed among those with whom they traded were gold, spices, sandalwood, incense, and perfumes from the East; ivory from Africa; and amber from the shores of the Baltic Sea. It is probable that before these articles reached them they passed through many hands. 

Copper from Cyprus and tin from the mines in Spain and the Scilly Islands they mixed to form the metal we call bronze. Other metals that they are known to have had are gold, silver, and iron. 

Historians tell us that the Phoenician artists were as skillful as their sailors were courageous. They made purple dyes, manufactured cloth and embroidery, and worked

MEDITERRANEAN LANDS 

169 

A. Ruins of a stadium in ancient Carthage. Many athletic contests were held in this structure. in gold, silver, copper, tin, bronze, and iron. 

They were also glassmakers and makers of pottery, but it is probable that they learned all of these industries from others. They used an alphabet of twenty-two letters, which was copied, with some changes, by all the peoples of Europe, one after another.

The trade and power of Phoenicia con tinued for a long time but finally declined, and other countries rose to take its place. 

The Greek and Roman Period. When new conditions along the shores of the Mediterranean brought about a decline in the power of Phoenicia, that of the Greek city-states was the first to profit from the change. The coast of Greece is much indented by the sea and there are many offshore islands in the Aegean. It was natural, therefore, that the Greeks should become seamen and colonizers. Greek settlements were made on many islands and along the Mediterranean coasts, and, for a time, they held control of trade and many of the trade routes of their day. They were not merely seamen and traders, however. They had worked out an excellent system of government. Their public men were orators and writers, and they were lovers of beauty. 

They showed their love of the beautiful in their public buildings, in their sculpture, and in the planning of their cities. Most of the great buildings of their days of power are now in ruins, and most of their statues and other sculptures have been broken.

Enough of each has been preserved, however, so that even today we may have some appreciation of their beauty. mans.

Greece was finally conquered by the Ro- 

Roman armies also conquered Carthage, took over its trade, and destroyed the city. Soon the whole of the Mediterranean world bowed to the power of Rome,

EUROPE 

and later their armies invaded the countries that we know as France and Great Britain. In many parts of the Roman 

Empire the remains of Roman works can still be seen roads, bridges, aqueducts, temples, and other structures. For years the Romans fought with the wild tribes in the forest regions of northern Europe and kept them from invading Roman lands. At last, however, these barbarians of the north forced their way through Alpine passes, and the 

Roman Empire fell.

Trade During the Middle Ages and Later. 

During the Middle Ages two cities of northern Italy became centers of trade. These were Venice and Genoa. Each in its turn carried on trade with the Far East and distributed the products of the East among the people of Europe. At the eastern end of the Mediterranean, the Turks partly blocked the trade routes, and the western world began to search for a new route to Asia. 

A few people began to believe that the earth | is round. Columbus discovered the New 

World, Magellan headed an expedition that sailed round the world, and Vasco da Gama rounded the southern point of Africa into the Indian Ocean.

As knowledge of the world grew, the interests of men and nations were drawn away from the Mediterranean, and its importance declined. The seaports on the Mediterranean peninsulas do not have near them any large areas where many goods are produced and consumed. In recent times, as we shall see, the Mediterranean became again an important trade route; but it will never again be thought of as the center of the world.

In 1869 the canal across the Isthmus of Suez was opened, connecting the Mediterranean 

Sea with the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean. 

Since that time ships from Mediterranean ports engaged in trade with the Far East have had a choice of routes. Three of these are by way of the Strait of Gibraltar. One is around the southern part of Africa, a second is around South America or through the Strait of Magellan, and a third, available only since 1914, is by way of the Panama Canal. 

A fourth route is by way of the Suez Canal and is much shorter than any of the others to most of the Far East ports. The Suez route is used also by ships from most north European ports and from some others on the 

Atlantic. The Mediterranean Sea has be come a great highway for the world's shipping.

Highway. You will remember that Great

Britain has lands under its control in many parts of the world (page 83). This fact has led to a vast amount of commerce between the home country and its foreign possessions. 

There is also much British commerce with other parts of the world, beyond the limits of the empire. To protect its shipping and its foreign possessions, Great Britain has a large navy. It has established stations where coal or oil can be purchased for refueling ships, at many ports both on continents and on islands of the sea. 

When you think of all these things, you will understand why Great Britain is interested in keeping the seaways of the world open. It is particularly interested in the Gibraltar-Mediterranean-Suez route.

This canal, which is a little over a hundred miles in length, has no locks. The part of the isthmus across which it was cut is in

About as much freight is carried through one canal as through the other. 

Mediterranean Trade of Today. A large trade with the East is carried on through the port of Marseille in southern France (page 132). Some of the finest modern ocean liners, as well as many freight steamers, have their home ports in Italy, France, and 

Spain. The Mediterranean is a highway, therefore, for three kinds of commerce: (1) trade that uses it only as a through route, (2) trade between ports on the Mediterranean and ports outside the Mediterranean, and (3) trade between Mediterranean ports.

- The Alhambra on the hill at Granada, Spain, is one of the most interesting buildings in the world. You will enjoy reading Washington Irving's stories about the Moors and Spaniards, in the book called The Alhambra. 

You have studied the Mediterranean region as a whole. You have learned about the size and location of the Mediterranean Sea, about its long history as the former center of world trade, and about its importance as a trade route today. You have found that the countries bordering the Mediterranean are not alike. Their people speak different languages, and there are differences in resources and industries, as you will see in studying the countries one by one. 

The Iberian Peninsula. At the western end of the Mediterranean, and between it and the Atlantic Ocean, is the Iberian Peninsula.

This peninsula, about equal to France in size, is divided between two countries, Spain and 

Portugal, both of them republics.

The peninsula is separated from France by the high wall of the Pyrenees Mountains, and from North Africa by the Strait of Gibraltar.

A very large part of the peninsula is a plateau with an average elevation of more than 2000 feet, and with some areas of much greater height. Towering above the general level of the plateau are many mountain ranges, most of which have an east-west direction (map, page 162).

On much of the east and southeast coast, from France to the Strait of Gibraltar, the edge of the plateau or the bordering mountains come close to the sea. The lowlands along this stretch of the coast are generally narrow, although they widen around Valencia and around Murcia and Cartagena. 

West of the Strait of Gibraltar and in 

Portugal the coastal lowlands are broader than those bordering the Mediterranean.

Along the northern coast of Spain the lowlands are narrow and are backed by hill lands that rise quickly to the foothills of the 

Cantabrian Mountains. The only other lowlands of the peninsula are found along

the valleys of the larger rivers. Two of the largest are along the Ebro and the Guadalquivir (map, page 162). 

Climate. Find Madrid, the capital of

Spain, on the map. It is in the central part of the country, a little to the north of 40° north latitude. This is almost the latitude of 

New York City. Using the maps needed, compare the latitude of Lisbon, the capital of Portugal, with that of San Francisco.

These latitudes show that the Iberian Peninsula lies in the track of the prevailing westerly winds. Blowing in from the Atlantic Ocean, these winds bring heavy rains to the Atlantic coast of the peninsula, especially in the northwest. Along the coast and among the lower hills the summers are mild and the winters cool. Snow and rain fall on the higher mountains, but much of the central part of the peninsula has little rain, with a continental climate of hot summers and cold winters. 

This is because the moisture-bearing winds from the Atlantic are largely shut out from the interior by the mountains or the steep margin of the plateau.

The Mediterranean coast lands are warm and sunny, and have little rain. The mountains and plateau protect them from the cold winds from the north and west. 

Agriculture. The chief industries of the 

Iberian Peninsula are agriculture and grazing.

On the plateau most of the rain comes in the winter. The cereal crops best suited to the cool temperature and light rainfall of much of the plateau are wheat, oats, and barley.

The same crops are raised in the rainier region of the northwest, as are also corn, rye, and some potatoes. In that region, too, there are many apple orchards.

The wheat crop of the plateau is winter wheat, which can be grown during the rainier season and harvested during the dry season of spring or early summer. On much of the plateau, crops must be raised by dry-farming methods. The land is plowed and cultivated several times, but is planted only every other year, as the rainfall of two years is needed for the growth of one crop. 

Some small parts of the plateau are irrigated, where water from the melting mountain snows can be used. Most of the larger streams flow for much of their length at the bottom of deep gorges and furnish irrigation water for fields in their valleys only. 

Grapes. Vineyards are found in many parts of both Spain and Portugal (map, page 128). As you will see, grapes are grown in many parts of the plateau, but the regions of especially heavy production are near 

Barcelona and in northwestern Portugal.

Many of the vineyards are on the terraced slopes of hills that get the sunshine, and very few of them are irrigated. Most of the grapes are used in making wine, but some are dried as raisins, and special varieties are packed in barrels with ground cork, and shipped fresh to American and north European markets. 

A thick red wine of Portugal known as port "wine is a favorite in England, and large quantities are sent to that country from the city of Oporto. A famous Spanish wine called "sherry" is made from grapes grown around Jerez, not far from Cádiz. 

Olives. - Olive trees, some of them of great age, may be seen in different parts of the peninsula (A), but chiefly in the southern part of Spain. They can stand long, dry summers and are therefore found growing in semi-arid regions. Spain produces more olives than any other country. Large quantities of green olives and some ripe olives are pickled and put up in casks for export. 35 30° 5°

Most of the ripe olives, however, are crushed for the oil that they contain. This oil when properly prepared is used by the people as a substitute for butter or lard, and much is exported. 

Other Products. On the sunny lowlands of southern and eastern Spain, especially around Valencia and Murcia, subtropical fruits and nuts are grown. These include oranges, lemons, bananas, and almonds. In a few small regions of high winter temperature, dates will ripen. Cotton and sugar cane also are grown where the temperature is favorable. All of these orchards and crops require irrigation. The irrigated districts are increasing in size.

In general the agricultural methods in use in Spain are very old-fashioned and the industry is in the hands of poorly educated people. The present government is doing what it can to help the farmers by spreading knowledge as to better methods and modern tools.

Grazing and the Animal Industries. - 

About half of the plateau area is used as pasture land. Spain has long been famous for its merino sheep and their fine wool. 

Much of its area furnishes poor pasturage at best, and from many sections the sheep are sent into the mountains for summer grazing. 

This makes it possible to save the plateau pastures for winter use. The fleeces of merino sheep grow heavy, largely because of the cold which these animals must endure during the winter and at night. 

Other animals raised include goats, cattle, and hogs. There are few horses, as the hardier mules and donkeys (B) take the place of the horse and are found in all parts of the peninsula. Mineral Resources and Industries. - Ever 

- Ever be bridged. since the time of the Phoenicians (page 168) the Iberian Peninsula has been looked upon as a land rich in minerals. In the northern part of Spain, not far from Bilbao, large deposits of high-grade iron ore have been mined for many years. The best of these are said to have been nearly used up. For a long time much of the iron ore mined was exported to England. Even today half of what is mined is exported, although blast furnaces have been built at Bilbao and at Santander. 

Other iron ore deposits are found farther west along the Cantabrian Mountains, and in the south not far from Málaga. 

Near the deposits of iron ore are the chief coal deposits of the peninsula, but Spain's total coal supply is much less than that of our own country, or of Canada, or of Great Britain, or of Germany. Some coal and some iron and steel goods are imported, showing that the output of the coal mines and the steel mills is not enough to meet the needs of the country.

For many centuries a large part of the world's supply of mercury, or quicksilver, has come from the mines at Almaden in the south-central part of Spain. Lead, copper, and zinc are all found in southern Spain. 

The zinc comes from a region near Murcia. 

Zinc is found also in the north near Santander. 

Fishing. - Fishing is carried on off the coasts of both Spain and Portugal. The chief fishing grounds are near the northwest and southwest points of the peninsula. Most of the fish taken are either sardines or tunnies. 

Railroads, Highways, and Air Routes. 

The Iberian Peninsula has very few railroads for its size. This is because there are not enough passengers or enough freight to pay for the expense of building and operating The peninsula also has few good roads for its size. The government is helping to rebuild the railroads and to repair the highways and build others. There are some fine motor roads, but ox-carts, loaded donkeys, and mule-drawn vehicles are much more common than motor cars or trucks on the highways of Spain. The map on page 133 shows that airplane routes keep the chief cities of both Spain and Portugal in touch with the rest of Europe. There are also wellequipped and well-managed Spanish steamship lines carrying transatlantic passengers and freight.

The People of Spain and Portugal. - The two countries of Spain and Portugal are separated from each other partly by the gorges of three rivers. But these gorges are no deeper and no broader than those that separate parts of Spain or parts of Portugal from each other. Not only are the products and industries of the two countries much alike, but so are the people. They may be divided into two groups: the so-called gentleman" class, and the laboring class. 

The "gentleman or upper class is largely made up of those who have been educated for a profession such as law or medicine, members of the government, and those who have property but no profession and live in idleness and luxury. Through the centuries most of the people belonging to this class have lived upon the work of others. They are gay and pleasure-loving. They have never developed or managed great industries. Many of their largest industries have been developed under managers who came from other countries, particularly from Great Britain and France. 

The people of the laboring class are for the most part poor and ignorant. Most of them know nothing about modern tools or modern methods of work. They are found as workers in the mines, as shepherds in charge of flocks, as farm managers and workers, as laborers in vineyards and orchards. In the cities you find them as porters and servants, and as workers in factories or small business places. 

Under such conditions it is natural for laborers to be restless and unhappy. 

When Spain and Portugal became republics the new governments hoped to improve conditions in their countries. But a civil war began in Spain in 1936 due to a rebellion against the new government. It took the form of a struggle between those who wanted to retain the government they had and those who wanted a government more like that of Italy or Germany. During this civil war there was an enormous loss of life and destruction of property. 

Cities. Because of the barren and semiarid conditions of much of the plateau, most of the people of the peninsula live near its shores. Madrid, however, the capital of 

Spain and a very large city, is in the center of the country. Chiefly because it is the capital it has become an important railroad and commercial center. It is a very beautiful city, with fine buildings and open squares, or plazas, that have been carefully laid out with beds of flowers and fine trees. Here also the visitor will find art galleries, museums, and several large educational institutions. 

Another city of central Spain is Toledo.

This is one of the oldest of Spanish cities, with dark, narrow, winding streets through which few vehicles can make their way. It was a Moorish stronghold and famous for its manufacture of fine swords - an industry that is still carried on. 

Most of the other large cities of Spain and 

Portugal are seaports. Let us visit them, one by one, on a voyage around the peninsula, beginning at the northeast.

Barcelona is the largest city in Spain, its chief seaport, and its greatest industrial center. There are mills for the manufacture of cotton, woolen, silk, and linen goods, for which most of the raw materials are imported. For which two of them does

Olives, olive oil, and wines are exported.

Valencia and Murcia are trade centers for the surrounding regions. Each city has silk mills using the raw silk produced near by. 

Most of the Spanish oranges and some other subtropical fruits and nuts sent to north European markets are shipped from the port of Valencia.

History. The history of Spain and 

Portugal is closely tied up with the development of the Mediterranean region, and with the discovery and settlement of the New World. Through explorations and settlements both countries built up great colonial empires that have since been largely lost. 

Before considering the remnants of these great empires still belonging to these countries, let us review some important points in

Spanish and Portuguese history. 

For many centuries the Iberian Peninsula was in the path of world trade, and was partly or wholly under the control of alien peoples,

one after another Phoenicians, Greeks, Carthaginians, and Romans (pages 168-170).

The Romans especially, for several hundred years, got a large supply of minerals and grains from this part of their empire. 

Roman power was broken by invaders from north of the Pyrenees, and for a time there was no orderly government. Later the 

Moors from northwest Africa conquered the land and ruled it for a time, making Granada their capital; but they were at last driven out. During their period of control they built roads, irrigation systems, and some very wonderful buildings, the remains of which may still be seen in Córdoba and Granada.

MOZAMBIQUE 

Perhaps the most famous of all the Moorish buildings is the Alhambra at Granada (172 A).

It was a fortress and the palace of the Moorish rulers. Very forbidding on the outside, A.-Spanish, Portuguese, and Italian possessions in it was a marvel of beauty within. Sadly marred as it has been by time, by the hand of man, and by earthquake, it is still lovely. 

There are courts with fountains and delicately colored tile floors and walls. Around some of these are balconies carried on slender marble columns. There are examples of fine wood carving which represent the patient labor as well as the great skill of fine artists. There are noble rooms with floors and walls of artistic colored tile, and inlaid ceilings of breath-taking beauty. 

Following the expulsion of the Moors came the age of discovery. As you know,

Christopher Columbus was in the service of Spain when he made his voyages to the New 

World. About the same time Portugal sent expeditions around Africa under the command of da Gama and Cabral. Magellan, another Portuguese who was at the time in the service of Spain, was (until his death in the Philippines) in command of the first expedition to sail around the world. 

Outlying Possessions. Based upon the discoveries of these and later expeditions, Spain and Portugal laid claim to many lands. 

Spain secured possession of large parts of 

North America, South America, and the 

West Indies; the Philippine Islands; and some small parts of Africa. The Portuguese possessions included Brazil, where the Portuguese language is still spoken; parts of 

Africa; and parts of Asia - particularly in India.

With the increase of population and the development of the natural wealth of the 

Spanish and Portuguese colonies, most of them have secured their independence or fallen into more powerful hands. The map on this page shows most of the lands outside of the Iberian Peninsula that still belong to Spain and Portugal. 

The Balearic Islands off the east coast of

Spain in the Mediterranean Sea are a part of that country. They have a Mediterranean climate and such products as wines, olive oil, fruits, and almonds. 

On the African mainland point out three areas belonging to Spain (A). One of these is Spanish Morocco, where grapes, cork, decorated leather goods, and tiles are produced.

A second, Rio de Oro, is at present valuable chiefly for its fisheries; other resources are as yet undeveloped. A third is the small area called Spanish Guinea on the coast of the Gulf of Guinea. It is a hot, rainy, denselyforested region from which small quantities of palm nuts, rubber, sugar, and cacao are obtained. 

The Canary Islands, off the northwestern coast of Africa, are probably the most valuable of the Spanish outlying possessions. 

They have a mild climate, and raise vegetables and fruits for European markets. On these islands, too, there are refueling and cable stations. Fernando Po and a few other less important islands also belong to Spain.

The Portuguese possessions are far more extensive than those of Spain. They include several islands and island groups, among them the Azores, the Madeira Islands, the Cape 

Verde Islands, and St. Thomas Island. Find them on the map. The Azores and the Madeira Islands (A) are sometimes visited by transatlantic and cruising steamers, and have refueling and cable stations. Fruits and vegetables are raised there. The Cape Verde 

Islands were discovered by the early Portuguese navigators when they were sailing south along the coast of Africa in their search for a route to the Indies. The island of St. 

Thomas produces a very large amount of cacao, and is an important source of supply for the chocolate industries of the world. 

The Portuguese colonies on the mainland of Africa include Portuguese Guinea, Angola, and Mozambique. Find them on the map.

The Guinea region is forested along the coast and grassland in the interior. Among its products are palm nuts and palm oil and hides from native cattle.

In Angola the coastal region is dry, and crops can be raised only where irrigation is possible. Some cotton and some sugar cane are raised, but farming is not extensive and the industry furnishes little for export. 

In the rainier sections farther north, however, there are coffee plantations from which a little coffee is exported. Many hides are exported from the cattle-raising regions on the savannas in the interior of the country. 

These hides go to our own country and to European countries, where they are tanned and used in the manufacture of a variety of leather goods.

Much of it is grassland where cattle could be raised, but the whole of the country awaits development.

ITALY 

The kingdom of Italy (map, pages 162-163) occupies the central one of the three great peninsulas of southern Europe that border or extend into the Mediterranean Sea; and also some islands near by. It is less than half as large as the Iberian Peninsula, but it has nearly one and a half times as many people. 

How has it been possible for Italy to support so large a population? Why have many 

Italians looked for homes in other lands? 

Surface. In shape, and in the division into highlands and lowlands, Italy is in sharp contrast with the Iberian Peninsula. The 

Italian Peninsula is long and narrow and shaped like a high-heeled boot with a wide, flaring top. The Iberian Peninsula is a compact land mass, roughly square, measuring about the same in average distance east and west as in average distance north and south. 

In Italy there is no great plateau. In the northwestern part of the country the Alps bend to the south and join the Apennines. 

The Apennines extend the whole length of the peninsula, and into the toe of the boot. The 

Iberian Peninsula is very largely a great plateau, although high mountains cross the plateau and border it on the north and south. 

In parts of Italy the mountains and hilly uplands occupy nearly its entire width. 

There are small lowlands along the Italian coasts, as there are along the coasts of Spain and Portugal, and in both peninsulas there are small lowlands along some of the rivers. 

But there is one great lowland in Italy with which Spain and Portugal have nothing to compare. It is the broad and fertile lowland drained by the Po, the largest river in Italy. It This lowland region of northern Italy was once a gulf opening into the Adriatic Sea. was filled by rock waste from the Alps and the Apennines, brought down by mountain streams which now make up the Po river system. Position. Italy's central position in the 

Mediterranean region is of great importance both to Italy and to much of Europe, for several reasons: (1) It gives Italy an advantage in trade with other Mediterranean lands. (2) Some of the European countries without a seacoast also find it to their advantage to carry on their trade with countries beyond the seas through Italian ports and by Italian ships. (3) Most of the steamers going to the

Far East from north European ports use the 

Mediterranean - Red Sea route. Mail and valuable goods that must be sent through as quickly as possible, and passengers who wish to shorten their time at sea, may be put on or taken off steamers at the Italian port of Brindisi. A passenger, for example, may leave

London several days after a steamer has sailed from Southampton, and fly to Brindisi in time to catch it. By allowing a somewhat longer time, he can travel by railroad and still have many hours at home after the sailing of the ship. 

Volcanoes and Volcanic Soils. On the map of Italy find the city of Naples. A few miles from this city is the active volcano Mt. 

Vesuvius (A). It has the shape of a cone with a hollow, or crater, at the top instead of a peak. Those who reach the top of the mountain can look down into the central crater and see it partly filled with red-hot, bubbling, molten rock. Clouds of steam that look like smoke can often be seen rising from the crater. 

The melted rock, or lava, sometimes pours over the side of the crater or breaks through it and flows down the mountain side. At times there are explosions in the crater, and clouds of dust and larger pieces of cooled lava are thrown into the air. They darken the sky, and the stones and dust fall on the mountain slopes and build them up.

Lavas break up in time, and with the volcanic dust form fertile soils. Such soils are found in large parts of the Italian Peninsula and the neighboring island of Sicily, where

ITALY 

183 volcanic flows occurred long ago. In such regions there are rich gardens and vineyards, and if there is no explosion or flow of lava for a long time, the farms may extend well up the slopes of a volcanic mountain. Sometimes a town will be partly or wholly destroyed by a volcanic eruption, being covered by rock ashes and perhaps by some lava. The people must then leave to save their lives, but they soon return and build homes again. 

In the year 79 a great eruption of Vesuvius buried the two cities of Herculaneum and

Pompeii, and in time they were forgotten. 

After many centuries, Pompeii and a part of Herculaneum have been uncovered. The volcanic material has been shoveled away, and many buildings that were only partly destroyed have been found, and also many useful and beautiful things such as household utensils, statues, articles of bronze and glass, and even pictures painted on the walls. 

Find the island of Sicily on the map. In 

Sicily is Mt. Etna, another volcano, about two miles high. How many feet is that?

At its foot are palms and lemon trees, on its slopes are oaks and chestnuts, higher up are evergreen trees, and around the top is snow all the year. Sometimes an eruption melts the snow, and lava flows down the slopes toward the towns and cities around the mountain. 

But as soon as the eruption is over, snow begins to gather again around the mountain top. 

A valuable product of volcanoes and volcanic rocks is sulphur, large quantities of which are found in Sicily. In the Mediterranean, not far from Sicily, is Stromboli, an island volcano that is always sending out steam and other gases. occur.

In southern Italy earthquakes sometimes In a severe earthquake the ground shakes enough to destroy buildings; cracks are opened in the earth's surface; and many lives are lost. 

Climate. Italy is as far north as our northern states, and yet it has a mild climate because it is protected by the high mountains on its northern boundary. Comparing the latitude of Rome with that of New York 

City, you see that Rome is a little farther north. Using the map on. pages 162-163, find the length of Italy in degrees of latitude, and in miles. How does it compare with the 

Iberian Peninsula? 

In the south of Italy the temperature is so warm at all times during the year that many tropical fruits and palm trees will grow there. 

The basin of the Po in the northern part of Italy is so well protected from cold north winds by the Alps that its summer season is warm. In the winter the temperature is usually mild, but snow sometimes falls. The shores of the peninsula and the islands are washed by the warm waters of the Mediterranean, and winds from these waters blow inland. Except in the higher mountains, frost is seldom seen.

The climate of the coast lands is Mediterranean, which means that it is hot in summer and mild in winter, and most of the rain comes in winter. In the summer the peninsula is in the belt of the northeast trades, and has little rain. Sometimes the sirocco, a hot wind from Africa, blows over Italy, but it brings no rain. tion.

As summer is the chief crop-growing season, winter rains do not help much in raising most crops. It is therefore necessary to use irriga- 

In the Po basin there is more rain and it is better distributed during the year. Yet water from the rivers is used to irrigate the fields so that more than one crop a year can be raised.

Italian Farming. The plains of the Po make up the largest area of good farm land in Italy. The soil is rich, level, and well watered. watered. Wheat, corn, and rice are the chief grain crops. Although much wheat is raised, not enough is grown to meet the needs of the people. The poorer people therefore use a great deal of corn, which is eaten as a thick corn-meal mush. Much rice is grown in the 

Po Valley, where the fields can be easily made

A. Gathering oysters off the coast of southern Italy. level and the crops flooded whenever necessary. Italy is the only European country in which much rice is grown. On the rich plains north and south of the Tiber, and around Naples, many vegetables are raised. In irrigated fields, two or more crops a year can be grown. They find a good market in these warm lands, for people in hot countries usually eat more vegetables than meat. 

Flax and hemp are raised for their fibers, which are used in the manufacture of textiles. 

Mulberry trees are grown in many parts of the peninsula, but especially on the plains of the Po. Their leaves are used to feed silkworms, and Italy produces much raw silk. 

You will remember that France imports raw silk from Italy for use in the manufacture of fine silk goods (page 130).

There are about as many grapes grown in Italy as in France (128 C), and much wine is made. Most of it is used by the people of 

Italy, although some is exported. Olive orchards are widely distributed through the peninsula (173 A). You will remember that grapes and olives are two crops that can be grown in regions where the summers are dry. 

They are usually grown without irrigation. 

Chestnuts, walnuts, hazelnuts, and almonds are grown, and some of each are exported. Many chestnuts are eaten in Italy, either boiled or roasted. They and other nuts largely take the place of potatoes, not many of which are raised.

More than half of the Italian people are farmers. In regions where modern machinery cannot be used with profit, much hand work is still done. Every bit of good land, and much poor land, is used. The Italian farmer is not an idler. For centuries the 

Italian people have spent an enormous amount of time and labor in building walls and in terracing mountain slopes. On these terraces, large or small, they have raised grapes, oranges, olives, and other fruits.

The Italian farmers for the most part know their business and work hard at it. In level areas, such as the valley of the Po, where modern machinery can be used, you will find the farmers using it. 

Large white oxen, with long horns, are

ITALY 

185 often seen at work on Italian farms, or drawing carts or wagons in city streets. Donkeys and some small horses also are used on the farms, or for drawing loads. Sheep raising is carried on throughout the peninsula, but is especially important in southern Italy and in the more rugged parts of the rest of the peninsula. 

Dairy cattle are raised, as are also goats, and the milk of both is used in the making of cheese. As in other Mediterranean countries, olive oil is used as a substitute for animal fats. 

Fishing (184 A) is an important source of food for the people, but not enough fish are caught to supply the demand, and many are imported. The chief fish caught are tunnies in the Mediterranean off the west coast of the peninsula, and sardines in the Adriatic.

Manufacturing. -Much of the manufacturing of Italy is based upon the use of raw materials found or raised in the country. 

Italy has very little coal and not much iron ore.

These are two serious handicaps. But hydroelectric plants have been built among the mountains to furnish power. Because of a great increase in manufacturing industries,

Italy has developed and is using far more electric power than Spain.

Among the manufactures based on local supplies of raw material are macaroni and other bread pastes made from wheat flour. 

The flour paste is run through machines which form it into long tubes or strings which are then hung over bars to dry. After they have hardened they can be kept a long time without spoiling.

A. - Central part of Rome, the "Eternal City." This bridge across the Tiber was built by the ancient Romans, but has been repaired in modern times and is still in use. Turn to the map on page 162 and notice several long, narrow lakes that reach from the plains of the Po back into the Italian Alps. 

These lakes are among the most beautiful in the world, and in the grandeur of the surrounding scenery they rival the lakes of Switzerland. Upon their shores cities and towns have been built. On the wooded slopes of the lower hills there are fine homes and lovely shaded walks and drives. From the lakes themselves, and from all about, you can lift your eyes to the higher mountain slopes and sunny skies.

At the mouth of the Po there are marshes, small islands, and lake-like lagoons of salt water, partly shut off from the sea by sand bars. In one of these lagoons the city of 

Venice (Venezia), one of the most picturesque cities in the world, has been built. Canals take the place of the broader streets of other cities, and boats are used instead of automobiles, carriages, or trolley cars. There are narrow winding streets that may be followed on foot, but they are little more than alleyways. There are also many bridges by which the canals can be crossed on foot. In going from place to place by canal you will probably use the picturesque gondola (186 A) which your standing gondolier keeps going by the skillful use of a single oar. If, however, you wish to go more quickly, you will use a launch or motor boat.

The largest of the canals is the Grand Canal, from the sides of which beautiful old palaces seem to rise out of the water. Many of these were built when Venice was the center of trade of the then-known world (page 170). Some of these wonderful homes of an ancient day are still used as they were when they were first built. Others have become hotels, and still others are used for some kind of business. Your gondolier will point out to you the ones where famous people have lived.

The capital of Italy is Rome (Roma) (A). 

Remember that the Roman Empire once included the Mediterranean world and its power extended far beyond the lands that border

MEDITERRANEAN LANDS EUROPE 

that sea.

That was the time of its greatest magnificence. Here may be seen the remains of temples, of memorial arches, and of the Colosseum, where fights between men and wild animals were once held, and where later Christian martyrs were thrown to the lions. 

Near the Colosseum there stood at one time many fine buildings surrounding an open space called the "Roman Forum." Here, in the days of Rome's greatness, statesmen and leaders spoke to the people. Ancient temples and beautiful churches are among the many other interesting buildings and places of historic interest that attract visitors to Rome. 

Some of the buildings erected in recent years are of great interest also.

St. Peter's, the great Roman Catholic church; the Vatican, a group of buildings in which the Pope makes his home; and some adjoining land, make up the Vatican City. Once a part of Rome, it is now an independent state the smallest in the world. 

Within this small area there are buildings to which some of the most celebrated architects, sculptors, and painters have contributed a wealth of beauty. 

Other Cities. Milan (Milano) is on the lowland of northern Italy, and on the route southward from two of the great railroad tunnels through the Alps. It is the most important manufacturing city and trade center of Italy, and its cathedral is one of the most beautiful in Europe. In this city, in the dining room of what was once a monastery, Leonardo da Vinci painted on the wall the well-known picture "The Last Supper." 

West of Milan is Turin (Torino), another manufacturing center. It is connected with 

France by a railroad through another of the great Alpine tunnels.

About midway between Milan and Rome is the city of Florence (Firenze), on the Arno River. Here are wonderful art galleries and a great cathedral with a fine bell tower. In the valley of the Arno the farm lands are among the best of all Italy. 

Naples (Napoli) is one of the large cities of Italy and a very important port. As a result of the development of hydroelectric plants in the near-by Apennines, Naples is also a manufacturing city of increasing importance. It has shipyards, plants for the making of railroad equipment, automobile factories, sugar refineries, and silk, cotton, jute, and woolen mills.

Not far from Naples is the tiny island of Capri. It is the home of many artists and has many caves that open to the sea. One of these is the "Blue Grotto." When the sea is calm enough, visitors are taken into the grotto by boatmen. The waters of the grotto appear a most beautiful blue, and the bodies of boys who dive for pennies look like burnished silver.

There are three ports in northern Italy whose trade is of especial importance to other European countries (page 181). These are 

Trieste, Fiume, and Genoa. Trieste and 

Fiume are at the head of the Adriatic Sea.

Trade with Austria through the Brenner Pass must go through Trieste. Fiume, farther east, is the port used by Hungary.

Genoa (Genova) has a larger commerce than any other Italian city. Goods are landed here not only for the densely populated Po Valley and its cities, but also for shipment to Switzerland and countries north of the Alps. At the time that Venice was at the height of its power, Genoa and Pisa were its chief rivals. With the discovery of the 

New World, all of these cities lost their early importance, but in recent years Genoa has recovered while the other two cities have not. 

Genoa has large shipyards, and manufactures cotton goods, motor cars, and hats. Extending west from Genoa along the coast to the French boundary is the winter-resort region known as the Italian Riviera (189 A).

Like the French Riviera, it has a mild and delightful winter temperature because the mountains at the north protect it from cold winds.

Sicily and Sardinia. - On the map, pages 

162-163, see the position of Sicily, between

North Africa and Italy. In the days when world trade centered upon the Mediterranean this island was important. It was on the route from Rome to Carthage and was visited by the ships trading between the eastern and the western Mediterranean. The small ships of that early day sought the protection of its shores. its shores. It became an important trade center, and many battles were fought for its possession. 

Chestnuts and tropical fruits, especially lemons, are raised in Sicily. For many years sulphur from the mines near the foot of Mt. 

Etna supplied the world market. Sulphur from mines in Texas has now largely taken its place, although Sicily still markets a large amount. Palermo is the chief city and trading center, and exports the products of the island.

Northwest of Sicily, and not far from the French island of Corsica, is the Italian island of Sardinia. Agriculture, stock raising, and

San Marino. In the Apennines, south of the plains of the Po, is the small independent republic of San Marino. It is protected by 

Italy, as Andorra is by Spain and France. 

Where the People of Italy Live. The map on page 81 shows that most of Italy has a dense population but that it is especially dense in northern Italy and in the lowland regions along the coasts. Its population has become so dense that many of the people have sought work or homes in other lands. 

With the improvement of conditions in in Libya and the conquest of Ethiopia many Italians are finding new homes in the lands under Italian control in Africa. A large number of Italians have, in years past, found work and new opportunities in the United 

States, Brazil, and Argentina.

In 1936 Italy annexed Ethiopia and the King of Italy was proclaimed Emperor of Ethiopia.

Italian Islands and Colonies. In the 

Aegean Sea near Asia Minor there are some small islands known as the Dodecanese. 

They belong to Italy although they are inhabited chiefly by Greeks. Farming is the main industry and grapes and vegetables the leading crops. The map on page 178 shows that the area in east central Africa under Italian control has been given the name of Italian Oriental Africa. It includes former Ethiopia and the older Italian colonies of Eritrea and Italian Somaliland.

Among the products of the country is some cultivated coffee and much that grows wild. 

There are also hides and skins, wax, grain, and tobacco. Deposits of iron, gold, coal, copper, salts have been located. There are extensive forests and there are cattle, sheep, goats, horses, donkeys, and mules. To open the country for settlement, the Italians are building an extensive system of roads. They make use, also, of the railroad the French built between Addis Ababa and a French 

Somaliland port on the Gulf of Aden. 

Libya is in northern Africa between Egypt and Tunisia. The interior of the country is a part of the Sahara, but there are oases where excellent dates are grown. Tripoli, on the Mediterranean coast, has an excellent harbor, and is the starting point of caravan routes into the interior. Along the coast where there is a little rainfall, barley, tobacco, and some fruits are raised. Sponges are found in the waters off the Libyan coast. 

Much salt is produced by evaporation of sea water.

GREECE 

The Balkan Peninsula is the easternmost of the three peninsulas of southern Europe. It has a very much indented coast line with many off-shore islands. It is divided into several countries. Of these countries Greece alone is really Mediterranean in character, and the only one you will study at this time. 

It occupies the southern part of the peninsula and is divided into two parts, northern and southern, by the gulfs of Patras and Corinth. 

You have already learned some things about this region and its people. In the early days it was not a single united country under one government. In many small areas separated from each other by mountains small cities or city states grew up. Each of these areas faced toward the sea. Off-shore islands could be seen, and beyond them there were other islands. The Greeks built boats, became sailors, and engaged in trade. Many 

Greeks still follow the sea. 

With the decline of Phoenicia (page 169) the Greeks for a time took over the trade with the East and along the Mediterranean. 

Along these same shores they founded settlements. Some of their city states became powerful and prosperous. With their new wealth they beautified their cities. They built temples (A) and great open-air theaters. 

Their sculptors carved wonderful reliefs for the temples, and beautiful statues that were set up in public places. Wealth made it possible for the most brilliant of their citizens to spend time in the writing of prose, poetry, and plays for their theaters. Some of their great men studied and taught philosophy, and others became orators and leaders of the people.

There was great rivalry between these city states, leading to wars that weakened them. 

When Rome became powerful the Greek states were easily conquered; they lost their trade to Rome and their other activities began a period of decline. As you read the following pages, see if you can tell why Greece is no longer one of the great nations of Europe.

Coast Line and Surface. The coast line of Greece is even more irregular than that of

the Balkan Peninsula as a whole. It has sometimes been called a " peninsula of peninsulas," and if you study your map (page 163), you will see why. Many of the smaller peninsulas are parts of mountain ranges, and the off-shore islands are the tops of ranges that extend out into the sea.

Between small peninsulas there are many bays, at the heads of which there are lowland areas of varying size, some large, others small. The waters of the Ionian Sea are on the west, and those of the Aegean Sea on the east. These two seas are nearly connected with each other by gulfs extending far into the land. By cutting a canal across the 

Isthmus of Corinth an actual connection has been made. Small ships can use this canal to get from one side of the peninsula to the other, and thus avoid a longer and somewhat dangerous trip around its southern end.

In the northern part of the Balkan Peninsula the Dinaric Alps swing to the southeast, and occupy much of its western part. They continue into northern Greece as the Pindus

Mountains, and under other names to the tips of the small peninsulas at its southern end. Branches of the higher north-south ranges extend eastward.

Most of Greece, therefore, is a land of mountains. Between ranges there are many small level basins where some farming can be carried on, corn being usually the chief crop. Besides the small coastal lowlands at the heads of bays, others extend for some distance along a few rivers. The largest of these are the plains of Thessaly, in which 

Trikkala and Larissa are located; around

Salonika along the Vardar River; and along the Maritza River on the eastern boundary. 

There are lowlands also in Macedonia, the region north of the Aegean Sea. 

Products. Only about one fifth of the land surface of Greece can be cultivated, and in some regions where crops can be grown, dry summers make irrigation necessary. In the valleys and on the lowlands, winter wheat, barley, olives, oranges, lemons, grapes, and some figs are grown. Along the shores of the 

Gulfs of Patras and Corinth, and in places along the west coast, small seedless grapes are grown. These, when dried, are called currants, and form an important export. Many of them come to the United States from the port of Patras. On the plains north of the 

Aegean Sea much tobacco is raised. So much is sent to other countries that it is the chief export of Greece in value.

On the rough pastures of the mountains of Greece many sheep and goats are raised.

Their milk is used by the people, or made into cheese. Some wool and many hides are exported. 

Iron, copper, zinc, and lead are found in

Greece, most of the deposits being in the mountains where there are few roads or railroads for their transportation. As a result, the mineral resources of the country are poorly developed. Transportation is chiefly along main river valleys, and very little across country. For much of the country there are not enough people traveling, or goods to be moved, to make it worth while to build good roads or railroads. The construction of these in so mountainous a country would be very expensive. 

Cities. Athens (Greek name, Athenai) is the capital and largest city of Greece. It has grown rapidly since the World War and is now a very modern city with fine buildings, broad streets, motor cars, trolleys, and a large stadium in which international athletic contests are frequently held. But Athens was also a great city in ancient times; and it has ruins of some famous buildings, among them the Parthenon, one of the most beautiful of ancient temples (191 A). Athens is several miles inland; its seaport is the smaller city named Piraeus. 

Salonika (Thessalonike), an important city of Greece, is at the head of a gulf of the same name. It has a large harbor, and railway

Some of the countries of southeastern Europe carry on their trade with Asia, Australia, and the eastern Mediterranean through this port. 

Greek Islands. Most of the Grecian islands are mountainous. Crete is the largest (map, page 163). Agriculture and the raising of sheep and goats are almost the only industries. Off the west coast, Corfu raises olives, and some of the smaller islands raise the grapes from which currants are made. 

The People and Their Manufactures. 

There is little manufacturing in Greece, because there are few raw materials to be manufactured, and the lack of coal is a serious handicap. Because of the general dryness of the country there is little water power to take the place of coal. Some olive oil, woolen cloth and carpets, pottery (A), and cigarettes are made, but most manufactured goods must be imported. The people are energetic and hard-working, and are doing all they can to bring prosperity to their country.

NORTH AFRICA 

When you were studying the Mediterranean region as a whole, you learned that it includes parts of southern Europe, the peninsula of Asia Minor, and North Africa (page 

165). You have since made a more careful study of the different countries that make up the European part of this area. Before going on with the study of eastern and southeastern Europe, it will be well to give a little time to the lands of North Africa which are included within the Mediterranean area. This is because their climate and products are so much like those of other Mediterranean areas that you have been studying. 

The Atlas District. The Atlas district includes most of Morocco, and northern Algeria and Tunisia. You know that Tunisia,

Algeria, and the larger part of Morocco belong to France, and the rest of Morocco belongs to Spain (pages 137 and 178).

Turn to the map on pages 162-163 and notice that the Atlas Mountains cross all three of these countries. They are high and rugged, with parallel ranges between which are inclosed high plateaus, or table lands. 

They have in general an east-west direction, and winds from the Mediterranean striking against their northern slopes lose their moisture as rain. At what period of the year do the heaviest rains come? (The Mediterranean climate is described on pages 165-166.)

In thinking of rainfall in mountain areas it should always be kept in mind that no mountain region is a high wall of uniform height. There may be several ranges instead of one, and there are high peaks and low valleys leading upward into the mountains. 

Between the ranges there are other and larger valleys, and sometimes there are broad plateaus.

The facts just given will explain why, through the Atlas Mountains, there are plateaus and valleys with enough rain so wheat and barley can be grown, and others where cattle, sheep, horses, mules, and goats are pastured. The Atlas district is a rich agricultural region that once supplied much grain for ancient Rome. Remains of the Roman occupation of the land have been found, such as the ruins of cities, irrigation works, and roads. Today, along the coastal plain known as the "Tell," fruits and vegetables are raised and shipped to France and to other European markets. In the Tell, and in the warmer valley lands, grapes, olives, oranges, and figs are raised, while dates are grown in the oases of the interior. As in other Mediterranean countries, the grapes are made into wine or dried as raisins. Some of the olives are pickled, but most of them are used in making olive oil. 

There are cork oaks and mulberry trees.

The first of these furnishes sheet cork for export, the second furnishes leaves for silkworms raised for their cocoons. Much tobacco is grown in Algeria. In the mountains there are deposits of iron ore, lead, zinc, copper, and phosphate rock. Mines of all these minerals are worked. 

The People. The population of the Atlas district is made up of natives, mostly Arabs and Berbers, and colonists who have come 

Changes are nevertheless being made.

Many of the native people have begun to lead a more settled life. The French are teaching them scientific agriculture and the use of modern tools. Wells for water are being bored, irrigation works are being built, and the railroads and highways are being extended.

There are mountain tribes and desert nomads of the interior who at times make war upon each other or upon the European colonists and soldiers. nists and soldiers. But with agriculture, grazing, native manufactures, and trade all increasing, most of the peoples of the coast lands are becoming more prosperous, peaceful, and industrious.

This is a great change from the time when this coast was the home of pirates who sailed out of their ports to attack passing ships. If successful in capturing a vessel, the pirates took whatever they wanted, and killed the passengers and crew or carried them off as slaves. It was the navy of our own country that succeeded in stopping this piracy a little more than a hundred years ago.

The chief cities and ports are Algiers (Alger), the capital of Algeria, and Tunis, the capital of Tunisia. Through these ports much trade of the Atlas district is carried on.

RUSSIA 

The great country called Russia, or the 

Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, includes the easternmost part of Europe and much of northern Asia. The European portion extends from the Arctic Ocean on the north to the Black Sea, Caucasus Mountains, and 

Caspian Sea on the south. Trace its boundaries on the map on the opposite page. The 

Asiatic portion is mostly in the northern part of Asia and stretches east from Europe to the Pacific Ocean. A smaller part takes in the southern slope of the Caucasus Moun- 

Before the World War, this vast area, with some additional lands, was known as the Russian Empire. Its ruler was called the 

Czar, and he had absolute power. In 1917, however, the people rose in rebellion, took away all power from the Czar, and formed a government of their own. Finland, Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania soon became independent republics, and other lands were made parts of Poland and Rumania (156 A). 

Other "republics" formed out of the old

Russian Empire, and certain other territories united to form a union of Soviet Socialist Republics a soviet being a committee of workers. Representatives from these republics met in Moscow to form an All-Union Congress. But this Congress was always under the control of self-selected leaders. leaders. In 1937 a constitution was adopted 199

EUROPE 

under which, in theory, the power of the central government is in a Supreme Soviet. 

This Supreme Soviet is made up of two groups of elected representatives who form (a) the Soviet of the Union and (b) the Soviet of 

Nationalities. 

The central government claims, as state property, the land, natural resources, means of transportation and communication, and the industries and much of the property formerly belonging to private owners. Today, however, as before the adoption of the constitution, the government is in the hands of self-selected leaders. They keep themselves in power by removing, in one way or another, all those who threaten their control.

As the name Union of Soviet Socialist Republics is a long one, the old name Russia is more often used, as in this book, to mean the whole Union.

The Largest Country in the World. - To get an idea of the great size of Russia, compare it with such other large countries as the 

United States, Canada, and Brazil, as you see them on a globe. Also, compare their areas as given in the Tables at the back of this book. You will find that Russia as a whole is more than two and a half times as large as the United States or Brazil, and much more than twice as large as Canada. 

In so vast a country you will naturally expect to find a great variety in climate, vegetation, natural resources, and the industries of the people. Let us see if this is true. 

Surface. Most of Russia in Europe is an enormous area of lowland plains. Those in the central and northern parts were glaciated during the ice age (map, 101 A), but those in the southern part were not disturbed by the ice sheet. The underlying rocks are horizontal and deeply buried. There is a low elevation stretching from the northeast to the southwest, and separating the rivers that flow generally toward the north from those flowing generally toward the south. In the western part of this low water parting are the Valdai Hills, which are the highest in the plains area. The region to which the name is given is really a low plateau that has been cut into low, rounded hills by the streams that flow out of it. The highest elevation is only 665 feet above sea level.

The only mountains in European Russia form parts of its boundaries. There is one such mountain area in the south and one in the east (map, page 198). At the south you find the high, rugged Caucasus Mountains. They are higher than the Alps, have few passes, and have always been a serious barrier to trade and travel. They are not, however, so serious a barrier as they were before the airplane came into use for carrying passengers, mail, and valuable goods of small size and light weight. By what other routes can you travel between southeastern Europe and western Asia and avoid the Caucasus?

Between the plains of Russia in the northern part of Europe and in northern Asia are the Ural Mountains. These mountains are very different from the high and rugged Caucasus. The Urals are old worn-down mountains so broad and low and with such long slopes that they are easily crossed at almost any point. They form no serious barrier to trade or travel.

South of the Urals the boundary between 

Europe and Asia swings west and then south to the shore of the Caspian Sea. This large body of water has no outlet. It is like the 

Great Salt Lake in the western part of our own country. The water that flows into it evaporates as it flows in. All of the salts that the streams carry into the lake are left there when the water evaporates. The lake water is therefore salt, and is increasing in saltiness. 

The basin in which the Caspian Sea rests is below the level of the world's oceans. 

If there were any place where the waters of the Black Sea or the Mediterranean could break through, a much larger area would be

ור A. 

Oil tankers on the Volga River near Gorki. At the left you see a large tugboat used for hauling the tankers. flooded. That is because there are lowlands surrounding the Caspian Sea that are also below sea level.

Most of Russia in Asia is a vast plain, the largest part of which slopes gently toward the Arctic Ocean. It extends to the north much farther than do the northern plains of European Russia, and reaches for a long distance north of the Arctic Circle. This northern plain of Asia is widest just east of the Caspian Sea and Ural Mountains, and it narrows more and more toward the east. 

Measure it on the map, page 278. 

In the southeastern part of Asiatic Russia there is an area of hills and mountains. 

These elevated areas begin at the southern margin of the plain and rise quickly toward the central highlands of Asia. Find them on the map.

Rivers. -The highest part of the plains region of European Russia is near the center. 

It extends across the plains from the region of the Valdai Hills in a northeast direction toward the Ural Mountains. It is only slightly higher than the rest of the plains area.

From the Valdai Hills and this central | upland the rivers of European Russia flow outward in different directions. Here, therefore, is another region of radial drainage, like that in Switzerland (page 152).

Because of the great size of the plains and the general levelness of the land, the rivers move slowly toward the sea. In such a country you would not expect many waterfalls and rapids. The only ones of great size are on the Dnieper, where it bends to the west. 

A great power plant has been built there. 

The plains of European Russia are crossed by thousands of miles of rivers that are used for the transportation of goods and passengers. 

In some places canals have been dug to connect rivers, so that boats can pass from one river system to another.

The Volga River, which flows into the Caspian Sea, is one of the greatest rivers of the world, and it carries a vast amount of commerce. See if you can trace its winding course across the map of European Russia (page 198) from the place where it rises near the Valdai Hills to the Caspian Sea. The 

Dnieper River flows southward through a rich farming region into the Black Sea.

EUROPE 

A. 

Caterpillar tractor hauling a day's cut from a Russian forest.

The Don, much shorter than the other two, flows into the Sea of Azov. These are the three chief rivers of southern Russia.

The commerce of the Volga is from place to place along its course, or to and from points on the Caspian Sea. The commerce on the 

Dnieper and the Don can reach the Black 

Sea. From Black Sea ports, by way of the water route past Istanbul to the Mediterranean, commerce can be carried on with any port in the world.

The rivers of the northern plains of Asiatic Russia follow the slope of the land toward the Arctic Ocean. On the map of Asia find the Ob, Yenisei, and Lena rivers. Which one of these is nearest to 

European Russia? Which one rises far to the south in the highlands of southeastern Asiatic Russia? The lower courses of all of these rivers and parts of most of their tributaries are frozen for many months in the year. This is true also of the northwardflowing rivers of European Russia. Why? 

If you will notice the high latitudes of the lower courses and the mouths of these rivers it may help you to find the answer to this question. Keep in mind the location of the 

Lena River. The coldest part of the world in which people live is found in the basin of this river. There is little commerce on these rivers because the country is sparsely inhabited, because they are frozen for many months at a time, and because they flow north while the commerce of this part of 

Russia moves east and west. 

Find Lake Aral and Lake Balkhash in southwestern Russia in Asia. Notice that streams flow into them but that they have no outlets. As you might correctly tell from that fact, the basins in which they lie are regions of light rainfall, like the basin of 

Great Salt Lake in our country.

Climate and Vegetation. The range in latitude in European Russia is from about 

40° north latitude on the west shore of the 

Caspian Sea to about 70° north latitude on the Arctic Ocean. Within this 30° range of latitude there are marked differences in climate, vegetation, industries, and density of population.

The prevailing winds are from the west, but they do not bring to Russia the even temperatures that are found in the lowland countries of west-central Europe. In western 

Europe their influence is to make the temperatures cool in summer and mild in winter (page 79). As they move eastward these westerly winds become warmer in summer and cooler in winter, and give Russia a continental climate-a climate of extremes of temperature. The difference between summer temperature and winter temperature for places in Russia, therefore, becomes greater from the west toward the east. As you would naturally expect, the temperature decreases from south to north, although at Astrakhan, near the mouth of the Volga, that river is closed by ice for over two months in winter. 

Throughout northern Russia, both in Europe and Asia, the winter temperatures are so low that the ground is frozen to a depth of many

feet. The short summers are usually warm enough to thaw out the surface, and as a result much of the land is swampy in the summer time.

The rainfall varies greatly in different parts of the country. It is about 24 inches a year in the west-central part of the country in the region of the Valdai Hills. From this region it becomes less toward the north, the east, and the south. In the north the average annual rainfall drops to less than 10 inches a year, too little for the growth of crops. This makes little difference to the farmers of Russia, because it is so cold in these regions that no crops will grow.

The rainfall in the central and southern parts of the country is of much greater importance. In these parts the temperature is favorable to the growth of trees or crops, and most of the soils are excellent. The average annual rainfall for much of this area is only 20 inches or less, and it varies so greatly from year to year that crop damage or failure frequently happens.

In the Caspian Sea region, where the summer temperatures are often very high, the rainfall is less than 10 inches a year, and part of the country is almost a desert. Farming is impossible without irrigation. 

The Tundras. You will remember that when you were studying North America last year, you learned about the tundras of northern Alaska and northern Canada. You found these tundras to be low, treeless plains, where the ground is frozen to great depths, and where there is a very sparse population. 

The surface thaws out during the brief summer, and there is a growth of reindeer moss and some grass. These furnish food for the herds of reindeer and the caribou that are to be found there. In studying Norway and 

Sweden, you found a similar region in which a nomadic people live with their herds of reindeer (page 106).

A broad belt of country in northern Russia, extending across the country from west to east, is just such a tundra region. The natural vegetation is lichens and some grass, with a few small shrubs. Here also you find many scattered groups of people with their reindeer. They live in sod houses or skin tents, and move from place to place whenever necessary to find food for their herds. In western European Russia, as in northern

Norway, Sweden, and Finland, these people are Lapps. In eastern European Russia, and in Asiatic Russia, there are various tribes or groups of the same yellow race, speaking different languages. For their food the people depend chiefly upon the milk and meat of their reindeer, but they also catch fish, and gather some berries. With the coming of winter these people move southward with their herds into the edge of the forest. There they are better protected from winter storms, and their animals have a better chance to dig through the snow with their sharp hoofs to get at the grass or moss underneath. The reindeer hides are used both for tents and for clothing. 

Forests. The forests of Russia are the largest in the world. The forest belt, like the tundra region, stretches across the whole of Russia, from the Baltic Sea to the Pacific Ocean. In the northern part, the trees are chiefly evergreens. Toward the south, the evergreens thin out and are replaced by deciduous trees; that is, trees that lose their leaves each winter.

In European Russia there is much lumbering going on in the evergreen forests. In the warmer season, logs are floated down the Dvina to Archangel, where they are sawed into lumber or made into wood pulp for export. Very little of this forest area has been cleared for crops, although some flax is grown for its fiber and crops of oats are raised. 

Taken as a whole, however, this European evergreen-forest region is very sparsely populated. As you know, this area was once covered by the European ice sheet, and there are many swamps and undrained lakes, as

Hunting and trapping have long been a very important industry in this region. Farther east little lumbering is done, because of the difficulty and expense of getting the lumber to market. 

Trees have been cut chiefly to meet local needs for timber and firewood.

A Region of Dense Population and Some Great Cities. The western part of the forest zone was largely cleared away many, many years ago. It is today the most densely settled part of all Russia, and within this area are two of the greatest are two of the greatest cities. It has also become the chief industrial region. 

Leningrad, first named St. Petersburg (and later Petrograd), is second in size among the Russian cities. For many years it was the capital of the country, but the government was transferred to Moscow after the revolution. Leningrad is located on the 

Neva River, the outlet of Lake Ladoga.

It is not far from the eastern end of the Gulf of Finland, an arm of the Baltic Sea. Improvements at the mouth of the Neva have made Leningrad the chief port of European

Russia. It is connected by a railroad line with Moscow (Moskva), the present capital.

Moscow, southeast of Leningrad, has grown rapidly since it became the capital of modern Russia. It is now much larger than Philadelphia, and about as large as Chicago. 

It is the railroad center of European Russia, and from it railroads lead out in every direction. Moscow is the European end of the 

Trans-Siberian Railroad. Trace this great route along its 6000 miles of length through European and Asiatic Russia to the Russian port of Vladivostok on the Pacific Ocean (see maps of Eastern Europe and Asia).

The government of Russia, in control of its industries, is increasing its manufactures (A). In recent years, Moscow has become a textile-manufacturing center, with cotton, woolen, linen, and silk mills. It also manufactures leather goods and machinery.

Moscow has naturally become also a trade center for the surrounding country. Here are gathered grain, furs, oil, and other products for export to other points in Europe, or to be sent to ports for shipment abroad.

Grasslands and the Black Earth Region. 

The region south of the old forest belt is a large area of grassland that occupies most of southern Russia in Europe and extends east ward into Asia. Find this Black Earth Region on the map, page 76. The soil is called "black earth" because it has been colored very dark by the decay of grass roots in it year after year for centuries. It is one of the most fertile soils in the world. Where there is sufficient rainfall, very large crops can be grown. 

This is the great wheat-raising region of Russia, and in the years of good harvests Russia is second only to our own country in the amount raised. Cattle are found on the farms all through the southern half of Russia.

The herds are cared for by tribes of wandering people whom we call nomads, because they move about from place to place in search of grass for their animals.

Mineral Resources of Russia. It is only since the World War that an active search for the mineral wealth of U. S. S. R. has been undertaken. Before the war but little was known about the mineral deposits of the Urals and nothing at all about those of Siberia.

Coal and iron have been found in the Ukraine. As the coal is a good coking coal, and as there are deposits of manganese near by, this region has become an iron- and steel-manufacturing center.

But the great surprise to the world is the vast wealth of mineral resources that the Soviet government has opened up in Siberia. 

All northern Siberia seems to be rich in minerals. But the chief areas now being developed are in the eastern and western parts of Siberia rather than in its central part. 

In the provinces of the Far East hundreds of mineral deposits have been located that will richly repay working. When all Siberia is considered, the deposits already located number thousands rather than hundreds.

One area in which coal has been found is said to have enough coal to equal the world consumption for 300 years and another area has even more.

A considerable number of mines have already been opened. As a result Russia now ranks second among the gold-producing countries of the world. It is even reasonable to expect that it will sooner or later reach first place. Only time can reveal to what extent the people of Russia will develop their mineral resources, and how soon. 

The oil fields of Baku on the Caspian have been mentioned. Oil has been found, also, along the Caucasus Mountains where wells have been opened, and in a number of places in Siberia. It is expected that, as the 

Siberian oil is made available, it will be used in oil-burning steamers along the north coast of Asia. The oil from these wells will be refined for use in Soviet airplanes also. 

Water from the Caspian Sea and other salt lakes is heated until the water evaporates, leaving the salt. The salt is then purified and prepared for use.

With such great mineral wealth as the 

Russians have discovered that they possess, it is natural to expect that they will push eagerly forward in the field of metal-manufacturing industries. Fishing. There is some fishing in the 

Russian lakes and rivers and in the Russian coastal waters.
