COUNTRIES AND PRODUCTS 

You have learned that Africa is largely under the control of European peoples who are spending vast sums of money to develop its resources and build up its industries. How successful have they been? There are also some small parts of the continent that have independent governments. What are their present industries and how successfully have they developed their resources? 

Egypt. Civilized people lived in Egypt and had a strong kingdom for thousands of years before the time of Christ. Much of their ancient history has been learned in recent years because scholars have been able to read the old inscriptions and other writings that have been discovered. Most of the inscriptions and other records that scholars have found in Egypt would have been destroyed in a land with a moist climate and severe changes of temperature. They have been preserved in Egypt because it is an arid country. The Egyptians took great care in embalming and wrapping the bodies of their dead, which are known as mummies. 

The mummies of some of the ancient kings have been discovered, and many beautiful and interesting articles used by them during their lifetime have been found in their tombs. 

The pyramids of Egypt, made of blocks of stone, were built as burial places for some of the kings. The building of such pyramids required the work of thousands of men for many years. The largest of them are about 

450 feet high. 

450 feet high. Temples with many huge columns were built in the same way. Single blocks of stone of great size were quarried, carved with inscriptions, and set up as monuments. These are known as obelisks. Some of these obelisks have been taken from Egypt and set up in foreign cities, as in Rome, in 

London, and in Central Park, New York.

The Sphinx is a giant statue carved out of rock, having the body of an animal and the head of a human being.

Egypt suffered under Turkish rule for many years. In 1883 it became a nearly independent monarchy, under British influence.

The people were justly taxed and were taught modern farming methods and the use of farm machinery. Since 1922 Egypt has been a sovereign state with its own king, but Great Britain continues to guarantee order and to protect the Suez route and neighboring colonies. 

Egypt is several times as large as the British Isles, but most of it is a desert like the Sahara. the Sahara. The Nile flows through it from south to north. For thousands of years the people have lifted or pumped the water over the flood plain and the great delta at its northern end. But the Egyptian ways were crude, and it was not until British engineers introduced scientific methods that the land was properly irrigated.

The floods in the lower Nile were largely due to the heavy summer rainfall of Ethiopia. 

Much of this highland area is drained by two tributaries of the Nile. As the heavy rainfall gathered in these tributaries, it hurried

AFRICA 

A. One of the locks in the Aswân Dam. On the right you can see a section of the first cataract of the Nile. on to the main stream and then flooded the lowlands, leaving a cover of fine, rich soil. 

One crop a year could be grown. 

The lower Nile began to rise in June and continued to September, reaching a height of from 30 to 50 feet above its low-water level. 

The Egyptians piled up ridges of earth to form shallow basins for holding some of the flood waters. These they built at various levels on lands that were usually flooded. 

The basins filled as the waters rose high enough to cover them. Later, when the floods went down, the water in these basins was used to irrigate the near-by fields. The basin system of irrigation is still in use in some parts of the Nile Valley, as are also some very old methods of lifting the water from the river to the fields. 

In spite of the great variation in the level of the lower Nile in Egypt, it is usually navigable as far south as the first cataract at 

Aswân (A). British engineers found that they could make a large lake south of this cataract, by building a great dam across the Nile at this point. The rocks of the cataract gave an excellent foundation for such a dam, and it was built. It is one and a fourth miles in length and 164 feet in height. The lake or reservoir is 200 miles long. Water from the lake can be let out into canals, and spread over a large area of fertile fields as needed. 

As a result, more than one crop a year can now be grown in parts of the valley that formerly produced but one, and fields are now irrigated that formerly were not reached by the annual floods.

Crops of both temperate and hot climates are raised, including a large amount of wheat and other grains. Many different kinds of dates are exported, both ripe and dried. The 

Egyptian cotton, grown largely in the Nile delta, has a long, strong, fine fiber and is one of the best cottons in the world. The country stands next to the United States and India in the export of this fiber. Some Egyptian cotton is used in American mills for making special kinds of goods, but most of it goes to England.

Cairo's dry and healthful air, and its historical interest, attract people of many lands, who make it a resort for the winter months. 

Alexandria is still the chief seaport of Egypt, as it was in ancient times. 

The Suez Canal extends from Port Said, on the Mediterranean, 103 miles to Suez, at the head of the Red Sea. Of this distance, true canals cover 76 miles, and lakes 27 miles. 

The canal was completed in 1869 after ten years of work. It is 41 feet deep, and all but the very largest ocean vessels can use it. | Before it was dug, ships for the Far East sailed around the southern end of Africa or South 

America,. and Mediterranean commerce was much less important than now. Now ships from London and other European ports go by the Suez route to the ports of southern and eastern Asia, Australia, and New Zealand.

In normal times about 5000 ships pass through the canal each year. The greatest number of the ships are British, but there are many under the French, Dutch, Japanese, Italian, and other flags. 

Libya. When you studied Spain, Italy, and Greece, you learned that the Mediterranean Sea is a vast body of water, and that long voyages are needed to go from one part of the shore to another. On a trip from 

Cairo, the great city of Egypt, to Tripoli, the traveler will go first to Alexandria and there take a ship, just as people did 2000 years ago. The ship will be much larger, safer, faster, and much more comfortable than in those old days. Use the scale of miles to find the distance from Alexandria to Tripoli. It

AFRICA 

is about 1000 miles. The distance looks short on our small map, but probably three days or more will, even now, be needed for the voyage; and in the old days a much longer time was necessary.

Libya is a country with a small and scattered population made up of Berbers, Arabs, Jews, and desert tribes. It is an Italian colony and is larger than Spain, France, and Germany combined. Yet, because it is mostly desert, it has fewer people than Hamburg or Glasgow. Without the Nile, Egypt would probably have as few people. 

Unfortunately, Libya has no river to moisten its desert soil.

Libya, like Egypt, was at one time a part of the Turkish Empire. The chief city is Tripoli. The sands and shoals of this part of the Mediterranean were feared by ancient seamen, and navigation is still dangerous. 

Along this shore Greek divers come every year to gather sponges from the sea bottom. 

In the deserts of Libya and in other parts of northern Africa, a plant known as esparto grass is found. It has strong fibers. The stems are gathered, bound into huge bundles, and carried by camels to the sea. There they are put on ships and sent to England, where they are used in the manufacture of paper. 

From Tripoli caravans follow desert trails across the Sahara to Lake Chad, the Niger

River, and parts of the Sudan country. 

Tunisia and Algeria. Tunisia and Al geria are the nearest and most useful colonies of France. All this region has the Mediterranean climate with hot, dry summers and rainy, warm winters. Such a climate favors the growth of many crops, as you know from your earlier study of this region (pages 166 and 195). 

Tunisia and Algeria are far more progressive countries than Libya. More railroads have been built there than in most parts of Africa, and there are thousands of miles of telegraph and telephone lines. Tunis and

Algiers (A), the two capitals, are well-governed cities, and are visited every winter by many 

Americans and other tourists.

They come from over Asia and cause here the greatest desert in the world. The desert area of North Africa is greater than the entire area of the United States.

Little grows in such a desert, for much of it is too dry even for grass. There are parts that are covered with sand dunes that the winds move ever before them. Whirling storms lift dust, dirt, and sand, and drive them across the desert. Men and beasts must lie down and protect themselves as best they can when such storms overtake them. 

There are other parts of this great desert area that are barren and rocky because all soil has been blown away. Then there are some higher parts of the desert plateau where a small amount of rain may fall and where the

AFRICA 

The caravans carry ivory, ostrich feathers, and skins from central Africa or the Sudan region to the Mediterranean coast cities. They carry back to the natives various products of Europe, such as cloths of cotton and wool, beads, paper, drugs, and sugar. The chief item in this list is cotton goods from Great Britain. 

The caravan trade is not so large as it was, for short railroads that lead out to the ocean are being built in the countries south of the Sahara, and goods are being shipped in and out by rail. Also, automobiles with a special kind of wheel are being used on the desert with considerable success. 

Courtesy Canadian Pacific Steamships 

A. A native kraal in southern Africa. Fences separate the small yards about the houses. See how neatly the straw roofs are made. ground water comes out in springs. Here are oases in which are seen palm trees, gardens, villages, and people.

Between the markets on the north, and the moist and fertile regions of the south, trade has been carried on by the nomads of the desert for thousands of years. The trade routes across the desert lead from oasis to oasis, and animals must carry both goods and men, for the routes are poorly marked and there are no railroads that cross the Sahara. 

Some caravans are small, and some have thousands of camels with their drivers and guards, and carry goods having a value of hundreds of thousands of dollars. A caravan journey across the Sahara may take several months, and is full of danger, for bands of robbers are common in the desert. They know where all the wells and springs are, and often demand money from passing caravans even when they do not plunder them.

Camels are the animals chiefly used to carry burdens across the desert, because they can go several days, if necessary, without drinking. Each animal carries a load of about 300 pounds, and a day's march may last sixteen hours. 

Central and Southern Africa. The cen tral and southern parts of the continent were almost as difficult for the white man to penetrate as was the desert. Along the east and west coasts, the lowlands of the rainy region are damp, unhealthful, and covered with a dense jungle growth. The coasts of the drier regions are barren and uninviting, and there are but few good harbors. Everywhere these coastal lowlands are narrow and are backed by the seaward-facing escarpments of interior plateaus. This part of the continent has always been the home of the black, or Negro, race. The first white men to enter it found most of the Negroes densely ignorant. For many years the few white visitors only made the condition of the natives worse. They came to Africa for little else than to buy Negro slaves from warring Negro tribes, or even to capture Negroes themselves. The captives were placed on ships and kept as prisoners during the voyage to America or to some other land where they were sold. The slave trade, however, was stopped by civilized nations more than a hundred years ago.

Some of them hunt; others tend a few sheep or farm a small patch of ground. They live in a warm region, where they can get along with little clothing and shelter, and where the forest and grassland provide enough food. 

Sudan Countries and Ethiopia. The Su dan is the region south of the Sahara. It extends from the Atlantic Ocean eastward to 

Ethiopia and the Red Sea. On the south are the Gulf of Guinea and the watersheds between Lake Chad and the Congo River system. The Sudan is not so hot and rainy as the tropical forests, nor so hot and dry as the Sahara. Many of the Negroes of the Sudan, west of Lake Chad, belong to the Hausa tribes. These tribes are among the best and most prosperous people of the African black race.

France governs the central and much of the western part of the Sudan. In the west the chief center for trade between the Sudan and the Sahara is the ancient city of Timbuktu on the northern bend of the Niger. It is the center of many caravan trails. The French plan to connect it by a railroad with their possessions in northern Africa. On the Gulf of Guinea are Nigeria and the Gold Coast, under British rule. Dahomey and the Ivory 

Coast are under French rule. These are tropical countries with a hot climate, unhealthful near the coast. However, these countries have valuable mineral and forest resources, fields that can be cultivated, and much pasture land. The Gold Coast produces more cacao than any other country in the world.

In the western part of the Sudan you will find the small republic of Liberia, and the 

British colonies of Sierra Leone and Gambia.

Egyptian Sudan, which is being developed under British control. The capital is Khartoum, on the Nile. The fierce natives were conquered by a British-Egyptian army in 

1898. Order was then established, opening the way for agriculture and civilized life. A railroad, part of the route from Cairo to Cape

Town, has been completed to a point some distance south of Khartoum, and a branch line has been built to the Red Sea.

To the east of Anglo-Egyptian Sudan is the plateau and mountain region often called Abyssinia. It is now a part of Italian Oriental Africa. Valuable mineral and other resources are known to exist in this area. 

Now that the Italians have taken possession of this region these resources will undoubtedly be developed.

At Kimberley in Cape of Good Hope are the largest diamond mines in the world. The gems are dug in a rough state out of masses of partly decayed volcanic rock. The native laborers are watched and searched to see that they do not steal the precious stones. When sold, most of the diamonds go to Antwerp or

Amsterdam to be cut and polished. After the diamonds are polished most of them are taken to the United States, which is the largest market for precious stones.

Madagascar. The island of Madagascar, off the southeast coast of Africa, is the largest island of Africa, and third in size among the islands of the world. It is larger than either 

France or Germany. Madagascar is under

French rule. There is a narrow plain backed by mountains along the east coast, and the interior is largely a high plateau. There is a broad coastal plain on the west. Being in the region of the southeast trade winds, the eastern part of the island receives a heavy rainfall (maps, page 248) and has a luxuriant growth of tropical forests. Farther west there is much less rain and the forests are replaced in part by grasslands or savannas.

Although the island belongs to France, there are but few French people living there, and most of the agriculture is in the hands of the natives. The chief crops are rice and manioc, from which a native flour and tapioca are made. Sugar cane, cacao, and coffee are raised, as they are in so many parts of Africa with a similar climate. Some vanilla beans are raised also.

Cattle raising is an important industry in the grasslands, and hides and meat are exported, chiefly to France.

Among the mineral resources is graphite, from which the lead in pencils, a mineral lubricant or grease, and stove blacking are made. Mica, a mineral that can be split into thin transparent sheets, is also found on the island. Mica is used in stoves and in the electrical industries.

The population of the island is nearly 4,000,000, mostly natives who are descended from Negro and Mongolian races. A railroad runs from Tamatave, a port on the eastern side of the island, to Tananarive, the capital. 

The French government has spent much money on roads, railroads, and in making harbor improvements.

AFRICA AFRICA AS A WHOLE 

It is possible to think of Africa as a continent of the past -a continent within whose borders great civilizations rose to power and passed away. To 

To this past belong the temples, palaces, monuments, and royal tombs of ancient Egypt. The ruins of these, scattered along the valley of the Nile, still tell us in their own voiceless way some part of the story of the great people who built them. In other ways, also, a part of the history of the days of Egypt's glory has come down to us. 

History tells us of other civilizations in northern Africa, not so ancient, but great in their time. Carthage, for example, was one of the splendid cities of the ancient world yet Carthage has been but a heap of ruins for hundreds of years. The Moors, long before the time of Columbus, carried their arts and learning from their homes in northern 

Africa across the Strait of Gibraltar. There we find even today the evidence of their learning. Yet they were finally driven back across the strait into Africa, where their arts fell into decay.

It is possible, and much more reasonable, to think of Africa as a continent of the future. 

Slowly, under the leadership of Great Britain, Italy, and France, prosperity is being brought back to Egypt, Libya, Tunisia, Algeria, and 

Morocco. You have already learned much about what France has done for Tunisia and Algeria and what is now being done in Morocco.

The work of Great Britain in Egypt is just as important. The building of the great dam at Aswân is only one of the ways in which Great Britain has been of help to the 

Egyptian people. Great Britain has helped them, also, to secure a better government; and British mills make use of much of their cotton crop. Most important of all, perhaps, is the fact that Great Britain is pushing forward the building of a great railroad to connect Cape Town (A) at the southern end of the continent, with Cairo, near the mouth of the Nile. As you have already learned, the political control of Africa is largely in the hands of 

Great Britain, France, and Belgium. The map on page 242 shows you which parts of the continent and its neighboring islands each of these countries controls. smaller areas are independent, or controlled by other countries. The lands controlled by 

Great Britain include (1) the whole of the southern end of the continent, (2) territories stretching from southern Egypt along the east side of Africa, to join with those at the south, (3) the entrances to the Red Sea and the Suez Canal, and (4) lands along the Gulf of Guinea.

The possessions of France are even larger than those of Great Britain, but as a whole are of less value, as such large parts of them lie in the Sahara. Belgium has a central | part of the continent in the basin of the 

Congo; and Portugal has two large colonies one bordering the east coast and the other the west coast of the southern part of the continent. 

Transportation. The transportation routes in the interior of Africa are very poor and the methods of transportation are not satisfactory. Small steamboats are in use on the navigable stretches of the Nile, the Congo, the Niger, and the Zambezi, as well as on the great lakes. well as on the great lakes. Short railroads lead inland from some ports, and the Union of South Africa, especially, has been active in railroad building (A). There are few roads on which wheeled vehicles can be used. 

The one long railroad line planned has not yet been completed, and the carrying of burdens by the native blacks is still common. 1

AFRICA 

Cape-to-Cairo Railroad. 

Cecil Rhodes, who was prominent in the settlement and development of South Africa, is given credit for thinking of building the Cape-to-Cairo Railroad. Parts of this route have already been built and it is being slowly but steadily extended. At the northern end of the route, a railroad has been built from Alexandria to 

Khartoum and beyond. At the southern end, the line has been constructed from Cape Town to the Congo. Between these two links in the route, steamships on lakes and rivers, short stretches of rail, and some overland travel by road must be used. It will probably be a long time before the railroad is completed and the whole of the trip can be made by rail. In the meantime, airplane travel has become more common, and many trips have been made into and across the continent. 

Products and Trade. In west Africa the region around the Gulf of Guinea is becoming an important producing region and trade center. Two great rivers reach the Atlantic within this region - the Congo and the 

Niger. You know that both of them are interrupted by falls or rapids, but there are long stretches of both rivers that are navigable. This fact has helped in the development of this region, as have also the short railroad lines connecting some of the ports with the country behind them.

Among the products that reach the Guinea coast from the interior are ivory, palm nuts, and palm oil. Peanuts from Gambia, cacao beans from the Gold Coast and from the

Portuguese islands, a small amount of wild rubber, and a little mahogany are other products. The mineral products of central and west Africa are increasing in number and value as further discoveries are made. Copper from the Belgian Congo is at present the largest in amount and the greatest in value, and enormous deposits have been located. 

There is tin in Nigeria, and some gold from the Gold Coast.

The east African coast is divided into two regions. The one to the north is almost a desert. The one to the south has abundant rains and a tropical and semitropical vegetation. This region is partly under the control of Great Britain, and partly under that of 

Portugal. Its chief products are peanuts, copra, and sugar. It is from this part of 

Africa that most of the native laborers in the gold and diamond mines (A) of South Africa come. This is largely due to the fact that railroads have been built into the mining regions from the coast, providing transportation for laborers, and for supplies and other A. East Africa, unfortunately for its people, is much farther from world markets than is the region around the Gulf of Guinea, and its trade will therefore be slower in developing.

South Africa gets rain enough for some crops along the coast, but the interior is chiefly a grazing region. It is largely given over to the raising of sheep and goats, and there are many millions of each. Cattle and horses are raised, but insects so annoy these animals that they are raised in much smaller numbers than in grazing countries where no such pests are found. The number of ostriches raised increases or decreases with changes in the use of their feathers.

The mineral resources of South Africa are of great value. Of these, the diamonds of the Kimberley region and the gold from the market for diamonds and other precious stones used in the manufacture of jewelry is sometimes good and sometimes poor, as precious stones are not always in demand. But gold, on account of its use as money, is in constant demand. 

Cities. From what you have learned about Africa you will not expect to find many large cities. The two largest are in Egypt 

Cairo, the capital, has a population of more than a million; and Alexandria (A), the port, has a population about half as large. These are the only cities in Africa with a population of more than half a million. 

Johannesburg, in the center of the goldmining region called the "Rand," is the largest city in the Union of South Africa. It has a population of about 380,000, most of whom make their living out of the mines or through trade. Cape Town, the chief port

AFRICA 

of South Africa, is next in size. It is a city with a beautiful and picturesque location. Another important city in the Union is 

Durban, a port which, like Cape Town, is a trading center and outlet for the mining regions of the interior. 

Algiers, with more than 250,000 people, Tunis, with more than 200,000, and Oran with about 170,000, are the chief ports on the western Mediterranean. Marrakech, with a population about as large as that of Tunis, and Casablanca, with a population a little less than that of Oran, and the smaller city of 

Fez are the three chief cities of Morocco.

Ibadan in Nigeria has a population of about 250,000, while Khartoum and Omdurman in the Anglo-Egyptian Sudan, Port

Said on the Suez Canal, and Constantinean inland city of Algeria-each have a population of over 100,000.

ASIA 

Asia is the largest continent. Its area is greater than the combined area of North and South America, or that of Europe and 

Africa. On a globe you will see that Asia is so large that by contrast Europe seems to be only one of its peninsulas. Indeed, some geographers like to think and speak of the two continents as one, called Eurasia. 1 Position. On maps and on a globe, study the position of Asia in our world. At the south, one of its peninsulas reaches within a short distance of the Equator. At the north, a point on the mainland is beyond 77° north latitude; that is, within less than 

13° of the North Pole. Asia Minor, the 

Asia Minor, the westernmost peninsula of Asia, stretches westward between the Mediterranean and

Black seas, and borders on the Aegean. 

Find the famous old city of Smyrna, the most western city of Asia. It is located close to 27° east longitude. In Europe this is about the same longitude as the boundary 

| line between Poland and Russia. In Africa this longitude is over 250 miles west of Cairo, in Egypt. The most easterly point of Asia is on the shore of Bering Strait, opposite 

Alaska. It is at 170° west longitude.

Comparisons. - In North and South 

America, the principal highlands have a north-south direction, and the central parts of the continents are lowlands. In Europe, the main mountain systems have an eastwest direction, and again the central part of the continent is a lowland. Africa has some scattered mountain areas, but most of it is made up of plateaus. Now study the physical map of Asia, page 278. Notice that the central part of the continent is a great highland and that the greatest lowland is the vast Siberian Plain that borders the 

Arctic Ocean. 

The surface features of Asia offer some interesting contrasts. On the northern border of India are the Himalaya Mountains (A). 277

ASIA 1 

One great peak, Mt. Everest, is over 29,000 feet in height, and is the highest mountain peak in the world. Look westward on your map to the Caspian Sea, on the boundary between Asia and Europe. The basin in which this sea lies, and some of the land surrounding it, are below sea level. 

North of the Himalaya Mountains is the 

Plateau of Tibet. This plateau is not only the highest in the world, but is very large. 

It is more completely shut in by mountains, deserts, and the great canyons of mighty rivers than any other of the world's plateaus. 

The people who live within its boundaries know little of the rest of the world and have no desire to increase their knowledge of it. 

There are many other contrasts in Asia that are equally interesting. When you study the climate of the different parts of the continent, you will find some of the hottest and some of the coldest parts of the earth. You will find also places where no rain falls from year's end to year's end, and others where the rainfall is as much as 

500 inches in a year. 

To understand what such a rainfall means, find out how much the annual rainfall is in the place where you live. 

North America, South America, and Europe have great plains opening out on the world's seas, and it is not difficult to get into the central parts of these continents. Even the mountains there can be crossed, and railroads have been built across them to connect coastal lowlands with interior plains. Deserts, forests, swampy grasslands, savage peoples, and wild beasts have at times made travel in Africa difficult, but men have penetrated to remote corners of the continent, railroads are being pushed through, and steamboats are in use on rivers and lakes.

In Asia, with a population of more than 

1,100,000,000 most of the people live in the lower lands around a great central highland. 

That highland is so large, so high, and so difficult to cross that it has kept the peoples of Asia apart.

Map Study.-1. Observe that the map shows 

Asia and all of Europe with the exception of a part of the Iberian Peninsula. Europe looks so small on this map because the scale on which it is drawn is considerably less than half of that used for the maps of Europe on pages 72, 74, and 76. If the map of 

Asia had been made on the same scale as that used for Europe, it would extend beyond the limits of two pages of this book. In comparing the sizes of continents and countries as shown on maps, it is important to notice the scale of miles used in each case. 

Thus on the map of Asia, one inch represents a distance of 945 miles. Compare this with the scales used for the other continents (see list of colored maps on page viii). 

2. What seas, mountain ranges, and river form most of the boundary between Asia and Europe? 

What oceans are north, east, and south of Asia?

Hindu Kush, the Karakoram, the Himalaya, and the Altai mountains. Locate the Pamirs, the 

Plateau of Tibet, the Plateau of Mongolia. Locate the Arabian Desert and the desert called the Gobi. 

4. In what parts of Asia do you find considerable extents of lowlands and plains? Name the large plain which occupies most of northern Asia. Point out the Lowlands of India. The Plains of China. 

5. Observe that the many great rivers of Asia flow from the central mountain and plateau region. 

Point out three large rivers that cross the Siberian 

Plain to the Arctic Ocean. Point out the Hwang, the Yangtze, and the Si rivers-the three great rivers of China. Point out the two rivers that drain most of the Lowlands of India. 

6. Look at the map showing the distribution of the population of Asia, page 287. Where do you find the regions of sparsest population? Where are the regions of densest population? Do you find that the population is very evenly or very unevenly distributed over the continent?

Central Highland. The vast ranges of the Himalaya 

Mountains extend east and west, and some of its ranges and hundreds of its peaks are more than 20,000 feet high. Daring mountain climbers have more than once attempted to reach the top of Mt. Everest, but no expedition has yet succeeded. 

That mountain is nearly twice as high as Mt. Blanc in Europe, and more than twice as high as 

Mt. Whitney in the United States. 

American Museum of Natural History, N. Y. City

A. - The camels of this caravan have halted beside some sand dunes in the desert called the Gobi. Some of these camels are shedding their hair. The camel men collect this loose hair and save it to sell. It is used in making rugs, coats, and artists' brushes. 

On the slopes of the Himalayas, and among its higher valleys, there are great fields of snow and wonderful glaciers. 

These glaciers, like others that you have studied, move out of the high mountain valleys where they are formed, and down their slopes. Finally, like other mountain glaciers, they move far enough down their mountain valleys to get into lower and warmer regions where they melt as rapidly as they move forward. A number of the great rivers of Asia have their sources in the 

Himalayas, or in other high mountains of the central highlands. 

Under various names great mountain systems extend westward from the Himalayas through Afghanistan, Persia, Asia Minor, and southern Europe. Trace these ranges and learn the location of the Karakoram Mountains and the Hindu Kush. Where are the 

Elburz Mountains? You may think of these various ranges of Europe and Asia as making one great line of mountains, from the Pyrenees in western Europe to the southeastern part of Asia.

North of the Himalayas, in all of central Asia, is a region of vast plateaus and towering mountain ranges. The plateaus of Tibet, Turkistan, and Mongolia are very large. 

Tibet and the Pamirs have an altitude of more than 15,000 feet, or about three miles.

Because the plateau of the Pamirs is so high, it is sometimes called "the roof of the world." Rising above the plateaus are many ranges of high mountains. They run in a general east-and-west direction, in about the same direction as the Himalayas. Among them are the Hindu Kush, Kunlun, Tien 

Shan, and Altai ranges. 

Turn again to the physical map. Find the Persian Gulf. Eastward find the Plateau of Iran, the Pamirs, Plateau of Turkistan, Plateau of Tibet, and the Gobi (A). The distance from the Persian Gulf to the Khinghan Mountains, at the eastern edge of the 

Gobi, is 4000 miles, with highlands all the way. This is the interior of Asia, and it covers an area as large as the United States.

It is because of the great differences in soils and because of even greater differences in the climate between the highlands and the lowlands. 

The high mountains of southern Asia are drained by great rivers. Among these rivers are the Ganges, the Brahmaputra, and farther east the Irrawaddy and the Mekong. Although you may never have heard of the

Mekong before, it is over 2600 miles long. 

Part of the Himalayas send their waters by the Indus River to the Arabian Sea. Find all of these rivers on your map. Find also the Euphrates and Tigris rivers, which flow southward into the Persian Gulf.

Rivers of Asia. Three of the great rivers whose headwaters flow for a long distance through the eastern part of the central highlands are the Yangtze, the Hwang, and the Amur. Find these rivers on the map of drainage basins (A) and the physical map (page 278). On the north slopes of the central highland the rivers of Siberia have their sources. They flow across the vast 

Siberian Plain and enter the Arctic Ocean.

They are navigable during the summer but are of very little value for this purpose.

Gulf of Siam between the two parts. Between the peninsula of Indo-China and

India and Arabia is the Arabian Sea. To what ocean do these waters belong? Find the Persian Gulf and the Red Sea (A) and the Gulf of Aden. You know it is by way of the Gulf of Aden, the Red Sea, and the Suez

Canal that ships make their way between the Indian Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea.

On the Pacific coast there are two large peninsulas. They are Chosen, or Korea, and, far to the north, Kamchatka. You will learn that these two peninsulas are of great interest to the people of Japan and Russia. 

Find six gulfs or seas on the Pacific border and learn the location of each of them. See how the south and east coasts of Asia are fringed with large islands. These include 

Ceylon, Sumatra, Java, Borneo, the Philippine Islands, and the islands of Japan. Find these islands on the map. 

On the east and on the south, the sea border of Asia is very much broken, with large lowlands and many islands, except in the far southwest. In these lowlands, except in the far northeast, and in many of the islands, the population is very dense and there are many great seaports and much trade. You will learn more about these things when you study the countries found in this part of the continent. 

In the west, Asia touches the Mediterranean, Aegean, and Black seas, and so opens out to the Atlantic Ocean. These shores, however, are not of great length, and are today of less importance in the trade of 

Asia than they were centuries ago. 

Asia has also an Arctic coast. You have already learned about its large rivers and its vast lowlands. Along this Arctic coast there are few people, no cities, and no ships. 

Climate. Asia has great extremes of climate. As you know, the climate of a place depends on its latitude; on its height above the level of the sea; on its nearness to the sea; and on the direction of the

Tropic of Cancer them is lost, long before they reach Asia. The climate of central Asia is continental; in places the summers may be warm, but the winters are bitterly cold. 

You know that the southeastern part of Russia in Europe is a steppe. This steppe area continues eastward eastward through

Turkistan and among the high plateaus of central Asia. Very little moisture can reach central and western Asia from either the Atlantic or the Indian

Ocean, and therefore much of it is desert. Another cause of the desert condition in the countries of southwestern Asia is that they are in the belt of the northeast trades. These winds have moved for long distances across the inland parts of the continent. They have gathered but little moisture, and they descend into the warmer land of southwestern

Asia as drying winds. They continue across 

Egypt and the Sahara also as drying winds, and are the chief cause of the great desert that stretches across much of Asia and Africa to the Atlantic Ocean. This is by far the greatest desert area in the world. A.

prevailing winds. Asia stretches through many degrees of latitude. It has land that is high and land that is low. It is bordered by cold seas and warm seas, and over large areas the prevailing winds change with the seasons.

Asia lies in the same zones as the continent of North America. The northern part of Siberia is intensely cold in winter. The region where the Lena River crosses the Arctic Circle is one of the coldest places known in the world. The average temperature there in January is 60° below zero. The southern part of the Siberian plain has a coldtemperate climate, somewhat like that along the boundary between our western states and 

Canada. As the westerly winds first cross

Europe and then pass for thousands of miles over the long stretches of Siberia, all the moderating effect of the Atlantic Ocean upon The northern part of Asia is cold, and the central and western parts are dry; but the southeastern parts are wet and hot, and they contain about four fifths of the population of the continent. Southeastern Asia, including the near-by islands, has about 700,000,000 people. It is far more densely populated than any other region of equal area in the world. This is due partly to its great and fertile plains, partly to its climate, and partly to its trade with other parts of the world. In eastern China the climate is tempered by the nearness of the ocean.

Monsoons.-The climate is warm in the southern lowlands.

They are south of the Tropic of Cancer, and are but little above sea level. The rainfall of southern Asia is brought chiefly by winds from the ocean in summer. In summer the land of India and of other parts of southern Asia is highly heated by the almost direct rays of the sun. The air expands, rises, and flows outward at some distance above the surface of the earth, so that the air that remains presses less heavily on the surface. The cooler, heavier air from the Indian

Ocean pushes in across the surface of the earth toward this area. Strong winds blow from the ocean over the land. A great amount of moisture is carried inland with them and falls as rain, especially on the

Over how many miles, then, does the Asian mainland stretch from its southern to its northern limit? Your answer will show a distance more than twice as great as that from New York to San Francisco.

LIFE IN ASIA 

Waste Lands in Asia. -There are large parts of Asia where you could travel for long distances without coming upon any settlement or even a single home. If you found any people in those lands, they would probably be nomads; that is, people who move from one place to another to find better hunting or to find fresh pastures for their herds and flocks.

You have now learned enough about Asia to know that there are large parts of it in which you would not like to live. Some are high and cold; others are covered with sand and have very little rain. On many of the mountains there are only bare rocks and snow and ice. Because of the thin air and fearful cold, you could not possibly live on them. In the far north the land is low and there is enough rain, but the soils are frozen to a depth of many feet, the rivers are often covered with ice, and there is little food to be had except reindeer meat, fish, and berries from some few low bushes. Yet there are people living in some of these regions. 

How, for example, do the people, few as they are, live in cold northern lands, and in the deserts and endless plateaus of central and western Asia? 

Certainly they cannot live by agriculture. Instead, they wander from place to place. 

The nomads of northern Siberia (Russia in Asia) live in the far north only during a short summer season. At that time they gather the wild berries, and catch fish not only for summer food but to dry for winter use. In the winter they move south into the edge of the Siberian forests. There 

Arctic Circle 

Forests they may have rude huts or live in tents. 

The women stay at home and prepare the food, make clothing out of skins, and care for the herds of reindeer. The men go out in the forest to hunt for animals that have valuable furs. At all seasons the reindeer is their beast of burden and is of value because of its milk, its hide, its meat, and its bones, which are used for making tools. After the winter is over these people go back again to cold and barren northern lowlands, or tundras, where their reindeer can find food during the short summer season.

The people of the deserts and steppes also are nomads. They have many horses, camels, cattle, and sheep. These animals need pasture, and as grass is thin over much of the area and the best is found in scattered patches, the people must be more or less constantly on the move to find food for their animals. These groups of nomads are not made up of a single family, but the sons and their families, and the servants as well, stay together, and thus the family becomes a tribe. The men of the steppe are expert horsemen from childhood, and wealth consists in owning many horses and other animals. Here, as in the tundras, the women do most of the hard work of the camp. The customs of these people make them independent and brave.

Animal Life in Asia. The animal life of 

Asia is of great importance. Some of the animals are of help; others are dangerous and destructive. To live in far northern Asia, the people depend on their reindeer and on fish. 

In the forest belt there are fur-bearing animals otter, beaver, sable, and ermine whose pelts are shipped to the fur markets of Russia, to the German fur center, Leipzig, and to other countries and cities. In the 

horses are kept by the wandering tribes. In these regions the camel is one of the important beasts of burden, because it can live without water for several days when necessary. In India, elephants are found wild in the jungle. They are also trained to carry people, to haul heavy loads, and even to handle timber with their trunks.

Lions (A), tigers (C), apes, and monkeys are found in the jungles. Crocodiles (B) are found in tropical waters, and serpents are found in the tropical forests. Insects of all kinds are numerous. Boring worms destroy timber, and the people have to take many precautions to preserve health and property.

In the East Indies, especially, there are many birds of brilliant plumage.

SOUTHWESTERN COUNTRIES 

The map of Southwestern Asia on the opposite page shows the countries west of India. The three largest of these are Persia (or Iran), Turkey, and Arabia, but the names and boundaries of others also are shown on the map. As you study the map, notice the waters that border this part of Asia. On the north you will see the Caspian and Black seas, on the west the Aegean, Mediterranean, and Red seas, and on the south the Gulf of 

Aden and the Arabian Sea. Between the

Plateau of Arabia and the Plateau of Iran are the Gulf of Oman and the Persian Gulf.

These two plateaus are still farther separated toward the northwest by the lowlands through which the Tigris and Euphrates rivers flow on their way to the Persian Gulf. 

Although southwestern Asia seems to include only a small part of the great continent, it is about four fifths as large as the 

United States. Yet it has only one fourth as many people as are found in our country, and ours is not one of the densely settled countries of the world.

Peninsula of Arabia. It is high, rugged, and barren, and only a small part of it has ever been carefully explored, most of it being known only to the nomads who wander across it. The plateau is, however, bordered by a narrow coastal lowland from the northern end of the Red Sea almost to the entrance of the Persian Gulf. There are lowlands on both sides of the Persian Gulf, and these extend northwest along the Tigris and Euphrates rivers - the Mesopotamia (betweenthe-rivers) of ancient days.

The Plateau of Iran also is high and barren, but there is a narrow lowland along the Arabian Sea. The mountains bordering the plateau are high and forbidding, with few passes across them to the interior. On the north of the plateau are ranges belonging to the great mountain system that extends through southern Asia and southern Europe. 

Trace the mountains at the northern edge of the plateaus of Iran and Arabia, and through Asia Minor to the Aegean Sea.

Notice especially the mountains east of the 

Caspian Sea, bordering the lowlands of 

Russia in Asia to the north.

Climate. -Study again the rainfall of southwestern Asia as shown on the maps on

A still greater contrast is shown between the population of southwestern Asia and that of such a densely settled region as west-pages 284 and 285. You will remember that central Europe. The combined area of Great 

Britain, France, Belgium, the Netherlands, and Germany is only a little more than one fifth that of southwestern Asia. But the combined population of these west European countries with their excellent climate, rich natural resources, many manufactures, and extensive trade, is more than three times as great as that of this part of Asia. Why should not southwestern Asia be as densely settled? Why are there so few people living in this part of Asia when there are so many living in India just to the southeast? 

Surface. - The surface of much of south-❘ western Asia is high and rough. On the map find the two plateaus of Arabia and Iran. 

The Plateau of Arabia occupies most of the much of this region lies in the path of the trade winds that sweep out of the northeast and on toward the southwest across Arabia and into North Africa. These are drying winds, and leave but little rainfall behind except on mountain slopes, in mountain valleys, and over the irregular surface of some parts of the plateaus. This general lack of rainfall leaves much of the region a desert. Within the desert areas there may be, from time to time, some scant rainfall along the higher slopes of its irregular surface or in valleys among its highlands. This rainfall may sink into the ground and come to the surface in some lower place as a spring to form an oasis. If there is too little rain for an oasis, there may still be enough for a

ASIA 

A. Nomadic Arabs in camp on the edge of the desert. thin growth of grass. All such bits of pasture land are known by the desert nomads. 

Because of the nearness of southwestern

Asia to the Equator, its temperature ought to be high at all seasons of the year. But much of the higher land is so high above sea level that it is usually cool during the winter, and temperatures below freezing are sometimes reached.

In the summer, even in the plateaus, the direct rays of the sun, which are north of the Equator at that time, bring hot days. 

Along the narrow coastal plains the heat is intense, except when winds from the bordering seas help to cool the air. The summer heat in the Tigris-Euphrates lowland is so great that it is one of the hottest spots on earth.

In a region of so little rainfall there will be few rivers. There are only two large streams in this whole area. These are the 

Tigris and the Euphrates. Their headwaters come largely from the mountains of northern Turkey, but after leaving the mountains they flow through broad, flat plains. 

Ever since the dawn of history, water from these rivers has been used to irrigate these plains, and it is so used today. These plains were among the most fertile lands of the ancient world. Here grew up, one after another, several great civilizations; each one lasting for a time, only to be conquered finally and to give way to the next.

The People of the Desert. The groups of nomads who live on the dry Plateau of Arabia, and in other dry regions of southwestern Asia, make a poor living and endure great hardships. They are a wild and independent people who measure their wealth by the number of animals that they own. 

Much of their life is spent in wandering with their animals from one small bit of pasture to another, where food and water for their camels, horses, sheep, and goats can be found. Occasionally some of them may visit an oasis in the desert or some small settlement on the desert edge to get food or other articles that they may need. They offer cheese, skins, wool, or camels' hair in payment for a saddle, dates, flour, or some coffee. After their trading is over they ride back into the desert to join their flocks again. 1 

Towns, Farm Lands, and Crops. There are many gardens or small farms in parts of southwestern Asia, where grain, vegetables, and fruits can be grown. Most of them

A. - Raisins being dried in the sun in Persia. Persian vineyards produce over 150 varieties of grapes, many of which are famous for their fine quality. are found in one or another of four kinds of locations: (1) small valleys among the mountains and on the lower slopes where rain or melting snow furnishes enough water for the growing season; (2) valleys where water for irrigation is drawn from the streams that flow through them; (3) true oases, around springs or wells in desert areas; and (4) land along the margin of the desert. In each of these regions small towns grow up, the size depending on the size of the area that can be cultivated. These garden and farm lands usually yield enough grain, vegetables, and fruit to support the population of the towns, and a small surplus to exchange with the desert nomads. 

Around each oasis you will find groves of date palms whose fruit is gathered, dried, packed in boxes, and sent by camels to some seacoast town for export. Coffee is grown in Yemen, in the southwestern part of the 

Peninsula of Arabia, on the Red Sea. It is grown on the hillsides where a small amount of rain and fogs drifting in from the sea furnish the moisture needed. Here is Mocha, the town that gave its name to a famous brand of coffee, years ago. Not much of this coffee ever gets into world markets now, because most of it is used by the Arabs, who are lovers of coffee.

There are valleys among the mountains of Afghanistan and Persia, and on the margins of the Plateau of Iran, where the climate is much like that of the Mediterranean borderlands. There is a small winter rainfall, and crops of wheat and barley are raised. 

Summer crops are irrigated, as they are along the Mediterranean, the water being taken from wells and streams. Figs, grapes, peaches, plums, apricots, and melons are among the fruits that are grown. Among the exports of Persia are sun-dried grapes, or raisins (A). Cotton and tobacco are grown on irrigated lands, and nut and mulberry trees are grown in protected valleys. There is a small silk industry in both Persia and 

Afghanistan, based on the use of mulberry leaves as food for silkworms.

In the more rugged parts of Persia, and in much of Afghanistan, little farming is done,

Courtesy Near East Foundation, N. Y. Cuy - An Oriental rug being woven on a hand loom in Persia. The loom master sings the count of the different colored knots to be tied for the pattern, as a guide for the other workers. and the people give most of their attention to the raising of sheep, goats, camels, and horses. Some of the most interesting industries of this whole region are based on the use of such raw materials as hides, skins, wool, and silk. The hides and skins are used in the making of leather goods, including saddles, pouches, and book bindings. The wool and silk are used in the making of fine rugs, shawls, and cloth. 

Oriental Rugs. The Persians, especially, are skillful in the making of fine Oriental rugs (A). These rugs are used on floors for their warmth and softness, on walls for their beauty of design and rich coloring, and as covers for great sacks of wool on which some Persians rest or sleep. Almost every district has its own patterns, colors, and methods of manufacture. Those who know about these can usually tell, by examining a rug, from what country and from what part of that country a rug came. The de- | mand for Oriental rugs is now so great that many of them are being made in workshops instead of in the homes of the people as formerly. 

Petroleum Production. It is probable that the mineral resources of southwestern 

Asia are not fully known. At the present time only petroleum is important. This is found in Iraq (Mesopotamia) and in Persia.

So much oil is now produced in Persia that it has become one of the most important oil regions of the Old World.

Why the Population Is Small. Some of the things that you have learned about this southwestern part of Asia will help you to understand why so large an area has so small a population. Review these facts briefly. 

A large part of the region is a desert. Parts of this desert are unexplored and unknown, and are believed to be unproductive and uninhabited. Other parts furnish scanty pasture and a limited water supply for the

SOUTHWESTERN COUNTRIES 

295 flocks of nomadic peoples. Farm lands and towns are found in mountain valleys where there is rain or melting snow, in irrigated valleys, at the edge of deserts, and in oases where water taken from springs and wells make them possible. There are no manufacturing industries except such as are carried on in the homes of the people or in small workshops, and such as use local supplies of raw materials. Mineral resources, except oil, are almost lacking, and trade is small in amount and limited to a few articles. 

Yet explorers have found the remains of many ancient civilizations, and of great cities that were built within this region. 

Out of it have come great religions. What is the story of the rise and fall of these ancient peoples? Will that story help you further to understand why this part of Asia has today so small a number of people? 

The Story of Those Who Lived in South western Asia Long Ago. In the Old 

Testament of the Bible, we find stories about the people who from time to time ruled in the valleys of the Tigris and Euphrates.

Some of them also extended their power beyond the borders of Mesopotamia; to the east, as far as India; to the west, as far as the Aegean and Red seas.

At a very early time the southern part of Mesopotamia was occupied by the Babylonians. Their royal city was at Babylon not far from the present city of Baghdad.

The northern part of Mesopotamia was occupied at about this time by a fierce, warlike people called the Assyrians. They had their capital city at Nineveh, across the river and not far from the present city of 

Mosul. Wars between these two peoples were carried on for a long time, but finally ended when the Assyrians were conquered, and Nineveh destroyed.

Later the Babylonians were conquered by the Persians, who came out of the plateau on the east of Mesopotamia. The Persians pushed their conquests both east and west, and for a time ruled over much of this region that we have called southwestern Asia. 

The Hebrews, wandering shepherds, came from Chaldea, the region to the south of Babylon, and we find interesting stories of their wanderings in the Old Testament. 

There you can read of Abraham, going from

Ur in Chaldea westward across the desert, and finally settling in Palestine. In one of the Hebrew homes the founder of the Christian faith grew up. So both Jews and

Christians are interested in Palestine and call it the Holy Land. 

Most of the people who live in southwestern Asia are not Hebrews or Christians, but 

Mohammedans. Mohammed was a religious teacher who lived in Arabia about six hundred years after Christ; and his followers are called Mohammedans. They believe that "There is one God, and Mohammed is his prophet." Their sacred book is the Koran.

So firmly did they believe in the teachings of the prophet, that they attempted to make people accept their faith by the sword.

Mohammed was born in Mecca, and was buried in Medina. To his followers both cities are sacred, and are visited by many thousands of pilgrims (296 A). Pilgrims from the north can make use of a railroad to

Medina, but from Medina to Mecca the journey is made by caravan. 

A Crossroad for Many Nations. This whole region has often been called a crossroad." What does that mean? From the time of the Phoenicians down to the time when the Ottoman Turks came out of central 

Asia and conquered all of southwestern Asia, it was crossed by trade routes. It was these 

Turks who blocked the trade between the East and the Mediterranean, and that, as you know, finally led to the discovery of the 

New World. 

During the thousands of years that trade was carried on across this southwestern part of Asia, two routes between the Mediterranean and Arabian seas were used. One

ASIA 

A. A pilgrim camp in front of a large Mohammedan mosque in a village outside Mecca (page 295). This is one of the places that must be visited by those who go on pilgrimages to Mecca. of these was by way of the Persian Gulf and the Euphrates Valley and overland to the Mediterranean. The other was by way of the Red Sea and across the Isthmus of Suez to the Mediterranean. Other trade routes crossed the plateau lands to points on the coast of Syria. Although the Turks blockaded the trade routes for a long time, they finally allowed the caravans to cross their lands again. But they ruled the nations they conquered with great harshness, and collected such heavy taxes that most of the people were always poor. Not only were the trade routes across and along the Mesopotamian valley reopened, but they are still Caravans still follow the ancient in use. trails, and goods are still carried in and out of the hidden parts of this region on the backs of camels. Caravans no longer follow the route across the Isthmus of Suez. 

The Suez Canal was opened in 1869, and became a link in a great water route connecting the North Atlantic and Mediterranean with the Indian Ocean. As a result of the World War, Turkey was forced to give up its control of most of the people that it had once governed. Both Turkey in 

Europe and Turkey in Asia are but small remnants of the once great Ottoman Empire. 

Other methods of transportation are coming into use. Motor roads are being built and automobiles can now follow the

SOUTHWESTERN COUNTRIES 

297 old paths across the deserts, through the mountains, and on the plateaus. The motor highways connecting the larger cities are being improved. Airplanes are also in use over a few routes.

The nations of Europe have much to do with southwestern Asia. Great Britain controls the Suez Canal and Aden on the route to India and Australia. Germany before the war was building a railroad from 

Berlin to Baghdad and on to the Persian

Gulf. The Germans were seeking for a larger trade with the East, over a route that would rival Great Britain's sea route through the Suez Canal. Russia is hoping to arrange for a route across Persia to the Indian Ocean. 

The French have a "mandate" for Syria and the British have one for Palestine, lands which were under the control of the Turks before the World War. This means that the country having the mandate must keep order and insure good government for these smaller, less influential countries.

Such a mandate is given by the League of Nations to some country strong enough to protect the dependent country, so that its people may have time to learn modern ways, with a view to taking over the control of their own affairs.

11. Why has southwestern Asia been called the crossroad of the nations "? Turkey. The westernmost country of 

Asia is Turkey. Turkey in Asia includes all of Asia Minor, or Anatolia, the peninsula that has the Black Sea on the north, the Aegean 

Sea on the west, and the Mediterranean Sea on the south. Most of it is a rugged plateau, bordered by ranges of mountains on the north and on the south.

The interior of the peninsula is a semi-arid region, bordered on the south by the Taurus Mountains. The chief industry there is the grazing of large flocks of sheep and goats.

Some wool is exported, but much is used in the manufacture of Turkish rugs and carpets, and in the weaving of woolen cloth. The famous Angora goats that supply the fiber for mohair cloth are natives of this part of Turkey. 

Along the Mediterranean shores of Turkey there are farming regions with a Mediterranean climate. Wheat, barley, tobacco, cotton, fruits, and nuts are grown in Turkey, largely by irrigation. The chief fruit-growing region is near Smyrna, where raisins and sundried figs are prepared for export. Much of the tobacco is exported for use in preparing special blends of Turkish smoking tobacco.

The country is rich in minerals, but little of the mineral wealth has been developed. 

Some petroleum is exported, but large deposits of coal and iron ore remain almost untouched.

Turkey, although the textile industries are increasing. There are cotton mills in Smyrna and Adana, and many rugs are made in the homes and workshops of the people. Adana is in the midst of a cotton-growing region where cotton production is increasing. Besides cotton mills it has cotton gins and cottonseed-oil mills.

Armenia, which for a short time after the

World War was an independent country. It is a mountainous land, and the chief industries are farming and grazing. The Armenians are of the white race and are Christians. They have long felt that they have been cruelly treated by the Turks, and have tried to free themselves from from Turkish

Under the new government, they are being treated much better. The small part of Armenia not in Turkey is a republic, and belongs to the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics. 

Syria, Palestine, and Trans-Jordan. 

Syria, which was made a French mandate after the World War, lies east of the Mediterranean. Here, to the north of Palestine, are the Lebanon Mountains, where the giant cedars mentioned in the Bible may still be seen.

Some agriculture is carried on in Syria, but irrigation is necessary. At the present time, less than a fourth of the land that can be used for crops is being planted. Cotton, silk, and tobacco are produced.

Aleppo is a commercial center in northern 

Syria. Damascus, in an oasis of southern

Syria, is the chief city of the country and a trading center (B). 

Near Syria is the large island of Cyprus.

Palestine is a small country, but is of great interest because here the most important events of Hebrew history took place. Here Here

The southern part of Palestine was the ancient kingdom of Judah, and the northern part was the kingdom of Israel, containing Nazareth, the home of Jesus.

Palestine is called in the Old Testament "a land flowing with milk and honey," but this statement is far from being true now.

ASIA Since those early days the country has been sadly neglected, its trees have been cut away, and much of the soil has been washed from the hillsides. At the present time it is beginning to prosper again under modern enterprise. 

Railroads extend from Haifa and Jaffa to 

Jerusalem. Another runs from Damascus to the sea at Beirut, and a long line extends from Smyrna to Damascus, and far southward through Trans-Jordan. Trans-Jordan is an 

Arab state under British protection. The railroad through it goes on to Medina, and may be continued to the outskirts of Mecca -the sacred cities of the Mohammedans.

Iraq and Arabia. - Iraq, also called Mesopotamia, is the region of lowland along the Tigris and Euphrates rivers. It was the seat of ancient empires and of the cities of Nineveh and Babylon. Here, as in Egypt, irrigation was practiced in ancient times, and its use is again increasing with the revival of agriculture. New irrigation canals are being built and the old ones repaired. One of the chief resources is petroleum, of which large amounts are obtained. Baghdad is the principal city, with many mosques with tall, graceful minarets. Goods and passengers are carried on the rivers by rafts and steamboats. Iraq is an Arab kingdom, until recently under the protection of Great Britain. 

Arabia is about one third the size of the United States. It is widest at the south and is mainly a high plateau with a very dry climate. The only important cities are

Mecca and Medina, one the birthplace, the other the burial place of Mohammed; and

Aden, on the southwest coast of the peninsula. This last-named city is owned by 

Great Britain and is fortified. It is an important fuel and supply station for ships using the Red Sea route. 

Oman is an independent state. Its seaport is Muscat, from which many dates are sent to the United States. In the Persian Gulf are important pearl fisheries. 

Persia. Persia, now called Iran by the

Persians, is an ancient country. Many centuries ago it was very large, reaching from the 

Mediterranean Sea to India. At that time it was the most powerful empire in the world. 

In the ancient capital of Persepolis its rulers built a magnificent palace that was burned down by Alexander the Great. Early in 

1933 the earth and sand that had so long covered the ruins of this palace were cleared away. away. Beautiful statues, great stairways (301 A), and other wonderful works of the ancient artists of Persia were found. They are described as the most beautiful ever found in Persia.

The Persia of today is a country nearly three times as large as France, but has less than one fourth as many people. So much of it is desert or barren mountain side that food for a large population cannot be raised. 

Much more of everything could be produced, however, if the people had the skill and the machinery that are common in 

Europe and America.

The surface of nearly all of Persia is a plateau with many mountains and valleys. 

Over much of the area the rainfall averages only about five inches a year. There are few rivers and many deserts. The streams usually disappear in the desert sands. The snow and rain of the mountains supply such streams as the country has, and the water is used in the valleys for irrigation. The northern part of the country, around the Caspian Sea, has a moister climate and considerable forest, but it is unhealthful. Silk, wool, cotton, tobacco, wheat, and barley are common products of Persia, as are fruits and gums. Many sheep and cattle are raised. 

Much of the wool is used in making rugs and shawls which are among the finest of those produced in Asia.

The cities have fine mosques and some beautiful shops. The houses are usually made of dried mud, and the windows open into an inner court, leaving the walls facing

Northern Asia. You learned much about northern Asia when you studied it as a part of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics. 

Remember the three belts of country that make up this great northern lowland of Asia.

In the far north are the tundras. South of the tundra belt is the forest belt, sometimes called the Taiga. And south of the Taiga is the region where wheat is raised. 

Most of these three belts are a vast plain with a gentle slope toward the Arctic Ocean.

Only on the south, hills and mountains begin to rise toward the central highlands of Asia. 

On the tundras there is little grass, with moss and wild flowers in the short summer,

For a long time only a few nomads lived in the tundra belt. Studies made in this region have shown that it has vast mineral wealth and a number of mines are now being worked. Several large mining settlements have been established with which communication is maintained by airplane from cities along the Trans-Siberian route. In summer timber is sent down the rivers to ports on the north coast which can be reached by ships during several months of each year.

The great forest is also being opened up by lumbermen and here and there small villages are beginning to appear. From the forest, also, hunters and trappers obtain the skins of ermine, sable, beaver, fox, mink, and marten, most of which are sold in the fur markets of Europe or in those of the United States.

The Trans-Siberian Railroad runs through an important farming area in which wheat growing and dairying are the leading industries. Along this route there are a number of large cities, including Sverdlovsk, Omsk, Novosibirsk, Krasnoyarsk, Irkutsk, and a number of smaller places. 

In recent years railroad building in Siberia has been very active. Much of the Trans- 

Siberian Railroad has been double-tracked, and a new line has been built from Taishet to a new port on the Gulf of Tartary. East of Lake Baikal a line paralleling but at some distance north of the Trans-Siberian route was opened late in 1937. It connects Kadrymskaya and Khabarovsk. Other routes are under construction. River boats and airplanes are used to transport goods and passengers. In the winter when the rivers are frozen, goods are drawn on ice sledges.

NORTHERN, CENTRAL, AND SOUTHWESTERN ASIA 303 Central Asia. Parts of the plateaus of central Asia are more than 15,000 feet above the level of the sea. This is in the region bordered by the Himalayas on the south, and the Hindu Kush, Tien Shan, and Altai ranges on the north. Not all of this region reaches this great height. sea.

These lands are far from the sea. The winds blowing into, or across this region, lose their moisture on the cold slopes of the bordering mountains. It is a region of little rain. Water is scarce, the grass is sparse, few crops can be grown, and there are not many people (map, page 287). From this high central part of Asia no river reaches the The streams dry up and are lost in desert sands, or they flow into salt lakes or marshes in the desert. Some few caravans cross these high and lonely plateaus and deserts between east and west, as they have done for thousands of years. Sometimes, American and European men of science go into central Asia to carry on explorations. 

But most of the vast uninhabited spaces of central Asia are little known to the modern world.

You will learn more about these interior lands when you study the provinces of China. 

So far in your study of the different parts of Asia, you have been studying regions in which the population is very sparse. On pages 305351 you are to take up those parts which are among the most densely settled regions in the world-southern and eastern Asia. It is here that 900,000,000 people live nearly half the population of the world.

INDIA 

In the days when the Phoenicians were masters of the trade of the Mediterranean world the name of India was often heard in their market places. It was spoken of as a land of splendor and magnificence, and of unbelievable riches. There were stories of gorgeous temples and palaces, of great empires, and great rulers. By sea routes and by caravans there came to these Mediterranean merchants lovely silks, incense and spices, gold and precious stones from India. 

From Phoenicia to Greece, from Greece to 

Rome, from Rome to Venice, Genoa, and

Pisa, passed the control of the trade through the lands of Europe. All through the hundreds of years that this trade lasted, the stories of a gorgeous East endured. So firmly fixed became the belief in the unlimited wealth of the Orient that when, at last, the trade with the East was shut off, Spain and Portugal began a search for a new route. 

You know the rest of the story. A New

World was discovered. It was at first thought by its discoverer to be part of the "Indies" (southeastern Asia and the East

Indies) for which he was searching. In that mistaken belief he named the native people of 

America" Indians — a name their descendants bear today. A new way to the East was found by the Portuguese. The decline of the 

Mediterranean countries set in, and the rise of the countries of western Europe followed. 

Through the years of later European history there were national disputes, rivalries, and wars that have lasted down to the present day.

In the struggle for India it was the British who at last won. The story of their conquest of India has its bright and its dark pages. 

Yet neither Germany nor Russia was content to let the British enjoy the trade with the East that they had won. Just before the outbreak of the World War, both Germany and Russia were trying to get to the Indian Ocean to absorb or sidetrack some of England's trade with the East.

There is a movement in India to force the British government to give up its control. In your study of this land of many millions, try to learn whether, after all, India is a great prize for Great Britain. Try to learn also whether British control has been or has not been a good thing for the people of India. 

Position and Size. - Study the map of 

India on the opposite page. At its southern end you will find Cape Comorin, about 8° north of the Equator. Southern India, therefore, is in a very warm part of the earth. 

Follow with your eye the heavy northern boundary line to the place where it bends farthest north. At that point it reaches 37° north latitude. That is nearly as far north of the Equator as Richmond, Virginia, and 

San Francisco, California. It is about 2000 miles from the northernmost to the southernmost point of India. 

See how nearly midway between these two points the Tropic of Cancer crosses India. 

The part to the south lies in the Torrid Zone. 

The part to the north is in the North Temperate Zone. Yet there are parts of the temperate region which are very hot, and others which are very cold. As you study 

India, watch for the reasons for these great differences in temperature in the regions north of the Tropic of Cancer. 

Look again at the northern boundary line. 

It runs from western Baluchistan to eastern Burma. Notice that this boundary is through mountains for almost all of the way. 

The total width of India is about 40° of longitude, equal in that latitude to more than 

2000 miles.

Making use of the scale of miles, measure the length of the coast line from the southwest corner of Baluchistan, around India, and south along the coast of the Malay Peninsula to 10° north latitude. What do you find?

There are really more than 5000 miles of sea coast, without measuring all the smaller

ASIA bends in and out. On the west of the Peninsula of India is the Arabian Sea; on the east is the Bay of Bengal.

The whole of India is three fifths as large as the United States. It is governed or controlled by Great Britain, yet in size it is equal to nineteen Great Britains, and has more than seven times as many people. 

The map colors (page 304) give a very clear idea of the surface of India. Study the colors that show elevations. South of the

Tropic of Cancer the country is largely a plateau with an almost unbroken range of mountains along the west coast, and other but more broken ranges along the east coast. 

This is the Deccan. On the west the coastal lowland of this plateau of southern India is narrow, but on the east it is much wider, and lowlands along the rivers extend back among the highlands. Follow the entire coast line. 

From the head of the Bay of Bengal, a wide lowland reaches north to the mountains and west along the broad valley of the Ganges. 

Similar lowlands are found in the northwest along the Indus River and the Arabian Sea. 

Most of the area between the high ranges at the north and the plateau of southern India is less than 2000 feet above sea level. 

On the north of India the high wall of the Himalaya Mountains shuts out cold winds from central Asia, and also makes it difficult for enemies to attack India by land. These mountains do for India, therefore, exactly what the Alps do for northern Italy, except that the Himalayas are about twice as high as the Alps, and have fewer and much higher passes. It is interesting, also, that Mt. Blanc, the highest peak of the Alps, is only about half as high as Mt. Everest, the highest peak of the Himalayas. This last-named peak, as you know, is the highest mountain in the world-reaching almost six miles above the level of the sea.

The passes across the Himalayas are from 16,000 to 19,000 feet above the level of the In crossing these mountains it is necessea. 

sary to climb higher to reach a pass than it would be to climb over the top of any mountain in the United States. Find the famous 

Khyber Pass between India and Afghanistan.

The British guard it carefully, and, as you have already learned, they have built a fine military highway for the use of troops and their equipment, in case of need. It would be very necessary in case of any Russian advance against India by way of Afghanistan. 

Climate of India. From what you have just read you will understand that the surface of India is divided into three well-marked regions of varying elevation. The southern part is a plateau with bordering mountains on the east and west, and with coastal lowlands and lowlands along the larger rivers. 

North of the plateau is a region of much lower elevation, especially along the Indus and Ganges rivers. North of that are the great mountains along the northern boundary. 

Such differences in elevation produce differences in temperature and rainfall. The regions of heavy and light rainfall depend, of course, mainly upon three things: (1) the direction of the prevailing winds; (2) whether these winds come from the land or from the sea; and (3) the differences in elevation of the lands over which the winds blow. 

In studying the climate of India, however, you will learn of changes in wind direction over the Indian Ocean that greatly influence the climate, especially the rainfall, of this great country. The monsoons have already been explained briefly on page 285. What causes the monsoons to change their direction as they do? 

In the summer time the plains of India and other parts of southern Asia are very hot. 

The air expands and flows outward at some distance above the level of the sea. The air that remains over these hot regions presses less heavily on the surface of the land. The cooler, heavier air over the ocean moves toward the land and pushes under the lighter air to be heated in its turn. During the
