The rainfall on the southern slopes of the Himalayas in summer is very heavy (A). 

It falls as rain on their lower parts and as snow on their upper parts. In places where the snow gathers in protected hollows it piles up in great masses and slowly changes to ice, forming large glaciers. Many rivers have their sources among these high mountains, and flow out upon and across the central plains on their way to the sea. 

On the slopes of the Himalayas there are extensive forests. At the foot of the mountains there are tropical forests growing for the most part in flat and swampy lands. 

Part way up the mountains, in a more temperate region, the ordinary hardwood trees are found. Higher still, are the evergreen forests, and as elevation increases these thin out and nothing is left but bare rock, snow, and glaciers. In the south edge of the Himalayas find Simla and Darjeeling (A). These places are at an altitude high enough to be cool and restful. Here British officials, business men, teachers, and others who live in India go for vacations. It has been found that people from cooler lands cannot live for a long time in hot tropical lowlands without an occasional rest in cooler places. Instead of going back to Europe, or the United States, for a rest in a climate to which they are accustomed, they go into the mountains.

Rivers. The Himalayas do more than stop the north winds and protect India from invasion from the north. The rainfall and the water from melting snow and glaciers gather into streams that unite to form great rivers. All of these mountain-born streams | carry with them rock waste to the foot of the mountains. In ages past this rock waste has been spread out to form vast plains. Another great stream of northern India is the Ganges (A). You can trace its course from its source in the Himalayas, east of Simla, to the south, then southeast, and east through a great plain. At last the river bends south again and divides into several branches, each of which makes its way across the delta lands to the Bay of Bengal. Taken together these make the "Mouths of the 

Ganges." You will need to be careful in following the course of the main stream, because it is joined by a number of tributaries which flow more or less parallel to it for a long distance. Some of these tributaries flow out of the Himalayas. Others come 

Others come from the plateau of Deccan to the south.

A third great river, which finally joins one of the delta branches of the Ganges, is the Brahmaputra. It rises in the southern part of Tibet, and flows a long, long distance in an easterly direction between the Himalaya and the Trans-Himalaya Mountains. It then turns southeast for about 150 miles and flows out of the mountains to a lowland plain. Through this plain, in northern Assam, the river flows a long distance in a general westerly direction before it turns south to join the Ganges.

These rivers have done for northern India what the river Po did for northern Italy.

They, like the Po, have brought rock waste out of the mountains and spread it out to

In that way it is like the valley of the lower Nile. The soil of these river plains is fine and fertile. Where there is enough rain, or where irrigation is possible, large crops can be raised, and on these plains you will find a very dense population. 

South of the lowlands of India is the Deccan. Much of it is a plateau over half a mile above sea level, and a large part is covered by lava from ancient volcanoes. 

This lava has decayed to form a fine, fertile soil, excellent for wheat and cotton. Along the western side is a mountain range called the Western Ghats. Along the eastern side, the Eastern Ghats are broken where the lowlands of the rivers reach a long way back into the plateau. You will notice that most of the rivers of the Deccan flow into the Bay of Bengal. In the fertile lands of their valleys, and on those of the plateau, there are thousands of villages and millions of farmers, but only a few large cities.

1. Much of the prosperity of the ancient peoples around the Mediterranean Sea was due to their control of the trade routes by which the silks, spices, gems, and other riches of India and the Far East were brought to Europe. 

2. The closing of the overland and sea routes over which trade had moved for centuries between the West and the East, led to the discovery of the New World and also to the finding of a new route to the East by "rounding the Cape " at the southern end of Africa. 

3. The Himalayas separate northern India much more completely from central Asia than the Alps separate northern Italy from central Europe. 

4. There are very great differences in the temperature and in the rainfall of the various parts of India. 

5. The monsoons are the chief cause of the heavy rainfall of the summers and the drier season of the winters in India.

Wheat is one of the leading crops, as you found it to be in our own country, in Argentina, in Russia in Europe, and in many other countries. It is raised principally in the drier parts of the Indus-Ganges plain, in northern India (310 B). There it is grown as a cool-weather crop, and much of it on lands that must be irrigated. From the central part of the Indus-Ganges lowland, the wheat-producing area extends southward in a broad belt into the Deccan. Much of the wheat raised in India is exported, because it brings a higher price in world markets than other cereals, which the natives eat. That means that by selling a bushel of wheat the native farmer will be able to buy more than a bushel of some cheaper grain. It is necessary for the poor people of India to use these cheaper grains because they must work for twenty cents a day, or less. Karachi, north of the Indus delta, is a shipping point for wheat, and at Bombay, farther south on the coast of the Arabian Sea, there are flour mills.

Barley is grown on the Indus-Ganges plain, some of it in the same regions that produce wheat. It is also grown between the wheatraising and the rice-raising regions, in the eastern part of the lowland. 

The greatest of the cereal crops of India is rice. You have found this crop growing in some of the other parts of the world, but in no other part of the world is so much rice raised as in eastern and southeastern Asia, and in near-by islands. It is the great cereal food of the Orient. In India it is grown chiefly in the lowlands of the eastern Ganges, and along the lower Brahmaputra. The region of heaviest production is the low, hot lands of the Ganges-Brahmaputra delta (A). 

Rice is grown, also, in the Deccan and in Burma, in lowlands along the coast, and along river valleys where the fields can be flooded when necessary. Much of the rice of India is used at home, but there is usually a surplus for export. Two crops a year are common. In all the densely settled parts of Asia it is usual to raise more than a single crop each year if possible.

Grain sorghum and millet are grown in the drier parts of the Deccan. These are used as food by the poorer people. 

One of the products of India that is raised largely for sale abroad, is tea (B).

ASIA A. 

Courtesy Jute Industries Ltd. of N. Y. Cuy 

Peeling off jute fiber after the jute has been gathered in shocks from the fields. 

Much fine tea is grown on the hillsides of Assam, and in the island of Ceylon. It is prepared from the leaves of a small shrub, which are picked by hand. The leaves, after withering, are rolled and dried; and the methods of preparation vary in the different countries where tea is grown. The tea plant is not a difficult shrub to raise, and the methods of preparing the leaves for market are neither elaborate nor expensive. The chief item of cost in the industry is the labor of picking and labor is cheap in India. 

Tea could be grown perfectly well in the southern part of our own country, but the cost of picking would be so great that it would not pay our farmers to raise it. 

A large amount of sugar cane is raised in the Ganges Valley. This crop needs more water than wheat, and therefore very little is grown in the dry northwest. Irrigation is necessary, even in the central lowlands where there is far more rain than in the northwest. 

Most of the sugar grown in India is used in the country itself, as it is a very valuable food. In total production, India ranks among the world's greatest producers of cane sugar. 

Two spices, cinnamon and pepper, are raised in India. 

Peanuts, castor beans, and flax, rape, poppy, mustard, and sesame seeds are grown and gathered for the oil that they contain. 

Some of these oils are used for food; others are used in the manufacture of various products such as ink, varnish, and paints. Both oil and oil seeds are exported.

Cotton is one of the most important of the crops raised in India. It is grown chiefly in the Deccan, east of Bombay, in the rich soils formed from the decayed lava flows in that region. But some is also raised by irrigation farther north. Much cotton is still spun and woven by hand. 

Some is manufactured in Indian cotton mills, of which there are several in Bombay. A large amount is sent to England, and a

INDIA 

313 smaller amount to Japan. In these two countries it is made into cloth, some of which may be sent back to India to be sold. The Indian fiber is not so long as that raised in the United States, and is somewhat more difficult to spin. It cannot be used, as the Egyptian fiber is, in the manufacture of the finest cotton goods. 

One of the fibers grown in India, and almost nowhere else in the world, is jute. It is a coarse fiber used in the manufacture of burlap sacking, rope, and string. A great deal of jute is sent from India to 

the United States, where it is manufactured. 

Jute is raised mainly on the low, wet lands of the Ganges-Brahmaputra delta (312 A).

Irrigation. The 

The lower Ganges flows through a region of heavy rains. During the summer monsoons the western coast of India, from Bombay southward, is well watered. The winter monsoons give rain to Ceylon and the near-by parts of the mainland coast. But much of India is so dry during at least a part of the year that for most crops irrigation is necessary. The natives dug irrigation canals centuries ago, but under British rule irrigation works have been greatly increased. Water for irrigation is now being supplied to more than 50,000,000 acres of land. This is over 

78,000 square miles-almost equal to the combined area of England and Scotland, and larger than Missouri. Various methods of storing water are used. There are huge, government-built reservoirs, cisterns, and and ponds. Yet in very dry years, when normal rainfall fails, the people of a large part of India are in danger of starvation. There has been much loss of life in this way, in spite of help from the government and gifts of private charity from other lands. 

A. A bullock cart on a road near Delhi. 

Animals of India. Some people in cold lands, such as the Eskimos in North America and the Lapps in northern Europe, live mainly on meat and fish. In India the people rarely eat meat. They live on grain, vegetables, and fruit. This is partly because the climate is hot and they do not care for meat, and partly because some of the most common of their animals are thought to be sacred. They would not think of killing a bullock or a cow. The bullock is thought to be very holy. One could walk up and eat the vegetables or fruit in front of a shop and the owner would not drive him away.

There are millions of cattle in India, but they are not kept as dairy animals. They are used to draw loads (A) and to till the fields. 

When they die their hides are sold, and hides are one of the large exports of India. The water buffalo loves the mud and is an ideal animal for use in the rice fields, just as the camel is the ideal animal for use in dry regions. There are goats and sheep also, but they too are kept largely for their hides and little of their meat is used. Horses are kept, but not in great numbers, and in the mountains there is an animal called the yak. 

The yak is like a big, shaggy ox and can

ASIA 

climb in the mountains where a horse cannot go.

Elephants are big and look clumsy, but they can be tamed and taught to do many kinds of work. Elephants have been trained to carry loads; to move and pile lumber in the forests and lumber yards; and to carry people either on ordinary roads or through forests where the plant growth is so dense and tangled that only an elephant could push its way through. 

There are many poisonous snakes and many insect pests, some of which are very poisonous also. They are not only out of doors, but they get into the flimsy houses and are dangerous and annoying. There are parts of the jungle in which you might meet a tiger, one of the fiercest and most dangerous of animals. Very likely you would not like to live in India, but if you had been born there you might consider it a pleasant home. 

Transportation in India. India has over 

42,000 miles of railroad. This is much more than any other country of Asia, but it is little as compared with the miles of railroad in the 

United States. Great Britain is only one nineteenth the size of India, but it has more than half as many miles of railroad. The railroads of India have all been built by 

British money and British skill. Naturally, the great network of railroads is in the central plains where the densest population is found and where the most goods need to be moved. 

There are, however, some railroads in the Deccan, but they are chiefly in the southern part. Trace the railroad from Calcutta far along the east coast of India almost to its southern tip. One railroad of special interest is the one that runs to Peshawar, near the Khyber Pass. Can you tell why? The chief railroad centers are Bombay, Calcutta,

Benares, and, far south along the east coast, Madras. Bombay is the most important because of its nearness to the Suez Canal. 

There are good automobile roads, and on these, and on thousands of poorer roads, many of the natives travel with their bullocks and their carts. A few ride sometimes on elephants. Many of the people of India are so poor that they must always walk. They have no money with which to pay railroad fares, and they own no automobiles or bullocks or bullock carts. locks or bullock carts. You would think it a great hardship if you always had to walk, although you may enjoy a long walk or hike once in a while.

Airplanes are coming into use for the few very wealthy people in India; they are also used by government officials and for government business. There is regular air service between the large cities, and air service between England and India has been established.

Cities. The large cities of India are few in proportion to the great population of the country. Great Britain, although much smaller and with a very much smaller population, has many more large cities than India; and the United States, with about one third as many people, has a great many more cities of large size. India has fewer manufactures and less foreign trade than either of the other two countries, and that explains why most of the people live in the country. They cultivate little farms instead of operating machines in mills or factories. 

Bombay has been called the "Gateway of

India." It surely is the door to India for visitors who come to it from the west, and as most of the people who visit India come from Europe, the city where they land will most likely be Bombay.

Make also a list, in order, of all the countries which would be passed.

Bombay is a city of many races. There are 

Europeans, Arab traders, Tibetans, Jews from Iraq, Japanese in a quarter of their own, and 100,000 Parsees. The Parsees are Persians who were driven out of Persia ages ago.

They are a strong race whose religion includes the worship of fire, and they keep a sacred fire which they never allow to go out.

Bombay has many factories and is the textile center of India. It has more than three million cotton spindles. Look on the map for the railway connections of Bombay, north, south, and east.

Calcutta is the great city of eastern India. 

It is 80 miles from the sea, on the Hooghly River, one of the mouths of the Ganges which flows across the delta to the Bay of Bengal. 

Calcutta has no fine harbor as Bombay has, but the river is dredged to receive large ships. 

It has a larger native population than Bombay, and many British people live there also.

It is the chief center for the manufacture of jute. The raw material comes from near-by lowlands. It is the center of the tea trade in northern India. Tea, burlap, and hides and skins are exported from Calcutta to 

Europe and America.

Madras is a port on the eastern coast. It has built fine sea walls out into the bay to form a harbor. From this city hides and skins are sent to the United States, and cotton to Japan.

ASIA 

Calcutta was long the capital of India, but in 1911 the government was moved to Delhi, which had been the capital centuries ago; and in 1931 it was housed in the addition to the old city called New Delhi. There were good reasons for making the change from Calcutta to Delhi. Some of these are: (1) The people in that region like the British rule better than do the people of Calcutta. (2) Delhi is much more central and easier to reach from most parts of India. (3) Its climate is better; and that, perhaps, was the chief reason for making the change. The summers are hot, but the officials then move up to Simla, farther north, which is a kind of summer capital. 

South of Delhi is Agra. In it is the Taj 

Mahal, a tomb built long ago by an emperor, to the memory of a beloved wife. It is of white marble, and many people think it is the most beautiful building in the world. 

In the Ganges Valley is Benares, a sacred city of the Hindus. It has many temples, and hundreds of thousands visit it on religious pilgrimages. The river is considered sacred and the pilgrims wish to bathe in it (309 A), drink some of the water, and carry more away in bottles. The water is very dirty, but these poor people believe they will be thought of much more highly if they use it. 

The chief city of the Deccan is the old walled city of Hyderabad, ruled by a native prince. 

It is larger than another city of the same name on the Indus. Hyderabad in the Deccan is a trading center far from the sea, with railroad connections to both coasts and the south.

People of India. - No other great country, except China and Japan, has so dense a population as India. Most of the people live in many little villages in the Ganges Valley and along the lowlands of the coast. the distribution of population on the population map of Asia (287 A). There are many peoples, and some of them are dark-skinned even though they belong to the white race.

There are more than a hundred languages in use, and there are such differences in religion that at times those who have different faiths quarrel with each other. A. One of the ornate and beautiful temples in India. 

About 70,000,000, or one fifth of all the people, are Mohammedans. 

Brahmanism is the religion of the Hindus, who make up most of the population of India. 

Their name for God, or the 

Universal Spirit, is Brahma; but they worship many gods. 

The people are divided into classes or castes, and the members of one caste will have nothing to do with the members of another caste. People of the lowest caste are considered outcasts. Modern government and schools and the teachings of missionaries are slowly breaking down the cruel caste system.

​The Taj Mahal, one of the most beautiful structures in India. This memorial building is 185 feet square and its dome has an inner diameter of 58 feet. It is set in the midst of a lovely garden.

Buddhism was founded on the teachings of an ancient prince in northern India, who was given the title of Buddha. He did not believe in castes and taught a life of purity and kindness. His followers are Buddhists.

There are not many of them in his native country, but there are hundreds of millions in other countries, mainly in China, Japan, and Indo-China. 

Government. - In

In the government of India, Great Britain has had a hard task. 

It rules the greater part of the country directly, while other parts are ruled by native princes acting under the protection and influence of the British government. The head of the Indian government, called the 

Viceroy, is sent out from Great Britain.

Many of the soldiers and police are natives. 

There are native Indian leaders, most of whom have been educated abroad, who are trying to secure home rule for India. The great mass of people, however, know little and care little, if only they have enough to eat and clothes to wear.

The English have done much for India. 

They have kept order and have prevented wild tribes from invading the country. 

They have improved the highways and built railroads. They have very greatly increased the area irrigated. They have made a market for cotton, wheat, jute, tea, and other products. They have helped in education, prevented famine, and improved the care of the health. They have stopped some bad customs and given more chance for happiness to women. It is very doubtful if any change of government at this time, such as is proposed by native leaders, would improve conditions. It is rather to be feared that without British money and British leadership the hard-won improvements would be lost. 

Burma and Baluchistan. - Burma is a large province with about 15,000,000 people of different races. Only a small part of the country is under cultivation. Mineral products include some petroleum (A). Rangoon is the largest city and chief seaport. It

ASIA Man- exports much teakwood and rice. dalay is the chief city of the interior. On what river is it? This province of Burma is on the east side of the Bay of Bengal, but it is governed as a part of British India. 

Baluchistan, in the northwest, borders the Arabian Sea, and is west of the Indus

Valley. It is a wild, mountainous country with few people, whose main industry is grazing goats, sheep, and camels. 

Ceylon. Ceylon has been for a hundred years under British rule. It is not quite half as large as Alabama or Illinois. The government is separate from that of India, although the island is so near. Both the summer and the winter monsoons bring rain to Ceylon. The winds of the winter monsoons are wet because they blow for hundreds of miles across the Bay of Bengal.

Much of the land is in large plantations owned by foreigners, for whom the natives work. There are few small farms. Tea is the leading crop. It is raised mostly in the southwest, where there is plenty of rain. 

Ceylon is one of the three most productive tea-growing regions of the world. Another Another large crop is plantation rubber. This industry got its start when seedlings were brought to Ceylon from Brazil. Now the cultivated rubber is raised not only in Ceylon, but also in other parts of the Far East. Much of the rubber of Ceylon is sent to the United States. 

Rice is an important food crop (311 A), but not enough is grown to supply the people, and much must be imported. Other products are spices, cacao, copra or dried coconut meat, and coconut oil. 

Sapphires, amethysts, rubies, and pearls are among the gems found in Ceylon, and there is a large amount of graphite, a mineral long used in making lead pencils.

The main port of Ceylon is Colombo (319A). 

It has a harbor protected by a breakwater, and is an important refueling station for many ships. It is on the route from Europe and the Suez Canal to eastern Asia. 

Problems to Think About. Here are a number of statements about India, with a question following each statement. Get clearly in mind in each case the facts upon which the statement is based, and then try to answer the question. 

1. Tea could be grown quite as well in the southern part of the United States as it can in India and other parts of Asia. It is not raised in our country, because it would almost certainly not be a profitable money crop. Why wouldn't it? 

2. The amount of land cultivated by an individual farmer in India seems very small indeed in comparison with what we would call a small farm in the United States. It seems small even in comparison with the small farms of the more thickly settled farming regions of Europe. How do you explain the need of such careful cultivation and the further fact that modern farm machinery is very little used in India? 

3. The United States has about 250,000 miles of railroad. India has about 42,000 miles. If India had as many miles of railroad in proportion to its area (three fifths that of the United States) it would have about 150,000 miles. If it had a mileage in proportion to its population as compared to the United States, India would have more than twice as many miles of railroad. What reasons can you think of to account for the fact that India's railroad mileage is so much less than that of the United States in proportion either to area or to population? 

4. India produces nearly all the jute raised in the world. The value of the jute exports ranks next to that of cotton, India's greatest export crop. 

Why is jute of such importance as a textile fiber? 

5. India's leading export is raw cotton and its leading import is manufactured cotton goods. 

Since India raises much cotton and has many cotton mills, and since, also, there is a great deal of spinning and weaving done by hand throughout India, what reasons can you find to explain the large amounts of manufactured cotton goods that are imported? 

6. India is one of the great wheat-producing countries of the world. Much of this wheat is sold for export and the people of India use cheaper grains, such as millet and sorghum, for food. 

Why do they not export the cheaper grains and use their wheat for food? 

7. India produces immense crops of rice and large crops of sugar cane. Why are these two crops of great importance to its people?

The capital is Bangkok, a city crossed by the Menam River and by many canals. On these 

On these waters thousands of people live in floating homes or houseboats.

French Indo-China has already been studied briefly as one of the possessions of France (page 138). It has an area about as large as that of Texas, with nearly four times as many people. It is chiefly an agricultural country with an area of very rich soil in the southwest. Its products are like those of the other parts of southern Asia that you have already studied. 

Rice is the chief crop (320 A), and the rich lowlands produce so much of this cereal that there is a large surplus for export. French 

Indo-China exports more rice than any other country in this part of the world except 

Burma. Sugar, cotton, and fruits also are grown on the lowlands, and tea and some coffee in lands that are somewhat higher. 

Large rubber plantations have been developed and much teakwood timber is taken from the forests. This wood, which is very hard and durable, is used in shipbuilding, in house construction, and in the manufacture of furniture. 

An oil having medicinal value is extracted from the wood, and a dye from teak leaves. 

Saigon is the chief port, and because of the nearness of the rice fields it has many rice mills. Hanoï, in the northeastern part of the country, is the capital. The chief railroad in the country extends northward from Hanoï across the border into China, and will sometime be connected with the railroad system of southern China. Airplanes are in use to some extent, but by far the most important transportation route of the whole country is the Mekong River, which forms a part of the boundary line between French 

Indo-China and Burma and Siam. In its lower course it crosses the southern lowlands, and it is there that it is most crowded with native boats. 

East Indies. The East Indies (or Malay 

Archipelago) are the islands lying between 

Asia and Australia. All except a few islands that are close to Australia are considered as belonging to Asia. The waters about them are not so deep as in most parts of the ocean. Looking on the map on page 356, you can imagine that all these islands make a sort of bridge between Asia and Australia. 

Notice that Sumatra, Borneo, and Celebes are crossed by the Equator. This means that each is partly in the Northern and partly in the Southern Hemisphere. Java and New 

Guinea are wholly in the Southern Hemisphere. All the East Indies are hot lands surrounded by warm seas. 

In the group are the Moluccas, or Spice Islands. These are the lands Columbus tried so hard to find; the lands which Magellan's men did find. Then, as now, men hunted for places where they could get the things they wanted. 

The East Indies are largely of volcanic origin. Active volcanoes are numerous and earthquakes occur frequently. The vegetable and mineral products are like those of the neighboring parts of the mainland.

More of these islands belong to the Netherlands than to any other country. They are known as the Dutch East Indies. All together, they have a surface almost one fourth as large as the United States, and contain over 60,000,000 people. The most important of the Dutch possessions, though not the largest, is the island of Java, which has over 40,000,000 people, and exports tea, rubber, tobacco, tin, copra, coffee, sugar, and cinchona (quinine). Almost all of the

Most of these products are taken to the Netherlands and are then sent to other countries. The relation of the Netherlands to these islands is like the relation of Great 

Britain to to India. In both cases small countries in Europe are guiding the government and the trade of very large eastern lands. Throughout the East Indies rice is the chief food crop (A). Batavia, the capital of 

Java, is one of the great trade centers of this part of the world. From it, rubber, coffee, sugar, and quinine are shipped to many parts of the world.

Sumatra is much larger than Java, but has fewer people. It produces tobacco and many tropical products. Near it are two small islands, Bangka and Billiton, which have rich tin mines. Borneo is the largest island of | the group. It is divided between the Netherlands and Great Britain. In Borneo, Sumatra, and Java, supplies of petroleum are found. The Dutch also hold Celebes, a part of New Guinea, and many smaller islands.

The Philippine Islands. - Northeast of 

Borneo (map, page 276) are the Philippine 

Islands. They have belonged to the United

States ever since 1898, when they were taken from Spain during the Spanish-American 

War. Like the other islands of the East

Indies, they are in the Torrid Zone. There are many hundreds of islands in the group, whose total area is about 115,000 square miles. Luzon is the largest and Mindanao is nearly as large, their combined area being about two thirds that of the whole group. 

The surface of the Philippine Islands is mountainous, with many volcanic peaks, and the islands are frequently disturbed by

INDO-CHINA AND THE EAST INDIES 

323 earthquakes. The whole island group is really | stations of the Pacific.

It is-a beautiful city only the higher parts of a mountain region, most of which is covered by the sea. 

The climate of the islands is like that of the other island groups in this part of the world. 

The temperature varies from warm to hot, and the rainfall is heavy nearly everywhere in the group. The seasonal variation in the rainfall is shown on the maps, pages 284, 285. 

A rather dry season comes in the winter, but rainfall is distributed so that the islands are largely covered with a dense plant and forest growth. Because of the dampness of the ground many of the native homes are raised on poles, to keep the floor of the hut dry. 

The houses of the poorer people and of the savage tribes are built of poles and thatched with grass or boughs.

Many kinds of trees are found in the forests, including a great variety of hardwoods. Since the United States took over the government of the islands, the forests have been divided into districts, which have been placed in the charge of expert foresters. 

The soils are deep and rich. In many places they have been formed in part out of volcanic rock, and made richer by the decaying plant growth of ages past. 

Copra, coconut oil used in the preparation of food products, and fresh coconuts are exported. From the abaca plant a fiber called manila hemp is obtained. It is used in the manufacture of ropes, and much of it is exported to the United States. Cane sugar and tobacco are other exports to our country. 

Other crops include rice, the chief food of the people, and corn, bananas, coffee, and spices. There are some deposits of soft coal, and other minerals have been found, but there is very little mining.

During the time the islands have belonged to the United States, good roads, railroads, and thousands of miles of telegraph lines have been built.

The chief city is Manila, one of the great trading centers and refueling and supply with a wonderfully soft and pleasant winter climate; and it is becoming popular as a winter resort. Iloilo, on the island of Panay, is the second city in size. ence. 

Ever since the islands were taken by the United States, some of the better-educated natives have hoped and worked for independ- In 1934 our Congress passed a law under which the Philippines adopted a constitution for self-government, were made nearly independent, and may become entirely independent in 1945.

CHINA 

On the map facing this page study the area on the mainland named "Chinese Republic" and included within the heavy purple boundary line. There is much confusion at the present time as to the size of the area to which the name may correctly be given.

This question is tied up with the question as to how much of the total area is actually controlled by the central Chinese government. 

For many years a large eastern part of this area has been called China propermeaning, of course, that it is the real China.

The rest of this area is divided into the great provinces of Tibet, Sinkiang, and Mongolia. 

China proper has long been, and is today, the real heart of the country. It is the part where most of the people live, where agriculture and the arts have reached their highest development, and where the chief cities have grown up.

The control of the central government over the three outlying provinces varies greatly. 

In Tibet it is very slight, and that province is practically independent. Sinkiang (or Chinese Turkistan) is largely desert, and the control of the central government there is very limited. there is very limited. In Mongolia, the 

Russians have been pushing in from the north, and in their presence is a threat of future trouble. A Mongol government for a part of this area has been set up. 

Manchuria, with a population largely Chinese, was formerly another outlying province of China. In 1932 and 1933 Japan sent troops to take possession of the province, gave it a new government, and proclaimed its independence under a new name Manchukuo. Later the Japanese seized a neighboring area. boring area on the southwest, and since then they have occupied more and more of eastern China by force of arms. No one knows whether the people of China will be able to make a successful stand against the invaders or how much of China will be lost if the Japanese succeed in their plans. Until these matters are settled, China will be treated in this book as though the entire country was still under Chinese control.

Part of the Great Wall of China.

The Chinese People and Their History. 

Until the middle of the nineteenth century the people of China proper lived almost by themselves. The mountains and deserts of the western provinces shut them away from western Asia and eastern Europe. There was a wilderness to the north until the 

Russians built a railroad through Siberia to the Pacific. The Himalayas and other mountains separated the Chinese people from India and Indo-China. On the ocean, it took months for a European sailing vessel to reach them, and, besides, the Chinese did not allow foreigners to trade in their coast cities. They were satisfied with their customs, learning, and arts, and they did not want to have anything to do with other nations. 

Confucius, born 550 years before Christ, was their great teacher and philosopher.

He taught the Chinese the best ways of life as he saw them. He said that people should not do to others things they would not like done to themselves. He thought the people should know their poetry and history, and so for centuries Chinese scholars have memorized the teachings of Confucius and the works of their poets and historians. The result of his teaching was that the Chinese liked to keep their old customs and to follow their old ways of living.

For ages the Chinese have known how to make exquisite silk goods and fine chinaware.

They made paper and published books long before Europeans invented printing. Instead of using type, however, they printed from blocks of hard wood, on each of which the words for a whole page had been cut. 

It is said by some that the Chinese invented the mariner's compass and made gunpowder before these things were known in Europe. 

But there are good scholars who do not think that these last two statements are true.

Twelve hundred years ago, the Chinese built a canal 700 miles long which is still used. 

Two hundred years before Christ they began to build the Great Wall (A), most of which

CHINA 

327 still stands to show their skill and industry. It extends more than 1200 miles from east to west, winds its way across hills and valleys, and has many watchtowers. It was built as a protection against Mongolian invaders from the north. It served its purpose, for at that time those wild enemies were horsemen, and they could not ride over or around the wall. A small Chinese army could defend the wall against them. 

This brief story of the Chinese people shows that for many centuries they have been an able and intelligent people, but they have been slow to adopt new customs. They have great respect for the past, and do not readily change from the habits and mode of life of their forefathers. Because of this, as well as for other reasons, they worship their ancestors. They like to think that old ways are best, and for a long time they opposed the building of railroads and the use of machines because they were afraid they would lose their work when railroads took the place of porters and junks, and when machines took the place of labor by hand. Yet the 

Chinese people are coming gradually to appreciate the modern ways of the western world.

The homes of most of the people are poor, being made of bamboo or dried mud. Little fuel is used, although China has much coal, and mines are in operation. Many of the people try to keep warm in garments padded with cotton (A).

Climate. The climate of China and its outlying provinces varies greatly in different sections. This is partly because the land extends across so many degrees of latitude. 

Most of it is in the North Temperate Zone, although its more southern parts are south of the Tropic of Cancer. If the United States extended through as many degrees of latitude, it would reach from Yucatan or Cuba north to Hudson Bay. Part of China is low and near the ocean, while the interior is high and far removed from the influence of the sea. 

Little moisture can reach the high interior provinces, because most of their area is in the course of the westerly winds. These winds have moved across Europe and western Asia

ASIA 

and have lost their moisture before they reach Sinkiang, Tibet, or Mongolia. The high wall of the Himalayas also shuts out moisture from the south. 

Much of China proper has a great deal more rain. All the southern parts are in the path of the monsoon winds that bring so much rain to India. The south coasts often have as much as 100 inches of rainfall a year. 

The rainfall is much less in the north, where it amounts to about 24 inches. In the regions of heavier rainfall, farming is very successful, partly because there is plenty of rain during most of the growing season and partly because full streams and canals supply water for irrigation whenever that is necessary. 

Violent storms called typhoons sometimes start in the East Indies and sweep the Chinese coasts, doing great damage. They are like the West Indian hurricanes.

In the following pages the words China and Chinese are used to mean China proper and its people. The outlying provinces (Tibet, Sinkiang, and Mongolia) will be described separately, later on. 

China proper is only about half as large as the United States, but it has over three times as many people. It is divided into eighteen provinces, somewhat as our country is divided into states. A complete census of 

China is not taken, and the population is not known accurately. The country is mountainous in the west, where it joins Tibet, and in the south, where it borders Indo-China and Burma. The main lowlands are in the east, especially along the great rivers. 

Northern China. - Northern China is in about the same latitude as northern United 

States. Compare the latitude of Peiping with the latitude of the city of New York.

The summers and winters are similar to those in northeastern United States. If you lived in that part of China during the winter time, you might find it a very cold country indeed, because there is very little fuel to burn and the houses are not kept warm. Much of the interior of northern China is covered with a fine, yellowish soil known as loess. There are places where this soil is hundreds and even thousands of feet deep.

For a thousand years Peking, now called Peiping, has been the most famous city of north China. It was long the capital of China, but it is not in a central location, and in 1928 Nanking was made the capital. Peiping is made up of two cities, each of which is inclosed within walls, with great gates (A) that were formerly closed at night and guarded by day. This custom is still followed when civil wars or invasions threaten the city. 

The inner city has magnificent palaces and fortresses. Part of it was built by one of the early emperors as a residence and was long used also by later rulers. This part is known as the "Forbidden City," because very few people were admitted within its walls during the time it was a royal residence. 

The outer city is where most of the people live. In its older part there are many little shops, narrow streets, and one-story houses. 

In the newer sections, however, the streets are broader; the houses and business buildings are modern and well built, and there are many interesting shops.

Peiping is a railroad center and is reached by trains from the north and south and from its port of Tientsin. On the north it is connected with Mukden, the railroad center and chief city of southern Manchuria. The railroad lines from Peiping reach Nanking,

Tientsin is the port of Peiping. These two cities are related to each other as are Paris and Le Havre in France. It is in much the same way that goods gathered into Paris from the surrounding regions move on to Le Havre, and through that port across the seas to all the world. 

Middle China. - The largest of the rivers of China is the Yangtze, which to the Chinese 3100 miles long, and is the main commercial river of China. Ocean steamers can go up this stream as far as Hankow, 600 miles from the sea. River steamers can go 400 miles farther. Native boats reach a point 1500 miles from the ocean. In some places men use ropes to pull the boats, and it is a common sight to see men with these ropes walking or running along the river banks. There are several large cities on the Yangtze, and the near-by country has a dense population. 

The map shows you that there is much lowland along the Yangtze River.

It ex- tends from Shanghai (A) and Hangchow past

Nanking, the capital, and past Hankow to 

Ichang. In these lowlands the climate is warm, and the millet and beans of the fields farther north give way to tea, rice, wheat, and cotton. It is in the combination of favorable conditions that you will find an explanation

ASIA 

of the dense population of this region, with its many large cities. Here are great lowlands with fine and fertile soils. There are many, many days of warmth each year.

There are abundant rains so well distributed that on most of the land two or three crops a year can be grown.

As most of the larger cities are on navigable waterways, ships can reach them. Some of these cities have factories, and all of them carry on much trade. From Ichang toward the west the lowlands narrow, but they still border the Yangtze as far as Chungking and beyond.

Not far from the mouth of the Yangtze is the city of Shanghai. This is the greatest of the Chinese seaports, and through it goes the trade of the southern part of the Plains of China. There are docks on both sides of the river, but not enough to take care of all the ships that come to this port. The commerce that must be handled is so great that the harbor is always crowded and many ships anchor in midstream, unloading and loading with the help of small boats that carry the cargo to and from the shore. More goods from our country enter China through Shanghai than through any other Chinese port; and from Shanghai, Chinese products are shipped to the United States. 

River boats are used to carry imported articles up the Yangtze to cities in the interior, but many of the imported products are for use in Shanghai. There are cotton and silk mills, flour mills, oil refineries, and plants for the repair and building of ships. 

Shanghai has become the largest cottonmanufacturing center of China, largely because it is near the chief cotton-growing region.

Hankow also can be reached by ocean ships. 

It is the center of trade for a large region and is the most important business center in the interior of China. Here and in the neighboring cities of Hanyang and Wuchang are iron and steel, cotton and silk, and flour mills. 

Southern China. South of the region that you have just been studying is a somewhat mountainous district. An island-like portion of it is cut off to the east by lowlands along a tributary of the Yangtze River. The northern border of the western part is indented by other lowlands. This highland rises toward the west and southwest, and in so doing cuts off to the east the fine farming and industrial region of South China. It is a region of heavy summer rainfall because of the summer monsoons which blow inland from the sea.

Southern China is drained by the Si River, which rises in the highlands farther west and has its outlet in the South China Sea. The lowlands through which it flows, and much of the higher land which surrounds it, are warm enough to grow two crops a year. In much of this area, rice is grown on lowland fields and on terraces that can be flooded. Tea shrubs are grown on the hillsides, and mulberry trees are grown for the raising of silkworms. 

Most of the tea and silk go to Europe and the United States. The population is so large that rice must be imported - most of it from Indo-China.

The island of Hong Kong off the coast, not far from the mouth of the Si River, and a part of the near-by mainland, are under the control of Great Britain. A great city, named 

Victoria, has been built on a fine harbor in Hong Kong and has become the center of British trade in this part of the Far East. It is one of the world's busiest ports and of the greatest importance to Great Britain (325A). 

Canton, on the Si River, is the largest city of southern China. Much of the city is like other Chinese cities that you have studied. The streets are narrow and the houses and shops are small and crowded close together. It is in this district that you will find the carvers of wood, stone, and ivory; and the makers of toys, fans, lanterns, and jewelry. All of this work is done by hand, as is also some weaving and embroidery. There

CHINA PROPER 

333 are a number of cotton and silk mills in 

Canton. Along the river front and in the streets near by, there are more modern buildings.

Many of the people of Canton live in boats on the river. Some of these boats serve only as homes from which the men, and sometimes the women, go to their work. Other boats are used in the river trade. There is a very large river trade with Hong Kong. Ocean steamers cannot get up the river as far as Canton, so both imports and exports for Canton, or for the country it serves, must be carried back and forth on smaller boats.

Transportation. There is probably no other great country in the world, with a civilized and intelligent population, that has such poor means of transportation as China. 

The whole country, large as it is, has only a few thousand miles of railroads.

There is no chimney. Why is this?

Thousands of years ago the Chinese began to cut away their forests, dig canals, and build terraces on which to grow rice and other crops. 

China was a densely populated and a great agricultural country long before the New 

World was discovered.

Most of the Chinese roads are very bad, and only recently have attempts been made to pave city streets, or to build sewers to carry off the filth of the cities. Goods are still carried on the backs of men and animals, or pulled along the streams and canals in boats. Both goods and men are transported on a kind of wheelbarrow with a large wheel in the center. Sometimes people are carried in chairs supported on poles resting on the shoulders of two men.

In recent years, however, there has been some improvement in means of transportation. Important railroads have been built and others are under construction. Automobiles and trucks are in use in the newer parts of the cities, and nearly 35,000 miles of automobile highways have been built. 

Some use is being made of the airplane, and you can go by airplane between some of the great cities.

Agriculture. -The rich lowland region of eastern China proper is one of the very densely populated parts of our earth. As most of the people are farmers (A) you can understand why farms are small, and why each farmer tries to raise all he possibly can on his little patch of land. In the United 

States a farm of a hundred acres is not considered a large one for a small family. In 

China, the man with five acres has a large farm, and the average is less than two acres. All of the work on these small farms must be done by hand (B). A few simple tools and perhaps a water buffalo, or oxen, are about all that the Chinese farmer has to help him in his work. He tries to raise as many crops a year on his land as he can. While one crop is growing he is starting the plants in a small seed bed for the next crop. If he is raising a that is planted in hills and climbs poles or trellises, he will plant still other seeds between the hills of the pole crop, or in the ground underneath the trellises. crop

The Chinese farmers have long known that it is necessary to change, or rotate, the crops. They save everything that can possibly be useful as a fertilizer; otherwise they could not have raised crops on the same ground for thousands of years. On the B.

335 steep slopes they have made many terraces to prevent the washing away of the soil, and to give them more farm land, as the farmers do in Italy and Germany. On the lower courses of the Chinese rivers rafts are built and covered with soil for making gardens. 

Thousands of people have their little homes on such rafts, for every foot of space is precious where so many millions of people must be housed and fed. 

The natural rainfall does not always provide moisture enough for the crops. In the plains, especially in central and southern China, water is raised from the rivers for irrigation, and for flooding the fields on which the immense crops of rice are grown. Rice makes up a large part of the people's food. 

Two crops a year of rice and other products are commonly grown. The Chinese raise fish in the irrigating ditches and plant mulberry trees along the banks, to furnish food for silkworms. China is one of the leading countries of the world in the production of raw silk (A). This is largely because it has the cheap labor necessary for feeding the worms and unwinding the silk fibers from the cocoons. Cotton is raised and is used in home and factory manufactures. the China supplies a large part of the world's tea. The tea plant or bush needs a warm climate, but will endure some frost. It requires plenty of moisture, but the water must not stand around the roots. Hence warm, well-watered but well-drained hillsides are good ground for the crop. Three times a year the leaves are picked, dried in the sun, heated, rolled in the hand, and then baked over charcoal fires. This process, which causes fermentation, makes "black tea." For" green tea," the leaves are roasted without being fermented. Some of the tea is pressed into "bricks," for convenience in packing in small spaces. Much of this brick tea is carried for great distances on pack animals. The cheaper bricks are made from the poorer leaves and small twigs.

The main crops raised in the different parts of China vary because of the differences in climate. Soy beans, wheat, and millet are raised in the north; and tea, rice, cane sugar, and bananas in the south. In the north, the farmers can raise but one crop in the short summer season. In the south, where it is warm during most of the year, they are able to raise two or three crops each year. 

Four fifths of the Chinese are farmers, and they are good farmers. For fertilizer they use everything that will make the soil rich and restore plant food taken out of the soil by the crops. They use muck, sewage, the waste from the house, and the muddy slime from the rivers. Because each family must get a living from a very small patch of ground, they must use every foot of it. 

They have no room for orchards, pastures, meadows, or wide roads. They do not keep cattle because they need all of their land to raise food for human beings. As a result they have very little milk to use. They do keep hogs and fowls, for these will eat things which might otherwise go to waste.

The coal and iron deposits of China are among the largest in the world. These minerals are not yet mined in large quantities, nor will they be until methods of transportation are much improved. Remember how in our country it has been necessary to transport iron ore from Minnesota and northern Michigan to the lower lake ports and Pittsburgh for manufacture. So in China transportation must be provided to bring coal and iron together, and to move the manufactured iron and steel products to market, before great iron and steel industries can be built up. There are rich deposits of copper, gold, silver, tin, mercury, lead, and antimony, all awaiting the time when metal-manufacturing industries may find use for them. Already some tin and copper are mined and exported, but only a beginning has been made in the mining, smelting, and use of metals on a large scale (A). 

Manufacturing. -There is is much fine handwork done in China. There are skillful workers who make beautiful articles out of a small amount of raw materials. Among these are silk weavers, carvers of ivory, and workers in metals. The Chinese are not only skillful, they are artistic, patient, and painstaking. They have learned how to do their work well, and they refuse to spoil it by being in a hurry. 

You have learned that a beginning has been made in the manufacturing of silk, cotton, and iron and other products in mills and factories in a few of the great cities of

Government. China was made a republic in 1912. The country, however, is 

The country, however, is so very large, and communication and travel are so difficult, that the people in different parts do not know each other very well. 

Because of this they do not always work well together, and so the government is not very strongly organized. Some of the eighteen provinces of China proper have been at times almost independent.

Although the Chinese find it hard to work for a common purpose, they usually unite to protect themselves themselves from foreigners.

Some foreign nations forced the Chinese government to grant them "spheres of spheres of influence" in China. This was a polite way of making the Chinese do as they wished and give them their trade. The Chinese government does not want the government of Japan, Great Britain, or any other foreign country to tell it what to do. It wants to get rid of foreign control. If a foreigner commits a crime in China, for example, the 

Chinese want to try him in their courts; they do not want him tried by foreigners. 

China is friendly to the United States.

Our government has never tried to force the Chinese to lease land to the United States or to grant rights to citizens of the United States that are not granted to the citizens of other countries. Our country wants the "open door" in China. This means equal rights for all to trade there. countries, and have taken back to China new ideas of freedom and progress. The old 

Chinese education meant studying the Chinese classics and poetry and committing to memory the works of Confucius and other 

Chinese philosophers and poets. Now the young Chinese want to study the sciences and industries of the western world instead.

Schools, colleges, and hospitals were founded by missionaries and others who wished to help the Chinese. Now, the Chinese having learned how to do so, want to manage these themselves.

OUTLYING PROVINCES 

Tibet. — Tibet is a high and mountainous plateau. The western part is from 14,000 to 16,000 feet above sea level and is very cold. The surrounding mountains rise much higher. As a whole the region is dry, but streams fed by mountain snows drain toward the interior of the country and end in swamps or lakes. The dryness of the air is so great that evaporation is rapid and the lakes have no outlet, and are therefore salt. The eastern parts of Tibet, however, are much lower, and many streams flow out of the highlands toward the sea. The people and the cultivated lands are mainly in the drainage basin of the Brahmaputra River. Barley thrives there, and it is the chief grain and the most important food crop. The herdsmen keep sheep, goats, and yaks-animals which can live where the grass supply is scanty. 

Yaks (A) are much like cattle, but they have coats of long, soft hair, and most of them are either black or white. Yak's milk is rich, and is made into curds, which are a favorite food of the Tibetans. Ropes and tent coverings are made of the hair, the flesh is good for food, and the animals are used to carry loads, but not to draw wagons or plows. Thus the yak is as useful in this high, cold region as the reindeer is on the 

Arctic plains. 

Cashmere wool, clipped from goats, is an important export, and brick tea from China proper is one of the chief imports. 

The Tibetans are so isolated by mountains, and so far from China proper, that they are but little controlled by the central government. ment. Lhasa, the capital, is regarded by the Tibetans as a sacred city. They try to shut out all foreigners, and only a few have ever succeeded in entering it.

MANCHURIA 

Manchuria, or Manchukuo, is east of Mongolia. It has extensive plains in the central part, with mountains and forests in the east. 

It is well watered, and has good soil and a favorable climate.

The forests are useful as a source of lumber, and in them, as in those of Siberia (page 302), fur-bearing animals are hunted and trapped. 

Cattle are raised on the plains, and fishing has become an important industry along the coast. Deposits of coal, iron, and gold have been found. Most of the people of Manchuria, however, are farmers, and agriculture is the chief industry. Among the crops grown are wheat, millet, corn, and barley. 

But in most parts of Manchuria the largest single crop is the soy bean, raised largely for food and for the oil it contains. The cake (A) remaining after the oil is pressed out is used as a fertilizer and as a cattle food.

Manchuria has more people than all the three outlying provinces of China already described. China proper is much warmer than Manchuria is, and the Chinese people love their home land and cling to the place where they were born and where their ancestors lie buried. Yet, in recent years, millions of Chinese left their old homes and sought new ones in this land of cold and snowy winters, where only one crop a year can be raised. They were forced to migrate because China proper is overpopulated and famine faces them every year or so; or else they migrated because of floods or because of civil wars.

In Manchuria the Chinese settlers found good soils and plenty of rain for crops, and in most parts of the country there is little danger from floods. But they did not escape from warfare. In 1932 and 1933 Japan, as you know, sent troops into this region and took its control away from the old Chinese government (page 325). The Japanese claimed that this was necessary in order to protect property owned by their countrymen. 

Since this was done, more and more natives of Japan have settled in this old province of China, and the Japanese have invested large sums in industries there.

Many years ago, the Russians laid a railroad across Manchuria from Siberia to Port

Arthur, where they built a great fortress on ground leased from China. Japan captured the fortress in a war with Russia in 1905, and gained control of Port Arthur, Dairen, and the Manchurian Railroad. Russia and 

Japan, one after the other, thus gained great influence in the control of Manchuria. 

When Japan set up the new government of Manchukuo (page 325), it made Changchun (renamed Hsinking) the capital. 

Mukden, in southern Manchuria, was the former capital of the province, and is still fur market. It has tanneries and manufactures flour, soy-bean oil, cotton goods, carpets, and rugs. Mukden is partly a 

Chinese and partly a Japanese city. High walls, pierced by narrow gateways, surround the old Chinese section. Many of the streets are narrow, and the plaster-covered stone or brick buildings are low and closely crowded. 

There are many little shops where articles are still made by hand, with the painstaking care of Chinese artists. Other parts of the old Chinese city have been cleared, and broad streets laid out, along which modern buildings have been put up. The Japanese part of the city is much newer and is laid out with wide, paved streets and large, modern buildings. 

There are coal mines near Mukden, and iron mines between Mukden and Dairen. 

Iron and steel plants have been built near the iron mines. Some of the mines and steel plants were developed by the Chinese, and others by the Japanese.

Dairen (339 A), in the region governed directly by Japan, is the chief port of Manchuria.

Some of the words that we use to give the idea of distance or direction are used in a very exact way. Others are used in a loose or inexact way. In the exact use of the words north and south, for example, we mean the direction along a meridian line, as shown on a map or globe. East and west are, in their exact meaning, directions along a parallel of latitude. Yet in this book the terms East, Near East, and Far East are used in a different way. When the people of western 

Europe were first trading with the people of Asia, they thought and spoke of the goods that came from Asia as coming from the "East." Later, the parts of Europe and

Asia around the eastern end of the Mediterranean Sea were spoken of as the "Near

East," and the lands of eastern Asia as the "Far East." That is the way we use the terms today.

China and Japan, therefore, are in the Far East. But we can actually reach these lands by traveling either east or west.

China, Japan, and other lands of the Far East are often spoken of as Oriental countries and their people as Orientals. The word 

Orient means East; and Oriental lands and people are the lands and people of the East. 

Japan is also called the "Land of the Rising 

Sun" because the sun rises in the east.

Japan is today the most progressive country of the Orient. This means that the people and government of Japan have adopted the ways and methods of the most highly civilized governments and people of what we call the Western World; that is,

They have sent some of their young people to be educated in Europe and in the United States. They have founded modern universities, built railroads and many warships, and created and trained a strong army and navy. They have established a great merchant marine and extended their trade all over the world.

These changes have come rapidly, as they began only a little more than seventy-five years ago. Nobody knows when the ancestors of the Japanese came over from the continent of Asia and settled on the Japan 

Islands. It was a long time ago. They were of the Mongolian or yellow race, like most of the other people of eastern Asia. 

The Japanese are different from the Chinese, partly because they have lived so long in a different land. 

In 1853 the United States sent Commodore

Perry to Japan in command of some of our warships. Our countrymen wanted to trade with Japan. But Japan had shut the doors of its country in the faces of all other nations and because of this had earned the name of the "Hermit Nation." Just what did this mean? Perry tried to arrange with the

Japanese government some way so our people could trade with the Japanese people. 

The fleet called again in 1854, and that time a treaty was made which allowed our people certain trading privileges. Then Japan opened its doors to the world. These doors are open still, but Japan, like other countries, looks carefully after its own safety and commercial welfare.

Snow-capped Fujiyama is the most famous of the Japanese mountains. It is an old volcanic cone, but it is not lost among other mountains or dwarfed by higher peaks. but lovely form. At its base are beautiful lakes.

The main islands are mountainous, and many are volcanic in origin. Some of the volcanoes are active, but many more of them have been dormant, or quiet, for a long time. 

Fujiyama (A) has had no eruption for many years, and always has a cloak of snow on its summit. It is over 12,000 feet high, and is one of the most symmetrical, or regular, in shape of the volcanic cones of the world. 

It is beautiful whether seen from the sea or from the land. To the Japanese it is a sacred mountain. They admire its beauty and they make pilgrimages to its summit. 

Earthquakes are frequent. Most of them are slight and do no harm. Some would not be known unless instruments were used

From whatever direction it is seen it has the same simple On one of these you see a native boat called a sampan. which make a record of slight earth quivers. 

Sometimes, however, there are earthquakes that are destructive. Large parts of Tokyo and other cities have at times been so shaken that they were left in ruins. Yet whenever such a thing has happened, the enterprising 

Japanese have quickly rebuilt, using steel in any high buildings to guard, so far as possible, against their falling in future earthquakes. quakes. Most of the dwellings, however, are low and made of wood. This is wise in an earthquake region, for although the houses may often sway they seldom fall.

The Japan Islands rise from a continental shelf, as do the British Isles off the west coast of Europe (map, page 278). It is

ASIA believed that they have been slowly sinking for a long, long time. The result is that the ocean waters have flowed into, or drowned," many valleys, and given the islands a very irregular coast line and fine harbors. 

Climate. Since Japan extends over a wide range of latitude, the average temperature of its northern part is much lower than that of its southern part. Differences in elevation also bring about a range of temperature between lowlands and mountain peaks that is almost equal to that caused by difference in latitude. But these facts are equally true of any country that stretches through many degrees of latitude across the North Temperate Zone, and that has high mountains. There are two other influences that are felt in Japan, however, that are not felt in all other regions of the kind just mentioned. One of these is that the Japan Islands are long north and south, narrow east and west, and are on their eastern shores washed by a warm ocean current (78 A). The other is that winds, very much like the monsoons of India, blow across the islands from the east and southeast in summer, toward the interior of Asia; and other winds blow from the west and northwest across the islands in winter, coming from Asia.

The summer monsoon picks up much moisture as it crosses the ocean before reaching Japan, and its temperature is still further increased by crossing the Japan Current. 

When this wind reaches the islands there is a heavy rainfall over the eastern lowlands and on the eastern slopes of the mountains. 

The influence of the ocean current upon the climate of Japan is much greater than that of the Gulf Stream along the eastern coast of the United States, because of the monsoon character of the summer wind over Japan. There is no such steady summer monsoon blowing across the Gulf Stream into eastern United States. The influence of the Japan Current is more like the influence of the Gulf Stream Drift off the northwest coast of the British Isles.

The winter winds are cold and dry. They blow out of the cold lands of interior Asia, but they do grow somewhat warmer as they move toward the southeast and over the seas that separate Japan from the mainland. 

They pick up some moisture, some of which falls as snow at the north and on the higher mountain slopes. You have learned of the fierce storms, called typhoons, that sometimes sweep northward in the region of these islands, and along the Chinese coast (page 328). 

These destructive winds frequently come at the time when rice is ripening and do great damage to that crop. In a country where there is never a large return to the farmer for his hard work, it is very discouraging to have crops destroyed in this way.

Which one has the greater density of population? You know, of course, that in both countries there is much waste land and some forested areas. So there are regions where the density of population is much greater than the figures show. Some farming districts of the island of Honshu have more than 1000 people for each square mile. 

As in other countries with modern industries, many of the people are gathered into cities, and most of these are in Japan proper. 

At present there are about 65,000,000 people in these islands. The population is growing rapidly, and Japan does not know where to settle her growing population. The problem is made more difficult because the Japanese are not allowed to enter as settlers into the United States, Canada, or Australia.

They have added Chosen and Taiwan to their empire and they are pushing into

Although the Japanese are of the Mongolian race, as are the Chinese, they are smaller and more keen and active. They are pleasant, gentle in their manner, soft of voice, and polite. They are quick and eager to learn new things and have rapidly adopted the use of modern machines and modern inventions. 

The Japanese are fond of lovely things.

They like the mountains, the forests, the shrubs, and the flowers (A). Their cherry trees are famous for beauty. Some that were given to our government have been planted in Washington, D. C., and every spring thousands of people visit that city to see the Japanese cherry blossoms.

There is little furniture in the homes of the Japanese except the thick mats on which they sit. They like one picture instead of many, and one stalk with blossoms if properly placed seems to them more beautiful than a large bouquet of gorgeous blossoms.

They think our homes have too many things. in them. They are neat in appearance, and few people in the world are as clean as they. 

Because Japan is so crowded with people, labor is very cheap, and only by great care is enough food secured to go around. One reason why the Japanese are not allowed to settle in Canada, Australia, and the United 

States, is that they are willing to work longer hours and for smaller wages than are the peoples of those countries. 

Government. The head of the Japanese nation is the Emperor (sometimes called the 

Mikado by Western people). There are two lawmaking bodies, one consisting of the nobility and the other chosen by the people. The Japanese are proud of their country, their government, and their people, and are very patriotic. ― -

Agriculture. The problem of supplying enough food for all the people of Japan is very serious. As in China, the people eat little meat. They do eat fish, which are abundant in the surrounding waters. There is only a little pasture land in Japan. This is partly because the land cannot be spared for this use, and partly because grass does not grow well in many parts. Grass does grow well in the north of Japan, and some cattle are raised there, but not many. The people depend chiefly on grain, vegetables, and fruit for their food, in addition to fish. 

Most of their farms are very small and are cultivated as carefully as gardens. The main crop is rice, and yet Japan proper has to import some rice to provide enough for its people. Other grains raised are millet, bar- ley, rye, and wheat. Much tea is raised (A), both for home use and for export.

The rice crop (347 A) of Japan is raised as in China and India, on wet lowlands which can be flooded. It is planted on terraced hillsides, also, where the plants can be flooded in the growing season. The rice is reaped by hand, and threshed by treading on it or by the use of a simple machine. The rice straw is used to cover roofs, or to make hats, mats, and baskets. If any is left it goes back to enrich the soil. 

Silk, as you know, is an animal product, but the silkworm eats mulberry leaves, and many mulberry trees are grown in Japan.

Much labor is needed to pick the leaves, and to feed the worms. It is even more work to unwind the small cocoons of silk

Do you wonder why our people do not raise silkworms? We could do it, for the mulberry tree will grow well in our country. We do not do it because labor costs too much with us and the business would not pay. Much of the raw silk and some of the tea used in the United States come from Japan. Tea especially is an important crop in the great island of 

Taiwan. 

Another product that comes from Taiwan is camphor. It is made from the chips or twigs or leaves of camphor trees. The 

Japanese are now careful to replace with young trees all camphor trees that die or are cut down.

Japan raises cotton, but there is not room for large fields, and most of the cotton for mills in Japan comes from the United States, India, and China. 

Minerals and Forest Resources. Coal and some iron are among the important minerals of Japan, and this is fortunate for the people, because modern Japan is building railroads, ships, and modern steel business and factory buildings. To keep all of these industries going, it is necessary to import much iron. The deposits of copper are large, and this metal also is of great value in the modern electrical industries now being developed in Japan. Petroleum is found on the island of Honshu, and Chosen yields copper, gold, and silver.

The Japanese are very skillful in the art of lacquering. From the sap of a kind of sumac tree they make lac, which is a varnish. 

They inlay woods in beautiful patterns, and then apply the lac, which when dried is given a high polish. As in India and China, many useful objects are made from bamboo. 

Bamboo is light, strong, and hollow, and the 

Japanese use it in 'making mats, hats, sails, house frames, poles, and water pipes, and paper, and furniture. They also use it for they use the young bamboo shoots for food.

Kyoto, the art center of Japan. waters around Japan moderate the climate and provide work for the people. Here are harbors and boats and shallow waters. In the shallow waters there are many fish, and, as you have learned, fish are a large item in the food of the people. The fishing is best in the northern waters, which are kept cool by an ocean current from the Arctic Ocean. 

Mackerel, cod, and herring are common there, as they are in the waters off the British Isles. It is probable that more than a million people are in the fishing industry, and they use hundreds of thousands of boats, big and little (351 A). 

Manufactures and Trade. - You know that most of the Japanese are farmers as most of the Chinese are, but manufacturing is being carried on in Japan much more than in China. Small articles of rare beauty are made in the workshops of the people (A), and the artist who can do fine wood, stone, or ivory carving does not need to work in a mill or factory.

Large factories are being built, however, to take over the manufacture of silk and cotton fabrics, paper, and to some extent chinaware. The Japanese also make many toys, lanterns, fans, and a great variety of small articles for trade with the Western world. Iron and steel mills and shipbuilding yards have been established, and give employment to many workers.

Most of the raw cotton for the mills making cloth and cotton yarn is imported, and the finished goods are exported. In this way Japan sells the labor of her people, both the labor in the factories and the labor of all those who handle the raw materials or finished goods on any one of the transportation lines.

The raw material needed in the silk industry, the paper industry, and in the iron and steel industries, comes in part from Japanese fields, and forests, and mines. 

Japanese ports are now open to the trade of all the trading nations of the world, and much of this trade is carried by the ships of the Japanese merchant marine. Yokohama, which is almost as large as Pittsburgh or San Francisco, is the port of Tokyo, the capital; and to this port go most of the goods and passengers from the United States. 

This trade is handled by large ocean-going ships, most of which are too large to be able to get up the bay to Tokyo. Where in the interior of Great Britain, France, and China are there large cities whose trade is largely carried on through near-by, but better-located, ports? Tokyo (341 A), with a population of about 5,000,000, is a modern city with fine public buildings, many lovely gardens, and thousands of simple, modest, but clean and pleasant homes. Yokohama (349 A) has a fine harbor with docks, piers, and all the equipment of a good port. In 

1923, most of Yokohama and a large part of Tokyo were destroyed by a great earthquake.

Yokohama, Japan. This is one of the most modern of the cities of Japan, as it has been largely rebuilt since the great earthquake of 1923 when much of the old city was destroyed.
