Tokyo has large suburbs, which if included in the city would more than double its population. 

Osaka, another very large city of Japan, is on a fine harbor and handles much trade. 

You might call it the "Pittsburgh of Japan," because of its large iron and steel plants or you might call it the "Manchester of

Japan," because it has so many cotton mills. 

Kobe has a deeper harbor and is a center for much foreign trade, especially that with 

China and India. Nagasaki, on the west coast of Kyushu, is a shipbuilding center and is an important refueling station for all ships using these waters. 

Trade with Russia through its port of

Vladivostok is carried on by ships using the Japanese port of Niigata, on the west coast of the island of Honshu. Two other important cities, both of which are ports with a growing trade, are Fusan in Chosen and Tamsui in Taiwan.

Much trade is carried on with Chosen, with Manchuria, and with China, in spite of the fact that Japan and China do not get on well with each other. Japanese freight and passenger steamers may be seen on all great trade routes and in most of the world's ports. This is a great change from the time when, until about seventy-five years ago, the Japanese people shut themselves in and locked the door upon the rest of the world.

Japan has a well-developed railroad system. 

There is a network of lines reaching all important points in the larger islands and in Chosen. One line runs the length of 

Taiwan, and the Japanese are much interested in the railroads of Manchuria. 

The Japanese have been active in aviation. 

There are airports in or near the chief cities, and regular airplane service between them. 

Airplanes are in use, also, between Japan proper and the territories on the mainland in which Japan is interested. 

Chosen. The peninsula of Chosen, west of the Sea of Japan, and south of Manchuria, has a length of about 600 miles. Most of its surface is mountainous, with a main

Most of the native people, called Koreans, are engaged in farming (A), which has been greatly improved since Japan gained control of the country. The leading crops are rice, barley, wheat, and beans. Two crops a year are grown on good lands. Some cotton is raised. Among the fruits of the country are apples, pears, persimmons, and some oranges.

The fishing industry is being developed as a part of the food supply of the people. 

There are rich, but largely undeveloped, deposits of coal, iron, copper, and silver which should prove of immense importance in the future. A very fine grade of crystal is also found.

Since Japan gained control of Chosen, roads and railroads have been improved and extended, and airplanes are in use. Trade, especially with Japan, is increasing, and much of it moves through the port of Fusan. 

Keijo is the capital.

Japan Proper and the British Isles Compared. -In some ways the Japan Islands and the British Isles are much alike; in other ways very different. Each group rises from the continental shelf of the near-by continent. Japan proper is somewhat larger than the British Isles and has a somewhat larger population. But the difference in each case is not so very great. Both Great 

Britain and Japan have become great manufacturing and trading countries. In their race for world trade, the British people have three advantages: (1) an earlier start, (2) a great colonial empire, and (3) established markets. 

Japan has cheap, abundant, and easily trained labor, a sense of the artistic and beautiful, and a tireless energy.

Both countries must import raw materials, but Great Britain gets many of hers from various parts of her own empire. Japan seeks to extend its empire, so that it also may be placed in the same favorable position. 

There are mountains and lowlands in both regions, but in Japan the mountains are higher and much more extensive than those in the British Isles. Both island groups are in the North Temperate Zone, yet northern Japan has much colder winters than the British Isles have in any of their parts. This is because the British Isles are in the region of the westerly winds which come over the ocean and give them an oceanic climate. In Japan the winter winds are from the cold, frozen, barren lands of Asia, and the temperature contrasts between summer and winter are greater.

Both countries have the sea all around them. Both are lands that long ago sank to a lower level and therefore have many bays and inlets. Long before men lived upon the islands, the British Isles had many volcanoes and were disturbed by earthquakes. 

Japan has volcanoes and earthquakes now. 

Great Britain has more pastures and more live stock, and imports meat and dairy products for its people, and wheat for white bread. 

In Japan most of the people live largely upon rice and vegetables. In both Great Britain and Japan proper, fish is an important food

ASIA AS A WHOLE 

To most of us Asia is a story-book continent. It is the home of strange peoples whose ways of living are very different from those in our own country. It is a land of vast highlands and high mountains. Within its borders are the highest mountain ranges and the highest mountain peak in the world. 

On its frozen northern plains, in its vast and lonely forests, on its steppes, its high plateaus, and its arid wastes small populations, mostly nomads, find a poor living. In contrast, some of its river valleys and lowland plains support a population of great density (A). 

Here you find lands that have been cultivated for thousands of years, and during much of that time they have been forced to yield two or more crops a year. Yet so carefully have these lands been tended that they are probably more fertile today than they were ages ago. 

Asia is a land of ancient civilizations whose days of glory and power belong to a great past. Yet off its eastern shores is an island group whose people today take high rank among the progressive nations of modern times. times. In southwestern Asia we find the records of several great civilizations. Although most of them long ago perished from the earth, we have learned and are still learning about them. The ruins of their temples, palaces, and great cities have been located, and many have been uncovered. Enough has been found to show that there were great artists and builders among all these ancient peoples. 

Out of Asia came the great religions of the world, and there the greatest of religious leaders lived and taught. It was in Asia that Jesus was born, and there he lived and taught his disciples. From the little area where his life was spent, Christianity has spread through a large part of the world.

ASIA AS A WHOLE 

353 Both in ancient and in modern times there have been some men in Asia who have enjoyed great wealth and have surrounded themselves with magnificence and luxury.

Most of those who were able to live such lives have belonged to the ruling class. They have been able to command the work of the people. The great majority of the people of 

Asia have for centuries lived in poverty and ignorance. They are so poor that famine is never far away. The failure of a single crop in the Ganges Valley, or in most parts of China, means that many must go hungry, and that hundreds will starve to death.

There are parts of Asia where vast deposits of coal and iron, large reserves of petroleum, and various other minerals are known to exist. 

It is upon such resources, little used by the ancient peoples, that the modern industries of the Western world have been built up. 

In the Western world, along with the mining, smelting, and working of metals, have gone the invention and use of machinery for great mills and factories, and the development of new means of transportation. - -

Additional Reading. Any encyclopedia will give you much additional information on points connected with Asia. The general article on that continent will tell you about its physical features, its climate, its peoples, its history, and its products. 

If you want to know more about special countries, cities, rivers, animals, or products, turn to the article on whatever topic you wish to investigate. 

You may, for instance, want to learn about the great religions that have arisen in Asia. In that case turn to the articles on Brahmanism, Buddhism, Christianity, and Mohammedanism. 

Carpenter's Asia (American Book Company) will take you on sight-seeing tours all over the continent. Huntington's Asia (Rand McNally & Co.) is full of interesting accounts of the peoples. interesting. Chamberlain's Asia (The Macmillan Co.) is another good account of the entire continent. Allen's Asia (Ginn & Co.) also covers the entire continent, with excellent accounts of the work carried on in the different countries. 

There are many travel books about different parts of Asia. Among those that you might especially enjoy are Franck's China and The Japanese Empire in the Travels in Many Lands series (Owen Publishing Co.), Johnston's China and

Finnemore's Japan in the Peeps at Many Lands series (The Macmillan Co.), and Tietjens's Japan, 

Korea, and Formosa in the Burton Holmes Travel

Stories (Wheeler Publishing Co.). 

Many books tell about child life among the peoples of Asia. Among these are Roy's When I 

Was a Boy in India (Lothrop, Lee and Shepard 

Co.), Price's The Middle Country, a Chinese Lad's

Adventures in His Own Land (World Book Co.), and Mirza's When I Was a Boy in Persia (Lothrop, Lee and Shepard Co.).

In connection with India, there are Mukerji's many splendid stories, such as Ghond, the Hunter; 

Kari, the Elephant; and Hari, the Jungle Lad (E. P. Dutton and Co.). And no one who reads 

Kipling's books will ever forget such wonder stories as his The Jungle Book (in two series); 

Kim; and Plain Tales from the Hills (Doubleday,

Doran and Co.) all dealing with scenes and incidents in India. Among Kipling's short tales that you will enjoy are "Moti Guj― Mutineer," the story of an elephant, and "Wee Willie Winkie,” the story of the colonel's son at an army post.

AUSTRALIA AND NEIGHBORING ISLANDS 

You have just studied Asia, the largest | Equator; but Australia lies between 10° continent, made up of many countries and and 43° south latitude. It is entirely south inhabited by various races. Far to the of the Equator, in the Torrid Zone and the southeast of Asia, separated from it by the South Temperate Zone. To this southern 

East Indies and by 2000 miles of sea, lies the location the continent owes its name, for smallest continent, Australia. All the land "Australia" means Southern Land. of Australia is one country, inhabited largely by one race, the white race. 

If you look at Australia on a globe, you will find that it is set off by itself, with no near neighbors except the East Indies on the north and New Zealand, about 1200 miles away, on the southeast. It is surrounded by the Pacific and Indian oceans.

AUSTRALIA 

Australia's isolation will be still more clear to you if you remember that it is 4500 miles from Africa and 9500 miles from South America. Every other inhabited continent is crossed either by the Arctic Circle or by the 

Early Settlers. - Captain James Cook, a noted English explorer, landed on the southeastern coast of this lonely continent in 1770, while on a trip around the world. He claimed the eastern coast for Great Britain. 

Eighteen years later the British made their first settlement, which later grew into Sydney. Men who had been put in British jails because they did not pay their debts, or for other reasons, were sent to this distant continent as a punishment. Soon other settlers founded colonies on the eastern and southeastern coasts. These parts of Australia have a mild climate attractive to white people of the Temperate Zone. 357

THE COMMONWEALTH OF AUSTRALIA

Some of them are still wild, untamed savages, but each year their number becomes less. 

The discovery of gold on the eastern coast in 1851 brought many more white settlers to the continent. It is interesting to know that although much gold was found and gold mines are still being worked, the majority of the gold seekers finally turned to farming and stock raising as surer ways of making a living. 

The Commonwealth. In 1901 the colonies which the settlers had founded united to form the Commonwealth of Australia. The several colonies became states under a federal government. Like Canada, Australia governs itself, although it is a member of the 

British Commonwealth of Nations, as you have already learned (page 83).

There are now six states and three territories. Look at the map on the opposite page. On the mainland you will find the states of Queensland, New South Wales, Victoria, South Australia, and Western Australia.

To the south of the mainland, separated from it by Bass Strait, lies the island state of Tasmania. Two of the territories, Federal Capital Territory and Northern Territory, are on the mainland; the third, Territory of Papua, is situated on the island of New Guinea to the north.

The Australian parliament meets at the national capital, Canberra, in Federal Capital Territory, as our Congress meets at Washington, and makes the laws under which the country is governed. 

Population. Nearly all the Australians are of British descent. The total population of the country is now nearly 7,000,000, or less than that of the city of London. There 

Size. Australia is nearly 2000 miles across from east to west, and it averages more than 1000 miles in width from north to south. Its total area, including Tasmania and Papua, is over 3,000,000 square miles.

It is about the size of the mainland of the United States, and nearly as large as Europe. 

You see that although Australia is the smallest continent, it is nevertheless a vast country.

Follow the coastline of Australia on the map on page 358 and notice how regular it is, and how little broken by bays. There are few natural harbors. Thirty miles or more off the northeast coast, a coral formation called the Great Barrier Reef extends about 1000 miles from northwest to southeast.

Surface. Australia is made up of a central plain bordered by mountains on the east, north, and west. Turn to the map on page 

358. It shows that on the east the broad plain slopes upward into a range of mountains called the Great Dividing Range.

None of the mountains are very high. The highest parts are toward the south, where the range is sometimes called the Australian Alps. Here there are a few peaks, all of which are less than 7400 feet high. The mountains of the northern and western borders of the continent are lower. In the south-central section, the land slopes toward the Great Australian Bight and there are no mountains. How much of the map is colored green? Yellow? What does each color mean?

Rivers. The longest rivers, the Murray and its chief tributary the Darling, flow westward and southwestward from the

Great Dividing Range to the ocean on the south. The Murray-Darling is the only important river system in Australia. Other smaller rivers flow from the mountains to the sea on the east, north, and west coasts. 

The central plain has no rivers, as the small streams in the interior dry up or enter lakes B.-

Climate. Study the wind and rainfall maps on this page. You will see that the winds bring a great deal of rain to the eastern parts of Australia. They rise in crossing the slopes of the Great Dividing Range and are cooled as they rise. In the Australian summer, the equatorial calms move southward over northern Australia, and as in other continents rain falls in this zone of calms. 

During this period northern and northeastern Australia have an average rainfall of over 40 inches (A). In the Australian winter, when the equatorial calm belt and the wind belts move northward, southwestern Australia gets some moisture from the prevailing westerlies of the Southern Hemisphere (B).

In the summer, the westerly winds are too far south to touch the mainland, although they bring some rain to the island of Tasmania at that time.

The interior and the south-central coast are dry, and much of the land is a desert. 

Much of the interior has as little as 5 inches of rainfall a year. Parts of the eastern and northern coasts have more than 50 inches.

A. Distribution of population in Australia. 

The climate of much of Australia is continental, hot in summer and cold in winter. 

Remember that Australia has its winter during our summer, and its summer during our winter. Explain why this is so. June, July, and August are the coldest months. 

January and February are the warmest. It It is never very cold on the continent, although in the south there are frosts, and the temperature is at times as low as 30°. Snow falls only in the mountainous regions. The north is much warmer, for it lies in the Tropics. 

Distribution of People. Since the east ern coast of Australia has plenty of rain, you will find that section of the country most densely populated. It is a region of forests and cleared lands where the people can grow crops, raise live stock, and engage in lumbering. By using the rivers, they can get their products to market. 

The population map (A) shows a large number of people on the eastern and south-❘ eastern slopes of the Great Dividing Range, in Queensland, New South Wales, and Victoria. Most of the large cities are found there. Few people live in the northeast because that part of the country is very hot. 

In most of the interior of the country there is little or no population because the rainfall is too scanty for agriculture or even for stock raising (maps, pages 364, 367). The southwest coast has a small population, but the number of people is increasing. As you have learned, this part of the continent gets some moisture from the prevailing westerlies, enough for farming and ranching. 

Cities. Sydney, the capital of New South 

Wales, is the oldest and largest city, with more than 1,200,000 inhabitants (357 A). It is the eastern terminal of the Trans-Australia 

Railroad, the only important railroad system. 

Perth is the western terminal. Because

Sydney is a seaport, much foreign commerce passes through it. Melbourne, the capital of Victoria, is the second city in size, with about 1,000,000 inhabitants. Adelaide and

Brisbane are other important centers of population. Hobart is the chief city in Tasmania. Of what states are these cities the capitals? Locate them on a map. Which are seaports? In a straight line how far is it from Sydney to Perth? From Melbourne to Hobart? 

Plant Life. The plants of Australia differ greatly from those of other continents.

Among the most curious of the trees are the bottle tree and the eucalyptus. The bottle tree, as the name implies, is shaped like a huge bottle with branches growing out of the top. The eucalyptus is tall, rising from two to four hundred feet in the air. It has leaves more gray than green. Instead of shedding its leaves, it sheds its bark every year. The wood is hard and durable, and is used for shipbuilding, paving blocks, railroad ties, and telegraph poles. The leaves are pressed for the eucalyptus oil used in medicines.

In the tropical north there are palms and bamboos, as well as ferns and grasses that grow to the size of trees. On the northeast coast bananas, oranges, pineapples, and sugar cane are grown. In the southeastern and the

A. Kangaroos. Notice the short front legs and the well-developed hind legs and tail. southwestern parts of the continent and in Tasmania, there are many vineyards and orchards. Seeds for the cultivated crops and the fruit trees were brought to Australia by the settlers. 

as Animals. The native animals are peculiar as the native plants. The kangaroo (A) is one of the most curious. Some of the kangaroos are as small as large cats; others are as tall as men. The front legs are short and weak, but the hind legs and tail are long and strong. Instead of running when chased, kangaroos leap over the ground, standing nearly upright and using the tail as well as the hind legs in jumping. 

A mother kangaroo carries her young in a pouch or fold of the skin on the under side of her body. Such animals are called marsupials. A marsupial found in the United 

States is the opossum. 

The platypus (B), an animal the size of a large rabbit, has webbed feet like a duck, fur like a seal, and a broad beak like a duck's bill. It is at home both on the land and in B.

A platypus. Notice the dark fur, webbed foot, and broad bill. the water. It hatches its young from eggs and, like the kangaroo, carries them in a pouch.

Emus, which resemble ostriches, and lyre birds are native to Australia. In the hot north, gayly colored parrots and other tropical birds are numerous. Many kinds of song birds are found along the eastern coast, and in the interior hawks and eagles fly over the desert. The common domestic animals have been introduced from other countries, and in the interior camels are used on the deserts.

The Pacific Slope. The Pacific Slope is the plain extending along the eastern coast, sloping east from the Great Dividing Range to the Pacific Ocean. Find it on the map on page 358, and notice how it curves eastward into the ocean. The Pacific Slope is long from north to south, but it is only from 70 to 

200 miles wide.

The rainfall on the Pacific Slope is plentiful and the soil is fertile. In Victoria, New 

South Wales, and the temperate part of Queensland are regions of small farms produc-

In the background are large straw ricks. ing mixed crops, of wheat farms, and of dairying. On the small farms corn, oats, and other grains, alfalfa, vegetables, and fruits are grown. Some of the fruits are exported, but most of the farm and orchard products are consumed in the near-by cities. 

Tasmania has a climate much like that of the temperate region of the Pacific Slope. 

The island is noted for its orchards, and it exports thousands of barrels of fine apples yearly. It also has farms and sheep ranches. 

Growing Wheat in Australia. The wheat farms are as large as those in the western part of our country, and, like them, use the most modern farm machinery. More than half of the cultivated land in Australia is planted to wheat. But, as the map on this page shows, the greater part of the wheat crop is grown in the southeastern part of the country. There is, however, a wheat-producing area in southwestern Australia also. The | best wheat land, as you have learned, is one which is temperate in climate, with a wet growing season and a dry time for harvesting.

ern Australia, is the Central Plain. This is a region of light or little rainfall, and the interior is a desert. The outer regions which slope up to the mountains, however, have a rainfall of from 10 to 30 inches yearly. 

Here are wheat farms and large areas covered with grass and shrubs which furnish pastures for beef cattle and sheep. These regions are called the grasslands or "the bush." Some of the wheat is ground into flour in mills in the cities, but much is exported, especially to Great Britain (363 A). Australia is one of the largest wheat-exporting countries in the world. In recent years only Canada and Argentina have exported more wheat than Australia, and in some years Argentina has exported less than Australia. 

Dairying. There are many dairy farms in New South Wales and Victoria. With the help of the government, dairying has made great progress in recent years. Butter, cheese, and dried or condensed milk have now come to be important exports. 

Other Products of Eastern Australia.- 

In the tropical northern part of the Pacific Slope, sugar cane, some cotton, tobacco, bananas, oranges, and pineapples are grown for the home markets. On the higher slopes of the range, lumbering is carried on. Most of the forests are of hardwoods, especially eucalyptus. Some of the timber is exported, although Australia has so few evergreen forests that pine and other soft woods for building purposes must be imported.

Australia leads the world in wool exports, furnishing more than one third of the world total. Although the sheep are raised for both meat and wool, and mutton is shipped abroad, wool is the most valuable single product of the continent. The greater part of the wool goes to Great Britain, where it is made into cloth of fine quality (page 91).

Much Australian wool, however, goes to 

France, Germany, the United States, and other wool-manufacturing countries. 

Sheep Stations. Sheep ranches, called sheep stations in Australia, are very large. 

Some of them have an area of over one hundred square miles. This is because in regions of poor pasture it takes several acres of land to keep one sheep for a year. However, this land is not costly to buy. Many of the station owners got their lands in the first place as gifts from the government; or they bought the ground for a small price per acre. 

Each of the great sheep stations employs many men. The buildings are usually many miles from any settlement where supplies can be purchased or work done. As a result, you will usually find at each station some one who knows how to do whatever needs to be done to carry on the work without help from the outside. You will find homes for the men, a store, a carpenter shop, a blacksmith shop, and other buildings, as well as an office where the business of the ranch is looked after.

When Australia was first settled, sheep were allowed to graze over the open range, but later the ranches were fenced in to keep out the dingoes, or wild dogs, which killed the sheep. Now, if you travel through Australia, you see thousands of miles of wire fences.

There is another reason for the fences. 

Rabbits, brought into the country as pets,

AUSTRALIA 

escaped and so increased in number that they began to destroy the pastures and caused great damage. They not only ate the grass of the pastures, but they destroyed the young trees by eating their bark. The government is trying to get rid of them, and offers a sum of money for each animal killed. Many thousands have been killed, but thousands still infest the grazing lands, as they have no natural enemies among the animals of Australia. 

Wire fences are now sunk deep in the ground, so that the rabbits cannot burrow under them. As the fence net is so small that the rabbits cannot get through, it is usually possible to keep them out of regions that have been cleared.

The most valuable and most common of the different breeds of sheep is the merino, brought to Australia from Spain. The merino is small, but its wool is fine and heavy. 

The event of the year on a sheep station is shearing time. Shearing gangs travel from station to station, and clip the wool with mechanical clippers, run by electricity, steam, or compressed air. The stations have large sheds built especially for shearing (365 A).

Here the shearers work steadily for many hours each day until all of the sheep have been shorn. 

Wool Shipping. The wool from each sheep is separated into different parts, because of differences in its length or fineness. 

It is sorted and baled, usually in 400-pound sacks. It is then ready for its long trip to market. Since the sheep stations are far from the railroads and steamships, it is difficult to transport the wool to shipping centers. Some ranchers, who live near good roads, use motor trucks. The majority, however, use wagons drawn by horses or oxen. Near the desert, camel caravans are sometimes employed. In the chief markets, Sydney, Melbourne, Adelaide, and Brisbane, wool is sold to buyers from many parts of the world, and shipped over the various ocean routes. 

Ocean Routes. -The most important ocean route to Europe from Australia is by way of Aden and the Suez Canal. Some of the ships on this route stop at Batavia, Singapore, and Colombo on the way. Another route is through the Panama Canal. Wool for the United States is usually shipped to 

San Francisco, or through the Panama Canal to the eastern seaports. Other sea routes pass around the Cape of Good Hope and 

Cape Horn. Trace all these routes on a globe, so that you will have a clear picture of them in mind.

Beef Cattle. Second in importance to sheep raising in Australia, is cattle raising. 

Both beef cattle and dairy cattle are raised. 

Much frozen or chilled beef, hides, and leather are exported, as well as the dairy products that you read about on page 364. Most of these exports go to Great Britain, which in return sends manufactured articles. 

Compare the cattle map (B) with the sheep map (364 A). You will find many cattle ranches, as well as sheep stations, in the grasslands of the Central Plain. But most of the cattle ranches are nearer the bordering slopes of the mountains, where there is more water and better grass. 

Australia pastures over 10,000 000 cattle. 

Most of them are beef animals, the profit coming from the meat and from the hides of the animals. The beef cattle are generally driven to market in herds, grazing as they walk the many miles to the cities. They travel over routes that are supplied with water. When the city to which they are being driven is reached, they are slaughtered. 

The meat is either sold to the home markets or chilled or frozen for export. The hides may be shipped as raw hides or made into leather before they are shipped.

Study the cattle map (B). It gives a very clear picture of the large area over which cattle are now being raised. Notice, however, that, on this map, each dot represents only 2500 head of cattle but that the sheep map on page 364 uses a single dot to represent 20,000 sheep.

AUSTRALIA 

The Western Coast. The Western Coast | territories and the Bismarck Archipelago to extends from the Indian Ocean to the mountains and plateaus which border the Central Plain on the west. It has few inhabitants except in the city of Perth. In the north it is too hot for farming. In the central region the rainfall is too scanty for crops, although there is some pasture on the slopes where cattle and sheep are grazed. 

The principal occupation is ranching, but gold has been found in several places, and there are a number of gold-mining towns. 

Farther south, where the rainfall is moderate and the temperature is mild, there are wheat farms and orchards. Some mixed farming also is carried on. Wool, hides, meat, and wheat are shipped from Fremantle, the seaport suburb of the city of Perth. But the

Western Coast of Australia has not been developed, for there is still much land in the east and southeast on which it is easier to make a living. 

Mines and Minerals. Australia is rich in mineral deposits. Formerly gold was the chief mineral, and in the early days many adventurers went to Australia hoping to make their fortunes. Some gold is still mined in the southwestern and southeastern parts, but coal is now the leading mineral product. It is mined largely on the eastern, southeastern, and southwestern coasts. Some of it is sold abroad, and to steamships which stop for fuel. Copper, lead, silver, zinc, and tin mines also are worked. Tasmania has especially valuable mineral deposits.

Rubies and sapphires are found in the northeast near the Gulf of Carpentaria, and opals are mined in the eastern part of the 

Central Plain. Pearls are taken from the waters of the Indian Ocean on the Western Coast. 

New Guinea. The island of New Guinea lies to the north of Australia. Find it on the map on page 356. The eastern half is divided between the Territory of Papua and the Territory of New Guinea. These two the east are controlled by Australia. The western half of New Guinea is controlled by the Netherlands. 

New Guinea is part of the East Indies, which are generally considered as belonging with Asia, as you have already learned elsewhere. But it lies near Australia and is somewhat like it in plant and animal life. It is a large island, with an area of more than 

300,000 square miles. It has lowlands and highlands, some of the mountains rising more than 15,000 feet above sea level. 

In the lowlands of Papua rubber and coconut plantations are being developed by the labor of natives who are being taught by white men. There are very few white men on the island, however, for the rainfall is heavy and the climate is tropical. The chief settlement is Port Moresby, where ships call to bring in supplies and to take on cargoes of rubber and copra, which, as you know, is the dried meat of coconuts. 

Australia as a Whole. In your study of 

Australia you have learned certain facts which you will want to remember. Check them, so that you will keep them in mind.

Australia is the smallest continent. It is far from other continents, and lies entirely south of the Equator in the Torrid and South Temperate Zones. It is all one country and inhabited largely by the white race. It is self-governing, and part of the British 

Commonwealth of Nations.

Most of the people in Australia live in the eastern and southeastern parts of the continent, where rain is plentiful and the climate is mild. The interior is largely uninhabited. 

A great part of it is desert. On the grasslands millions of sheep and cattle graze. 

Grazing and agriculture are the main occupations. Wool, mutton, beef, hides, leather, wheat, butter, cheese, dried or condensed milk, and fruit are the chief exports. 

Australia imports most of its manufactured articles because it is a new country and its

NEW ZEALAND 

New Zealand lies about 1200 miles to the southeast of Australia. Like Australia, it is part of the British Commonwealth of Nations (page 83), and self-governing. Find New

Zealand on a globe. Notice that it is half way round the world from the mother country, England.

New Zealand consists of two large islands, separated by Cook Strait, and many small islands. It is about the size of Colorado, more than 100,000 square miles in area.

The New Zealanders are very progressive, and have passed many laws that make the country a pleasant place for people who must work. Old-age insurance protects the worker when he becomes old. Sickness funds take care of him when he is unable to work. The law fixes the number of hours a day or a week he works. It also sets up the wages he must get for his labor. 

Surface and Climate. Mountain ranges form the backbone of both North and South 

Islands. Turn to the map on page 358, and see how much of the islands is over 2000 feet above sea level. The highest peak is Mt. 

Cook, named for the explorer James Cook. 

How high is it?

In the mountains the scenery is magnificent. Some of the peaks are at all times covered with snow. In the higher ranges, there are great glaciers. There are many picturesque waterfalls, active volcanoes, geysers, and other hot springs. In the moun- tains are also fertile valleys and plateaus, where crops are raised. where crops are raised. Most of the rivers. are short mountain torrents. Bordering the coast are many fertile lowland plains..

The climate is mild, except in the high mountains. There are no great extremes of heat or cold. The rainfall is heaviest on the western side, because the prevailing winds are westerlies. On the eastern side the rainfall is sometimes so light that irrigation is necessary for farming. 

Animals. New Zealand has animals as odd as those of Australia. There are various kinds of marsupials, black swans, and gaylycolored birds. The native kea parrot has caused much damage to the sheep herders. 

It alights on the backs of sheep and kills them with its sharp beak, to eat the fat surrounding the kidneys. Rabbits destroy pastures, as they do in Australia. In the mountains red and fallow deer and wapiti supply game for sportsmen.

ISLANDS OF THE PACIFIC 

Thousands of islands are scattered over the Pacific Ocean, but only the larger groups are important. Turn to the map on page 

356, where you will see these larger groups. 

The smaller ones are not shown. You learned about the East Indies when you studied Asia and New Guinea when you studied Australia (page 368). 

The Larger Islands. East of New of New Guinea is the Bismarck Archipelago, belonging to the Commonwealth of Australia. Southeast of these are the Solomon 

Islands under British control. Also under 

British control are Santa Cruz, the Fiji

Islands, Tonga Islands, and Cook Islands. 

The New Hebrides are governed jointly by Great Britain and France. New Cale- 

Zealand and the United States. All these islands are south of the Equator. Find them on the map. They are the most important of the many you see there.

Formation. Some of the Pacific Islands are the tops of volcanic mountains. Most of the volcanoes are dead, but a few are still active. These high islands are mountainous, and therefore usually have a heavy rainfall. 

They are often covered with dense forests. 

Other islands are coral formations, and are rather flat, or low. The scenery on some of them, especially Tahiti, is beautiful, and many artists have visited them. 

Their Importance. Coconut, banana, and breadfruit trees grow in abundance on most of the islands. Food is so plentiful, and the climate is so warm that life is easy. The natives are therefore not very industrious, but they are certainly a very happy people. 

Copra is the chief export. But the principal value of the islands is their use as coaling stations and harbors for the ships that must pass their way.

The Food Grains. Among the food grains of the world the most important are wheat, rice, and corn. Wheat is the grain most commonly used by the people of the "West," and rice is the chief cereal of the "East." Corn, although used in various ways by man as a cereal food, is used principally in fattening meat animals. It provides a food for man, therefore, chiefly in the form of meat. 372

From the New World its cultivation has spread to other continents as shown on the map (B). In our own country, it is the most widely cultivated of all the grains.

Beef cattle are no longer shipped alive in any great numbers from the countries where they are raised to the countries where the meat is to be consumed. Half carcasses or other cuts are sent as fresh meat thousands of miles in refrigerator cars or ships, and arrive at their destinations in perfect condition.

Coal. You will notice from the map below (B) that coal-producing regions are most numerous and extensive in the continents of North America, Europe, and Asia.

Some coal-producing areas are shown, also, in South America, Africa, and Australia, but none of them are large, and their total output is small. The coal mined in those continents is largely for local use. 

More coal is mined in the United States than in any other country. Our chief coalmining states are Pennsylvania (34%, including both bituminous coal and the world's chief supply of anthracite), West Virginia (23%), Illinois (11%), Kentucky (9%), Ohio (4%), Indiana (33%), and Alabama (23%).

In the United States, Pennsylvania (30%), Ohio (24%), (24%), Illinois (10%), Indiana (9%) and Alabama (8%), lead in the production of pig iron.

The countries that lead in the production of steel ingots and castings are the same as those that lead in the production of pig iron, and usually in the same order.

THE EARTH AND THE SOLAR 

Ancient Beliefs. The famous Greek named Ptolemy, when living in Alexandria in Egypt about eighteen hundred years ago, spent much time in studying the movements of heavenly bodies. In spite of all his study, however, he believed that the earth, not the sun, was the center of our solar system. 

He knew five of the other planets of that system and studied their movements. But he thought that they moved around the earth instead of around the sun, as we now know that they do.

Ptolemy was, for his time, a man of great learning. If, with all his study, he could make the mistakes that he did, we need not wonder that many others made the same mistakes. The people of Ptolemy's day knew very little about the earth and its movements, about our solar system, or about the vast size of the universe. They thought that the sun and stars and planets all really

SYSTEM 

moved around the earth each day as they seemed to do. The men of ancient times knew that the moon and the five planets and the sun also seemed to move around more slowly among the stars. They thought that the movements were really what they seemed to be, and so they called all seven of those bodies "planets," or wanderers. 

The stars and planets that shone so brilliantly in the cloudless night skies of 

Egypt and southwestern Asia must have seemed both beautiful and mysterious to shepherds watching their flocks at night and to others who studied the heavens. The men of ancient times thought of the stars as belonging together in groups, and to these groups they gave names. One group in the north, if its stars are connected by straight lines, has the form of a long-handled cup or "dipper," and that group is now commonly known by the name of "the Big Dipper." 381

A. A large telescope in an observatory. It is so mounted that it can easily be kept pointing at any visible star or planet. 

Many star groups in ancient times were thought to have the forms of animals or men. The Big Dipper, for example, with other stars near it, was imagined to have the form of a huge bear the tail of the bear being the handle of the dipper. 

The Telescope. The invention of the telescope (early in the seventeenth century) gave to those who studied the heavens the astronomers a new and very useful tool. With it one can see many parts of the universe that cannot be seen by the naked eye. In the years that have passed since the telescope was invented, many improvements have been made, and larger and more powerful instruments have been built. Each new and improved instrument has made it possible to see farther and farther into space and to add new stars to those that had been seen before. No one believes that with the most powerful instruments yet made we can see to the outer limits of our universe. No one knows whether such outer limits exist. 

In 1934 a mass of molten glass was poured into a mold. With infinite care, the glass was cooled, ground, and polished into a giant reflecting mirror. This mirror, with a diameter of 200 inches, is larger than any other astronomical mirror that has ever been made. When the telescope in which it will be used is completed on Mt. Palomar, California, astronomers will be able to look twice as far into space as they have ever looked before.

Nearly all of the stars of the universe seem to be fixed in their position in relation to each other. It is believed that around some of these fixed stars, which are like the sun in our own solar system, planets like our earth may be swinging in great orbits. Each of these fixed stars shines by its own light, as our sun does. The planets that swing around them, if there are such, could be seen only by the light from their central sun; and that light -star light to us is so faint at our great distance that no such planets have yet been seen. 

The Solar System. Our own solar system is the only one about which we have learned much. The sun is at its center, and around the sun nine large planets swing in their orbits, at various distances and at different rates of speed. Named in order of their distances from the sun, and beginning with the nearest one, these nine large planets are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune, and Pluto. There are also hundreds of small planets called asteroids revolving around the sun in orbits which lie between those of Mars and Jupiter. 

The planets are of greatly different sizes. 

The asteroids are tiny planets, all too small to be seen by the naked eye; the largest of them has a diameter of less than 500 miles.

Mercury, Venus, and Mars are smaller than the earth, and Pluto is only a little larger. 

But the other four planets are much larger. 

Jupiter, the largest of the planets, has a diameter more than ten times as great as that of our earth, and Saturn's diameter is over nine times as great as the earth's. 

The average distance of Mercury from the sun is about 36,000,000 miles, and that of Pluto is about 3,700,000,000 miles. Compare these distances with the earth's average distance of 93,000,000 miles. You will find it difficult to give any real meaning to distances as great as these. The only dis- The only distances that we can really understand are those that we can measure by our own experiences. But great as these solar system distances are, they are very small as compared with other distances in the universe. 

Astronomers measure the distances of the stars by light years. A light year is the distance that light will travel in a year. 

As light travels about 186,000 miles in a second of time the distance it would travel in a year would be about 5,900,000,000,000 miles. There are star clusters, well known to astronomers, that are at least 900,000 light years away from our earth.

What are some of the important facts that have been learned as a result of the long study of our solar system by many astrono- ― - mers since the time of Ptolemy? Ptolemy knew but five of the large planets besides the earth those that can be seen with the naked eye. With the telescope we have learned of three more - Uranus, Neptune, and Pluto, although the most distant one, Pluto, was not discovered until 1930. With the telescope, too, it was found that some of the planets in our solar system have other bodies revolving about them as the moon revolves around our earth. We now know that the earth rotates on its axis once in twenty-four hours; that the sun is the center of the solar system; and that all the planets, including the earth, revolve about it. We know also, very accurately, the time taken for each planet to travel once around the sun, the full length of its orbit. For most of the planets we know also the length of time in hours or days that it takes for each one to rotate on its axis. 

Mercury and Venus. In the case of 

Mercury, the rotation and revolution of that planet take the same length of time 88 days. This means that the same part of the planet is always turned toward the sun. 

On that side the temperature is said to be hot enough at all times to melt lead. The other side is always turned away from the sun, and although the temperature is not known, it is probably always very cold.

Part of the crescent moon as seen through a large telescope. Notice the rough surface, which can be seen clearly because the moon has no atmosphere. Day and night at most places on the moon are each about 250 hours long; and the temperature varies from over 210° at midday to about 250° below zero during part of the long night. 

Venus is one of the planets whose period of rotation is not known. Astronomers guess it to be several times the 24 hours that it takes the earth to rotate on its axis. The reason why the period of rotation for Venus is unknown and why no part of its surface has been studied is because it is hidden by fogs at all times. A study of this atmosphere shows that there is much carbon dioxide present, and but little oxygen. Growing plants make use of carbon dioxide and give off oxygen, and scientists, therefore, have wondered if there may not be both plants and animals living on the surface of Venus. 

The Moon. The third planet in distance from the sun is our earth, and about this planet we naturally know a great deal more than about the others. We know also more about our moon than about other heavenly bodies, because it is so near that we can see it clearly. The moon has a diameter somewhat more than one fourth as great as that of the earth. It has no atmosphere, and its surface can be photographed and studied because it is not hidden by clouds. Its period of rotation and its period of revolution are the same, as is the case with Mercury.

The result is that from the earth we are always looking at the same side of the moon. 

We see the moon, as we see the planets, only by reflected light-the light received from the sun.

When people think of the moon they usually have in mind its glowing loveliness in the sky and the changes through which it seems to pass from new moon, when the part toward us is unlighted, to the time about a month later when it is again new moon. 

During this time the amount that is lighted changes from night to night. At first it is a small crescent, which grows wider and wider until the full moon can be seen. After that

The next four large planets are giants in comparison with the others. 

They are Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. Each of these planets has a dense atmosphere, and because of this fact but little is known about the surface of any of them. 

Two facts in which you will be interested are connected with the moon. One of these facts is that in A.D. 325 it was agreed to fix Easter on the first Sunday following the full moon (Paschal Moon) after 

March 21. In early Christian time the moonlight was of great advantage to the pilgrims who traveled at night to attend the Easter festivals. The other fact is that it was largely from the study of the moon that Sir Isaac Newton, the great

English mathematician and astronomer, gained facts that helped him to learn about gravitation the pull that each body in space has for each other body. Before this discovery astronomers wondered why the planets did not fly off into space. Newton explained, for example, that the earth and the moon attract each other and that this pull is just strong enough to keep the moon in its orbit around the earth instead of either moving off into space or falling down upon the earth. Other heavenly bodies attract each other also — more and more strongly the nearer they are to each other. The position of each planet, at any moment, is due in part to the speed of its own motion and in part to the result of all the attractive forces at work upon it. As you have already learned, it is the pull of the moon upon the waters of the earth, as compared with its pull upon the solid earth, that is the chief cause of the tides. 

Jupiter and Saturn each have several moons, moons, or satellites, swinging in orbits around them; and Saturn also has rings which, it is believed, are made up of vast numbers of very tiny satellites or small fragments. It is because the orbits of these tiny bodies are all in about the same plane that they give the appearance of rings.

Looked at edgewise a ring cannot be seen with even the most powerful telescopes. 

It can be seen only when, in Saturn's revolution around the sun, it is turned at an angle to observers on the earth. The rings are usually seen at an angle because the orbits of all Saturn's satellites are tilted at an angle to the plane of Saturn's orbit around the sun.

The Outer Planets. The first planet whose orbit lies outside that of the earth is Mars. This is another planet that may possibly be inhabited by some kinds of life like those on the earth. Mars has an atmosphere. Its day is only a few minutes 

All five of the outer planets are far enough from the sun so that they receive very little heat. 

Finding Direction. You know the meaning of the terms of direction in most common use, such as north, south, east, and west. 

You know also that northeast is halfway between north and east, and southeast is halfway between south and east. What do northwest and southwest mean? Other directions shown on the compass card (A) are in more common use at sea than on land.

Meridians and parallels.

This whole system of directions has been worked out in relation to north and south. 

The rotation of the earth on its axis fixes two points on the earth's surface which are at the ends of the axis. These two points are called poles. One of them is the North 

Pole, and the other is the South Pole. Any great circle on the earth's surface passing through these two poles is called a meridian circle. Every part of such a circle is a north and south line. Half of a meridian circle, extending from one pole to the other, is called a meridian. Lines running around the surface of the earth and crossing all meridians at right angles are parallels, and are east and west lines. Meridians and parallels are shown on most globes and maps, so that you can get the direction of one place from another.

Measurements and Locations. The par allel that circles the earth midway between the poles is the Equator. You can easily find it on a globe. 

Distances on the earth are measured north or south from the Equator as a zero line. 

The meridian that passes through Greenwich, a part of

London, England, is used as a zero, or prime, meridian, from which distances are are measured 

Prime Meridian

east and west over the surface of the earth. 

You know that all circles, whether large or small, are divided into 360 equal parts called degrees. Each degree is divided into 60 equal parts called minutes, and each minute is divided into 60 equal parts called seconds. The same system of measurement is used for angles. Thus angles of the same size, at the center of a circle, will be measured by the same number of degrees on the circumference of the circle, no matter how large the circle is (B).

Distances on the earth's surface may be measured in miles or parts of a mile, or they may be measured in degrees or parts of a degree. The distance from the Equator to either pole is 90 degrees (90°), because it is one fourth of a meridian circle of 360°. It is possible to find the distance of any place north or south of the Equator in degrees, minutes, and seconds, and this is called its latitude. The highest possible latitude is 90°.

The position of a place on the earth's surface east or west of the prime meridian can also be measured in degrees, minutes, and seconds, and this is called its longitude. 

The degrees of longitude, however, vary greatly in length on different parts of the earth's surface, because the circles called parallels vary in size. 90° 90° 90° 

B. Angles in circles. 

East longitude and west longitude meet at the meridian of 180°, half way around the earth from the prime or zero meridian. To locate a place on the earth's surface, its latitude is given as north or south of the Equator, and its longitude is given as east or west of the zero or prime meridian.

Measurement of Time. -The rotation of the earth through one full turn gives a length of time called a day. Each day is divided into twenty-four hours, each hour into sixty minutes, and each minute into sixty seconds.

One full revolution of the earth about the sun gives a period of time called a year. Vancouver? 120° yo Seattle Portland and clocks are now used instead of sundials and hourglasses. 

In our country twelve o'clock comes both at noon and at midnight, and so we have all the hours from one to twelve before noon (A.M.) and after noon (P.M.). In some countries, however, watches and clocks are made to show twenty-four hours. In those countries the time we call one o'clock in the afternoon becomes thirteen o'clock, our two o'clock in the afternoon becomes fourteen o'clock, and our midnight becomes twenty-four o'clock. 

Standard Time. Local time varies from place to place, because noon varies from place to place. Because it is often necessary that people in a large area should be able to do things at the same time, the United States has been divided into standard time belts.

Within each of these belts, the same time is used for all places, instead of the local time for each place. The standard time chosen for each belt is the local time of a selected. meridian. Map C shows you the standard time belts of our country. Learn their names.

In passing from one time belt to another when you travel west, you need to set your watch back one hour; but when traveling east, you must set it ahead one hour. o Paradise Through the centuries men have invented ways to measure time. One of the early ways was to use the sundial (A). This instrument is placed so that the sun causes its upright part to cast a shadow on the level surface on which it stands. The position of this shadow is marked for noon and for the hours of sunlight before and after noon. 

One way of measuring units of time, such as an hour, was by using an hourglass (B). In such a glass, sand runs from one half of the glass to the other through a narrow opening. 

Just enough sand is put in the glass to take an hour in flowing from the upper part to the lower. The glass can then be turned over to measure the next hour. Other such glasses have been made to measure longer or shorter periods of time. Watches Huntington

LIGHT AND AND HEAT 

You know that the earth is a great ball, or sphere, that it rotates on an axis, is lighted and heated by the sun, and makes a journey around the sun once every year. You may think of the earth's pathway around the sun, which is called its orbit, as being in a plane, or perfectly level surface; and this plane is usually spoken of as the plane of the earth's orbit. The axis of the earth stands at an angle of 66° to the plane of its orbit. In other words, the axis is inclined 231° away from a line that would be perpendicular to the orbit. As the earth moves from one part of its orbit to another, this angle remains the same. The position of the axis at any moment of time is parallel to any former position. 

How the Earth Is Lighted. Only half of the earth at a time can be lighted by the sun, because the earth is a sphere and only half of it at a time can be turned toward the The half that is turned away from the sun is in darkness. The fact that the earth rotates on its axis means that the half that is lighted and the half that is in darkness are always changing. You can see how this 

You can see how this is by holding up a globe in front of a lamp in a darkened room and spinning the globe on its axis. sun.

If the earth's axis were perpendicular to the plane of its orbit, the circle of illumination, or line separating the lighted half of the earth from the unlighted half, would always pass through the poles. It would divide all parallels into two equal parts, and all places on the earth would have equal lengths of day and night. But with the axis inclined as it is there are only two times during the year when the days and nights are of equal length in all parts of the earth. From the diagram on page 389 find which dates these are. On those dates, also, the sun's rays that strike vertically upon the surface of the earth are on the Equator. 

At all other times during the year the vertical rays of the sun are either north or south of the Equator. When they are north of the Equator some part of the earth's surface around the North Pole, larger or smaller, will be included within the lighted portion of the earth for all twenty-four hours of each day; in other words there will be no night there. At the same time, some part of the land around the South Pole, larger or smaller, will be in the unlighted portion of the earth for all twenty-four hours of each day; in other words the night time there will be continuous. When the vertical rays of the sun are south of the Equator some part of the earth's surface around the South 

Pole will be continuously lighted for a time.

At the same time some part of the surface around the North Pole will be continuously dark. A study of the diagram will show how these changes take place and at what dates the area in darkness is greatest in each of these polar regions.

The North Pole itself will be in light from 

March 21 to September 21, and the South

Pole will be unlighted during that half year. 

The South Pole will be in light from September 21 to March 21, and the North Pole will be unlighted during that same second half year. 

The vertical rays of the sun are farthest north on June 21. At that time all of the area included between the North Pole and the parallel of 66° north latitude - the 

Arctic Circle will be lighted for all twentyfour hours of at least one day. At the same time, all of the area included between the South Pole and the parallel of 661° south latitude - the Antarctic Circle-will be in the unlighted half of the earth for all twentyfour hours of at least one day.

LIGHT AND HEAT 

ZONES AND HEAT BELTS 

Zones. You will find it interesting to compare the two maps on the opposite page. 

For convenience of study they show meridians and parallels as straight lines. The upper one shows the surface of the earth divided into five zones. The names given to these five zones are "heat" or "temperature" names. The boundaries of these five zones, however, are fixed by the way in which the rays of the sun meet the earth's surface at certain times each year. 

The Torrid Zone is bounded on the north by the Tropic of Cancer, which is 2340 north of the Equator. This is the line that marks the northern limit reached by the direct rays of the sun on June 21 each year. The Torrid

Zone is bounded on the south by the Tropic of Capricorn, which is 23° south of the Equator, and marks the southern limit reached by the direct rays of the sun on 

December 21 each year.

The North Frigid Zone is a cap around the North Pole, reaching as far south as the Arctic Circle. The South Frigid Zone is a cap around the South Pole, reaching as far north as the Antarctic Circle. These circles are 

231° from the poles and are fixed in the following ways: when the direct rays of the sun, on June 21, are on the Tropic of Cancer, horizontal rays of the sun touch the earth's surface 231 beyond the North Pole, or at the Arctic Circle. At the same time, other horizontal rays of the sun touch the earth 231° short of the South Pole, or at the Antarctic Circle. Six months later, when the direct rays of the sun are on the Tropic of Capricorn, the sun's rays reach beyond the South 

Pole and fall short of the North Pole 2310, again fixing the position of the Antarctic and 

Arctic circles.

Between the Arctic Circle and the Tropic of Cancer is the North Temperate Zone, and between the Antarctic Circle and the Tropic of Capricorn is the South Temperate Zone. Notice carefully the position of all the zones on a globe. 

When you learn that a country is in one of the five zones, you have learned something about its position on the surface of the earth, and much about the direction of the sun's rays there. You have also learned something but not all all about its climate, especially its temperature. 

Heat Belts. The heat belts, shown on the lower map on the opposite page, are divided in another way. The hot belt is that part of the earth where the average temperature at the earth's surface at sea level is more than 68°. The cold caps are regions where the average annual temperature at sea level is less than 50°. In the temperate belts, therefore, the average annual temperature at sea level is more than 50° and less than 68°. To get sea-level temperature for a place that is above sea level, 1° of temperature is added for each 300 feet of elevation. For example, in the hot-belt part of South America, the northern Andes are included. Of course the actual annual average temperature of the mountains is much less than 68°. But if the average is taken for any point in the mountains and to that temperature 1° is added for each 300 feet of elevation above sea level, the temperature as it would be at sea level is found. 

You will see that each heat belt varies in width although the zones shown in the map above do not. This is chiefly because of the way land temperatures are affected by the prevailing winds blowing across the sea to the land in different parts of the earth. 

You will notice that the hot belt is on both sides of the Equator, but more in the Northern Hemisphere than in the Southern 

Hemisphere. The North Temperate belt is much broader than the South Temperate belt, more irregular in outline, and includes nearly half the land surface of the earth. It is in these temperate belts that the most progressive peoples of the earth live.
